short_description: Excision, nasal polyp(s), extensive Notes: (30115 would normally require the facilities available in a hospital setting) (To report bilateral procedure, use 30115 with modifier 50)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider removes a complicated nasal polyp or polyps from within the nasal cavity. The provider performs this detailed procedure with the help of a snare, or a wire loop, and a low power current to remove the obstruction that the polyp is causing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider identifies the location of the polyp or polyps. The provider may then use either a snare or forceps to remove the more complicated polyps. If the provider chooses the snare, which is a wire loop, he passes the loop over the polyp or lesion, and pushes the sheath of the snare against the base of the polyp. He then uses the snare, or a scalpel to detach the polyps from their base, or he may pass a low power current through a polyp, which cuts the stalk. This method also aides in the coagulation of blood vessels around the stalk to minimize bleeding. He may leave the excision site open to heal, or for larger polyps that leave a larger defect, he may suture the defect closed. Finally, the provider may pack the nasal cavity, leaving the packing in place for 24 hours. Terminology Concha Bullosa: An air filled cavity within the concha or the groove located high up in the bones comprising the nasal passage. Forceps: A two bladed instrument a provider uses to compress or grasp. Nasal polyp: A noncancerous soft and painless growth of tissue within the nasal passages. Tips For a concha bullosa resection with polypectomy procedure, remember that 30115 is not an endoscopic procedure; therefore, report 30115, depending upon the destruction method and approach, along with the endoscopic procedure 31240, Nasal sinus endoscopy, surgical; with concha bullosa resection. Also, CPT® considers polypectomy inclusive as a means of gaining access to the sinus; without removing the polyps the surgeon could not perform the concha bullosa resection. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider excises or destroys a lesion present within the nose through an external approach, in which he creates a full thickness incision in the nose to destroy the intranasal lesion. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider performs a lateral rhinotomy, or incision into the nose. The incision extends from the inner end of the eyebrow, moving down along the outer wall of the nose, over to the nasolabial fold, and passes along the nasal alar base to the philtrum, or groove of the upper lip. The provider then dissects the nasal soft tissue down to the level of bone, providing good nasal cavity access. When he identifies the lesion or lesions, and depending upon the size and location of the lesion, he may remove it with a scissor or knife. He may also use other techniques such as a laser, cryotherapy, a chemical method, or other methods. After, he removes or destroys the lesions, he applies an antibiotic at the site, and leaves the wound open to heal. Terminology Cryotherapy: A technique in which the provider freezes a lesion to destroy it. Chemical method: The provider uses a chemical to destroy the lesion. Dermis: Layer of skin between the epidermis and subcutaneous tissues. Epidermis: Thin outer layer of the skin. Full thickness incision: An incision extending through the dermis. Intranasal: Within the nose. Laser therapy: A strong beam of light is used to destroy a lesion. Lesion: Any abnormality in the tissue. Nasal alar: Area of the face next to nostrils where cheeks meet the edges of the nose. Nasal cavity: A large air filled cavity present behind the nose. Nasolabial folds: Two folds that run on each side of the nose to the corners of the mouth. Subcutaneous layer: The deepest layer of skin; also called subcutis. Tips Use 30117, Excision or destruction, eg laser, intranasal lesion; internal approach, when the provider performs the excision or destruction of intranasal lesion through an internal approach. short_description: Insertion, nasal septal prosthesis (button)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider inserts a silastic button prosthesis to repair a tear of the nasal septum. Explanation This procedure describes just one of several techniques that a provider may use to place a silastic button prosthesis to repair a septal perforation. With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider examines the anterior nasal cavity. He inserts a piece of paper into the nostril and measures the septal defect as well as the length of the septum from top to bottom, and marks the defect on the piece of paper with a marking pen inserted through the other nostril. He trims the rims or flanges of the silastic button so that it will lie an equal distance between the perforation and the upper and lower limits of the septum and smooths the edges of the flanges. He lubricates the button and uses sutures to collapse the button like an accordion. He then inserts the prosthesis into the desired location and cuts the sutures holding it in a collapsed form. The button expands, and he confirms the fit and that all tissue margins are covered to prevent crusting and bleeding. Terminology Perforation: A tear, break, or hole in the wall of an organ or vessel, such as that caused by erosion or wearing away of diseased tissue in an area; e.g., an ulcer or dilated veins. Prosthesis (pl. prostheses): An artificial or man–made replacement for a body part; also known as a prosthetic or prosthetic device. Septum: Wall or partition between two cavities or open spaces; examples include the septa between the ventricles and the atria of the heart and the nasal septum. Silastic: A rubber type material. short_description: Removal foreign body, intranasal; requiring general anesthesia
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes a foreign body from a patient’s nasal cavity. Due to the shape and or deeper position of the foreign body, the provider administers general anesthesia to the patient. A general anesthetic may also be necessary if the patient is unable to tolerate the procedure or if there is edema, or swelling, near the foreign body. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the nasal mucosa to access an intranasal foreign body, or an object deep in the nasal cavity. Using forceps, the provider grasps the foreign body and removes it through blunt dissection. Finally, she closes the small wound by suturing the mucosa in a single layer. Use this code to report an intranasal foreign body removal that a provider performs with the patient under a general anesthetic. Terminology Forceps: A two bladed instrument a provider uses to compress or grasp. Foreign body: Any object that may be accidentally inserted into a cavity like the nose, and it does not belong there. Intranasal: Within the nose. Nasal cavity: A large air filled cavity present behind the nose. Nasal mucosa: Moist tissue lining the nasal surface. short_description: Rhinoplasty, primary; lateral and alar cartilages and/or elevation of nasal tip Notes: (For columellar reconstruction, see 13151 et seq)
lay_term: The provider performs rhinoplasty, a surgery to repair or change the shape of the nose, on a patient who has not had the surgery before. The procedure includes surgery on the lateral (side) and alar (tip) cartilages, elevation of the nasal tip, or all of these. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses either an open or closed approach to perform rhinoplasty, changing the shape of the nose for functional or cosmetic reasons. Open rhinoplasty, also known as external rhinoplasty, involves small, visible incisions, such as the transcolumellar incision that goes through the skin of the columella, the tissue that separates the nostrils and connects the tip of the nose to the base. After making one or more incisions, the provider can fold the nasal skin upward to visualize the nasal skeleton. Open rhinoplasty may allow for easier surgical access than closed rhinoplasty, which is also known as endonasal rhinoplasty. The closed approach involves making surgical incisions inside the nostrils, preventing visible scarring. In either approach, the provider makes the necessary changes to the cartilage and soft tissue, as desired. This procedure involves changes to the lateral (side) and alar (tip) cartilages, nasal tip elevation, or all of these. The provider may use a variety of surgical maneuvers. For instance, alar cartilage helps give the nasal tip its shape, and the provider may alter or remove part of the alar cartilage, which may raise the nasal tip. The provider also may use suturing techniques to change the shape of the alar cartilage. For the lateral cartilage, the provider again may use various techniques, such as suturing, taking care to preserve airway function. The procedure may involve graft placement. (Obtaining tissues for grafts may be separately reportable.) The provider completes the surgery on the lateral and alar cartilages and/or nasal tip and closes the incisions. Tips This code is specific to primary rhinoplasty, which refers to rhinoplasty on a patient who has not had the surgery before. In contrast, secondary rhinoplasty refers to surgery after a previous rhinoplasty, often because the previous rhinoplasty resulted in a complication, did not achieve the desired functional or cosmetic results, or did not treat the patient’s issues properly. Obtaining tissues for grafts may be separately reportable. Check coding guidelines. Read Less

short_description: Repair choanal atresia; intranasal
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically repairs an intranasal choanal atresia, an acquired or congenital condition, causing a blockage of the choana, an inverted funnel shaped passageway from the back of the nose to the upper throat that allows for breathing through the nose. The provider performs the repair through an intranasal approach, where he inserts surgical instruments through the nostrils. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses a nasal speculum to expose the nasal mucosa and atretic plate in the nasal cavity. He then uses a decongestant to open the blocked nose, and then he uses a diamond burr to drill the atretic plate. Next, he punctures and enlarges the blocked choanal openings and places a silastic stent in each nostril to avoid further stenosis or blockage. He keeps the stent in place for up to eight weeks to ensure the patency of the newly created openings. Terminology Atretic plate: A plate at the end of the nasal septum that is continuous with the choanal opening, an opening between the nasal cavity and the nasopharynx. Burr: A surgical instrument used to drill through the bone. Decongestant: A drug used to relieve nasal congestion. Intranasal: Within the nose. Mucosa: Moist tissue that lines the surface of parts of the inside of the body. Silastic: A rubber type material. Speculum: An instrument a provider uses to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure; it has two blades that are hinged and the provider closes when she inserts the speculum and then opens when they are in place. Stent: A small rubber type tube that is used to treat a narrow passage. short_description: Sinusotomy, maxillary (antrotomy); radical (Caldwell-Luc) without removal of antrochoanal polyps Notes: (To report bilateral procedure, use 31030 with modifier 50)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider enters the sinus using an osteotome and removes the entire mucosa of the antrum creating a nasoantral window. He then removes the diseased materials. Explanation Radical maxillary sinusotomy is a common procedure that a provider performs when a malignancy or other disease is present in the sinus cavity. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the upper gums exposing the canine fossa. He then uses an osteotome to enter the sinus and removes the entire mucosa from the antrum, creating a window that connects the maxillary sinus to the nose, improving drainage. The provider may create multiple openings. He then removes the diseased material and closes the incision in the gums with a single layer. The provider takes care to avoid injury to the infraorbital nerve. A typical goal of the procedure is to relieve chronic sinusitis by improving maxillary sinus drainage. This code does not include removal of antrochoanal polyps. Terminology Antrum: A natural cavity that may have a specific meaning in reference to organs or sites. Antrostomy: A surgical opening into a bone or other anatomical structure. Antrochoanal polyps: Single polyp that appears in the maxillary sinus and expands the sinus ostium; this causes the nasal cavity to move back into the nasopharynx. Canine fossa: A large and deep depression on the external surface of the maxilla, which is the upper jaw. Infraorbital nerve: Continuation of the maxillary nerve in the socket of the eye; supplies mucosa of the maxillary sinus, upper incisors, canines, premolars, upper gums, inferior eyelid and conjunctiva, superior lip, and part of the nose. Maxillary sinus: A large pyramid shaped sinus, or cavity, located on either side of the nose below the eye and above the teeth; also called antrum of Highmore. Mucosa: Lining of the part of the body that secretes mucus. Nasoantral window: An aperture between the nose and the maxillary antrum. Osteotome: Surgical instrument for cutting bones. Sinusotomy: Incision into the sinus. Tips This code represents a unilateral service, meaning performed on one side. lay_term: The provider performs a complete excision of the ethmoid air cells (anterior and posterior) with exploration of the frontal sinus; he may or may not remove tissue from frontal sinus. The procedure is performed to treat chronic sinusitis. Explanation After appropriate preparation and administration of anesthesia, a rigid or flexible endoscope is inserted into the nasal cavity. Using cutting forceps, the provider resects the uncinate process, a hooklike extension of the ethmoid bone, and widens the maxillary antrum. He identifies the posterior artery and protects it from injury. The provider removes the diseased and loose bony partition from the lamella papyracea. He also performs frontal sinus exploration and removes diseased tissue from the frontal sinus if necessary. Throughout the procedure, the provider carefully avoids a CSF leak and retrobulbar herniation. Finally, he removes the forceps and scope from the nasal cavity. He packs the nasal cavity with epinephrine–soaked cotton balls. short_description: Laryngectomy; total, without radical neck dissection
lay_term: The provider removes the larynx (voice box) without radical neck dissection. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, prior to starting the main surgery, the provider performs a separate incision for tracheostomy that allows the patient to breathe during the surgery. short_description: Pharyngolaryngectomy, with radical neck dissection; without reconstruction
lay_term: The provider performs pharyngolaryngectomy, in which the provider removes the pharynx and larynx. The provider commonly performs this procedure in patients with difficulty swallowing. The provider then makes a horizontal neck incision in the skin at the level of the thyroid cartilage. He exposes the larynx by raising the flaps from under the muscles extending from the collar bone to the jaw of the patient. These muscles are called the platysmal muscles. He then removes all or part of the hyoid bone, which is the bone present at the root of the tongue. It gives structural support to the tongue. The provider performs excision of lymph nodes. The provider does not reconstruct the pharynx and larynx at this session. short_description: Intubation, endotracheal, emergency procedure
lay_term: The provider inserts a flexible tube into the trachea (windpipe) typically via the mouth in an emergency situation to maintain an open airway in a patient with a compromised airway. Explanation The provider first inserts a laryngoscope to view the vocal cords and the upper part of the windpipe. He then inserts an endotracheal tube through the mouth and into the trachea just above where it branches into the lungs. Once the tube is put in place, a balloon at the tip of the tube is inflated to keep the tube locked in position as well as to protect the patient from choking due to blood or other secretions/discharges in the airway. He removes the laryngoscope. The tube may be connected to a ventilator for assistance in breathing. The provider listens to breathing sounds through a stethoscope for any abnormality. The patient may be administered general anesthesia during the procedure to prevent discomfort. Terminology Laryngoscope: A small instrument used to look for any abnormality inside the larynx (voice box). Trachea: Respiratory tube, also known as the windpipe, composed primarily of muscle and cartilage that connects the pharynx (throat), and larynx (voice box) to the lungs. Ventilator: A mechanical device that provides breathing assistance to a patient or, if necessary, breathes for the patient. Tips Code 31500 separately when there is enough medical documentation to support medical necessity. If billing this code for an anesthesiologist, please note that a general anesthesia service includes this procedure so you cannot bill it separately, unless the documentation proves the medical urgency otherwise. Additional Info Endotracheal intubation is the process of inserting a flexible tube through the mouth and into the trachea to maintain the respiratory function in a patient who has a severe illness, is undergoing major surgery, or when the patient cannot breathe on his/her own. The exterior end of the tube may be connected to a ventilator to maintain respiratory function. Conditions that necessitate endotracheal intubation include head trauma, airway obstruction, respiratory failure, respiratory arrest, and coma. Patients undergoing endoscopic surgery of the airways or bronchoscopy as well as patients under general anesthesia also need it. Any condition that prevents the patient from breathing normally, making the situation life threatening, might necessitate an endotracheal intubation. Read Less

short_description: Tracheotomy tube change prior to establishment of fistula tract
lay_term: The provider changes the tracheotomy tube before a fistula tract is established. This tube change helps prevent infection before the fistula tract matures. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider removes a previously placed tracheotomy tube in the patient’s neck and inserts a new tube. This change prevents an infection prior to final formation of a fistula tract. A typical tube change involves placing an obturator in the outer cannula, a hollow tube that holds the tracheostomy open and that is typically connected to a neck plate. Then the provider removes the inner cannula. The provider then places a new tube while securely holding the obturator inside the outer cannula. After placing the new tube, he removes the obturator. The provider inserts the inner cannula and locks it into place. Terminology Fistula: An abnormal passage made between two structures in the body or between a structure and the exterior of the body; this may be surgically prepared or occur as part of a natural process. Obturator: A metallic or synthetic device used to close an opening. Trachea: Windpipe. short_description: Laryngoplasty; for laryngeal stenosis, with graft, without indwelling stent placement, younger than 12 years of age Notes: (Do not report graft separately if harvested through the laryngoplasty incision [eg, thyroid cartilage graft]) (Do not report 31551 in conjunction with 31552, 31553, 31554, 31580) (To report tracheostomy, see 31600, 31601, 31603, 31605, 31610)
lay_term: The provider performs a laryngoplasty, or surgical repair of the larynx (voice box) and/or its structures, in a child younger than 12 years of age, using a tracheotomy to access the larynx; after dilating and releasing webs as necessary, he places a cartilage graft on the larynx for stability of the larynx and trachea (windpipe) and to correct laryngeal stenosis, or narrowing. Explanation When the patient, under 12 years of age, is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin of the neck as well as the trachea to access the larynx. He may dilate the trachea and remove any web tissue found to free up the vocal cords as well as the affected area of the posterior glottis. The provider then accesses the larynx. He carefully divides any web structures and covers raw surfaces with mucosa. He may use a submucous resection technique (by which he opens the membrane over the mucosa, excises some of the mucosa underneath and then replaces the membrane over the area) in order to remove a laryngeal web from the area of stenosis. Finally, he places a cartilage graft to provide stability to the larynx and trachea. Often, the graft material is autogenous costal cartilage that may be removed in a separate procedure. He then reinspects the area, controls any bleeding, and closes the incision with sutures. This procedure is performed without placement of an indwelling stent, a tubelike device that keeps a passage open. Terminology Arytenoid: Cartilage present at the back of the voice box, responsible for production of specific voice sounds. Laryngeal web: A condition present from the time of birth in which a web of thin or thick filaments is spread between the vocal cords; this condition may cause difficulty in speaking, hoarseness of voice, or respiratory symptoms. Tracheotomy: A surgical procedure in which an incision is made through the neck and into the trachea to make an artificial opening; a tube can be inserted to assist breathing or for inserting instruments to examine the trachea and larynx. He may dilate the trachea and remove any web tissue found to free up the vocal cords as well as the affected area of the posterior glottis. The provider then accesses the larynx. He carefully divides any web structures and covers raw surfaces with mucosa. He may use a submucous resection technique (by which he opens the membrane over the mucosa, excises some of the mucosa underneath and then replaces the membrane over the area) in order to remove a laryngeal web from the area of stenosis. Finally, he places a cartilage graft to provide stability to the larynx and trachea. Often, the graft material is autogenous costal cartilage that may be removed in a separate procedure. He also places an indwelling stent, a tubelike device that keeps a passage open, through the tracheotomy for added stability and to prevent restenosis. He then reinspects the area, controls any bleeding, and closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Arytenoid: Cartilage present at the back of the voice box, responsible for production of specific voice sounds. Cartilage: A strong but flexible tissue found at the ends of long bones, between the ribs and sternum, and in the nose and ears. Glottis: The part of the larynx that contains the true vocal cords, which expand and contract down to a narrow opening that is no more than a slit, and where certain sounds are produced. Laryngeal web: A condition present from the time of birth in which a web of thin or thick filaments is spread between the vocal cords; this condition may cause difficulty in speaking, hoarseness of voice, or respiratory symptoms. Tracheotomy: A surgical procedure in which an incision is made through the neck and into the trachea to make an artificial opening; a tube can be inserted to assist breathing or for inserting instruments to examine the trachea and larynx. Tips For the same procedure for a child younger than 12, report 31553 (Laryngoplasty; for laryngeal stenosis, with graft, with indwelling stent placement, younger than 12 years of age). For the same procedure without indwelling stent placement, report 31551 (Laryngoplasty; for laryngeal stenosis, with graft, without indwelling stent placement, younger than 12 years of age) in a child younger than age 12 and for a patient 12 or older, report 31552 (..., age 12 years or older) For other laryngoplasty procedures, see 31580–31591 (Laryngoplasty, ...) The graft is usually a cartilage graft, which may be taken from the ear, septum of the nose, rib cartilage, or other location, for which an additional code may be reportable; however, a thyroid or cricoid cartilage graft harvested through the laryngoplasty incision cannot be reported separately. short_description: Laryngoscopy, direct, operative, with arytenoidectomy; with operating microscope or telescope Notes: (Do not report code 69990 in addition to code 31561)
lay_term: The provider uses a laryngoscope to look directly inside the larynx, which is the voice box, to detect the presence of any abnormalities. The provider also performs arytenoidectomy, in which the provider excises the arytenoids cartilage present at the back of the voice box. He performs arytenoidectomy under the guidance of an operating telescope or microscope. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a laryngoscope into the throat and directly views the laryngeal and hypopharyngeal structures. Then the provider identifies the arytenoids cartilage. Under the guidance of an operating microscope or telescope, the provider makes an incision in the aryepiglottic fold, which is the opening of the larynx that is narrow in front and wide behind. He releases the soft tissues and muscles. The provider then removes the arytenoid using such techniques as microsurgery or laser. The provider may also perform a widening of the posterior glottis. Finally, he closes the incision with sutures if needed. Terminology Arytenoid: Cartilage present at the back of the voice box, responsible for production of specific voice sounds. Arytenoidectomy: Surgical procedure in which the provider excises the arytenoids cartilage; it is generally performed to improve air flow through the airway. Direct laryngoscopy: Involves the use of a laryngoscope in the mouth to directly view the larynx and adjacent structures; a direct laryngoscopy almost always takes place in the operating room under general anesthesia or conscious sedation. Glottis: The part of the larynx consisting of the vocal cords and a slit–like opening between them; it affects voice modulation when it expands and contracts. Hypopharyngeal structures: Muscles and tissues present below the pharynx, which is a passage that connects the nose and the mouth to the esophagus, which is the food pipe. Laryngoscope: A small instrument used to look for any abnormality inside the larynx, which is the voice box. Read Less

short_description: Laryngoscopy, flexible or rigid telescopic, with stroboscopy
lay_term: The provider uses a flexible or rigid laryngoscope to look inside the larynx, or voice box, to detect the presence of any abnormalities. He also performs stroboscopy, which is a method of examination of the vocal cords in which the provider illuminates and vibrates the vocal folds with a bright light for a fraction of a second allowing the examination of the voice box structure and function. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a flexible or rigid laryngoscope via the mouth or nose to view the laryngeal and hypopharyngeal structures along with the vocal folds. The provider also performs a stroboscopy where he beams a pulsed light source inside the throat/nose area to visualize vocal fold vibration. This provides real–time, slow visualization of the patient's vocal fold vibration and vocal fold closure permitting observation of how the vocal folds move and the identification of possible lesions and/or other abnormalities. The exam is usually recorded for playback at varying speeds to allow for detailed analysis and clinical voice evaluation. Findings are then used in planning treatment. Terminology Diagnostic: Refers to procedures performed for the purpose of determining the type of disease and its causes. Hypopharyngeal structures: Muscles and tissues present below the pharynx, which is a passage that connects the nose and the mouth to the esophagus, which is the food pipe. Larynx: Part of the respiratory system that produces voice and helps with swallowing action and breathing; also known as the voice box. Stroboscopy: A method of examination of the vocal cords in which the provider illuminates and vibrates the vocal folds with a bright light for a fraction of a second to examine the voice box structure and function. Tips There is no code that specifically denotes videostroboscopy. You should use 31579 for a laryngoscopy using equipment that flashes a strobe light. The provider has the patient make sounds so the vocal cords will move and appear to be in slow motion while being examined. Reserve 31579 for videostroboscopy with a rigid or flexible scope. Do not use the code for simply making and viewing a video of the procedure. Read Less

short_description: Laryngoplasty; for laryngeal web, with indwelling keel or stent insertion Notes: (Do not report 31580 in conjunction with 31551, 31552, 31553, 31554) (To report tracheostomy, see 31600, 31601, 31603, 31605, 31610) (To report removal of the keel or stent, use 31599)
lay_term: The provider performs laryngoplasty, a surgical procedure in which the provider repairs or alters the larynx (voice box) or its structures. He performs this procedure to remove a congenital or acquired laryngeal web, a membranous structure spread in the larynx and vocal cords, sometimes from birth, that narrows the airway. The provider removes the laryngeal web and places a keel, or stent to prevent scar tissue from forming, and web reformation and restenosis. After the larynx has healed, the keel or stent may be removed in a separate procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider commonly performs a tracheostomy to access the larynx, which is the voice box, and to access the laryngeal web around the vocal cords. He may opt to use another mode to reach the larynx. The provider removes the web tissue and inserts a keel, an artificial device that creates some space between the vocal cords or stent. He secures the device in place, then sutures and closes the incision. After the larynx has healed, the provider accesses the larynx via the same laryngotomy incision during a later, separately reported procedure, to remove the keel or stent. Terminology Keel: A medical device to keep the laryngeal lumen open and the repair, or reconstruction supported and stable Laryngeal web: A condition, sometimes present from birth, in which a web of thin or thick filaments is spread between the vocal cords; this condition may cause difficulty in speaking, hoarseness of voice, or respiratory symptoms. Larynx: Part of the respiratory system that produces voice and helps with swallowing action and breathing; also known as the voice box. Lumen: The interior, open area of a vessel or organ; a tubelike cavity. Stenosis: Narrowing in a tubular or hollow structure, such as an artery, valve, the colon, throat, or ear canal. Stent: A tubelike device used to maintain the opening of a tubular structure. Tracheostomy: A surgical procedure in which an incision is made into the trachea, through the neck, and a tube inserted to make an artificial opening to assist breathing. Read Less

short_description: Laryngoplasty; with open reduction and fixation of (eg, plating) fracture, includes tracheostomy, if performed Notes: (Do not report graft separately if harvested through the laryngoplasty incision [eg, thyroid cartilage graft])
lay_term: The provider performs laryngoplasty, the surgical repair or alteration of the larynx (voice box) to repair a fracture of the larynx; the provider may also perform a tracheostomy as part of this procedure to allow the patient to breath during the procedure. A fracture may occur due to a penetrating or blunt injury caused by a motor vehicle accident (MVA), sports injury, or assault. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized the provider may first perform a tracheostomy, that is, he makes an incision into the trachea through the neck and inserts a tube to make an artificial opening to assist breathing. Then the provider makes an incision on the neck to access the cricoid and laryngeal cartilage, separating and retracting muscle and tissue as he goes. Next, depending upon the type of injury, he makes an incision through the thyrohyoid membrane or the thyroid cartilage over the larynx and dissects down to reach the fractured larynx for repair. He manipulates the laryngeal tissues to realign them and stabilizes the structure using wire sutures or miniplates. He then reapproximates muscle and tissue and closes the incision, placing a nasogastric tube as necessary. Terminology Cricoid cartilage: Ringlike cartilage at the base of the larynx, which is the voice box in the throat. Hyoid bone: A small bone at the base of the lower jaw that is shaped like the letter U and serves to support the tongue to facilitate speech and swallowing; it is the only bone in the human body that does not connect to any other bone and is instead connected only through muscle tissue. Larynx: Part of the respiratory system that produces voice and helps with swallowing action and breathing; also known as the voice box. Open reduction: A surgical procedure in which the provider exposes the fracture fragments for repair by dissecting the tissues. Thyrohyoid membrane: A wide, fibroelastic sheet of the larynx; also known as the hyothyroid membrane. Thyroid cartilage: A firm structure that is present around the wind pipe and contains the voice box and forms the Adam’s apple. Read Less

short_description: Laryngoplasty, cricoid split, without graft placement Notes: (To report tracheostomy, see 31600, 31601, 31603, 31605, 31610)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a laryngoplasty, the surgical repair or alteration of the larynx, or voice box in a procedure, known as a cricoid split. This procedure may be necessary for congenital or acquired subglottic stenosis, a narrowing of the airway below the vocal cords and above the trachea, which may be congenital or occur due to trauma or infection. A cricoid split includes transection or division by cutting across the circular laryngeal cartilage, or cricoid without placing a graft in order to enlarge the subglottic airway. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates a horizontal neck incision through the muscles to expose the trachea. He continues the incision down dividing the muscle and locates the cricoid cartilage. He transects (divides) the cartilage by cutting across the cricoid ring in order to enlarge the subglottic airway. The airway may be stented intraoperatively or an endotracheal tube may be placed postoperatively to maintain an open airway. He then closes the wound, and places a drain. Terminology Cricoid cartilage: Ring–like cartilage at the base of the larynx, which is the voice box in the throat. Endotracheal tube: A flexible tube inserted into the trachea via the nose or mouth to maintain an open airway. Larynx: Part of the respiratory system that produces voice and helps with swallowing action and breathing; also known as the voice box. Stenosis: Narrowing in a tubular or hollow structure, such as an artery, valve, the colon, or ear canal. Trachea: Respiratory tube composed primarily of muscle and cartilage that connects the pharynx, or throat, and larynx, or voice box, to the lungs; also known as the windpipe. Read Less

short_description: Laryngoplasty, medialization, unilateral
lay_term: The provider restores the function of the larynx, or voice box, by moving a displaced or paralyzed vocal cord, which is displaced to one side, back toward the midline (medialization) in order to improve breathing, vocalization, and swallowing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in a skin crease over the larynx and cuts a hole in the larynx to gain access to the vocal cord. He inserts an implant, graft, or other material into the larynx so that it moves the vocal cord toward the midline. He passes a flexible laryngoscope through the nose, which has been sprayed with lidocaine anesthetic, and into the throat to examine the vocal cord position and make any needed adjustments. During this part of the procedure, the patient is allowed to recover a bit from anesthesia and asked to make sounds. If no more adjustments are needed, the provider controls any bleeding and closes the incision. Terminology Laryngoscope: A small instrument used to look for any abnormality inside the larynx, or voice box. Unilateral: On one side only, generally applied to structures situated symmetrically on both the right and the left halves of the body. Vocal cords: Small band of muscle in the larynx that produces the voice; also known as vocal folds. Tips This procedure is for medialization of the vocal cord on one side through an incision in the larynx. For a laryngoscopy with injection procedure to move the vocal cord toward the midline, report 31574. Read Less

lay_term: The provider removes a narrowed segment of the trachea, or windpipe, and joins the two ends back together to relieve subglottic stenosis, narrowing of the airway at the level of the cricoid cartilage, ringlike fibrous connective tissue at the base and back of the larynx, the part of the throat above the trachea. Explanation The patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, and a shoulder roll placed to extend the neck. The provider intubates the patient with a small diameter endotracheal tube (ETT) or places an ETT through a tracheostomy during resection and replaces it with an oral ETT just prior to reconnecting the thyroid cartilage and cricoid remnant. The provider incises the skin over the lower neck near the collar bone and exposes the airway from near the base of the lower jaw to the uppermost part of the sternum, or breastbone. He retracts the muscles in the front part of the neck and divides the thyroid isthmus, the band of tissue joining the lobes of the thyroid gland, in the midline. He identifies the distal (far) end of the stenosis and mobilizes the trachea circumferentially to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage. He bluntly dissects the anterior (front) wall of the trachea to the lowest portion of the tracheal cartilage. He identifies the muscle over the cricothyroid and moves it upward out of the way. He incises the perichondrium, the dense fibrous connective tissue covering the cartilage, on the upper and lower border of the cricoid cartilage and excises the front segment. He dissects along the inner aspect of the cricoid cartilage to protect the recurrent laryngeal nerves, which are located below and behind the structure. He uses a rongeur to further excise the thickened tissue causing the stenosis within the inner channel of the cricoid ring. He uses a bur to thin the posterior lumen (the back of the channel) but preserves about 50% of the wall thickness. He identifies the distal and proximal margins of the stenosis and resects it all in one piece. He may develop advancement and/or rotational flaps in order to facilitate reattachment of the two ends of the resected trachea. If necessary, the provider may also harvest and insert a cartilage graft. He places retention sutures through the sides of the thyroid cartilage and cricoid remnant. He uses a submucosal stitch that encircles the far end of the tracheal ring. He uses, the retention sutures to bring the segments together and attaches them to each other using a posterior to anterior (back to front) running stitch. The provider checks for bleeding, closes the incision, removes the endotracheal tube, and completes the procedure. Terminology Cartilage: A strong but flexible tissue found at the ends of long bones, as well as in the nose and ears. Cricothyroid membrane: An elastic tissue cartilage that is attached to the cricoid cartilage, the ring of cartilage around the trachea. Resection: Surgical excision or removal of tissues, organs, or other structures, in whole or in part. Trachea: Respiratory tube composed primarily of muscle and cartilage that connects the pharynx, or throat, and larynx, or voice box, to the lungs; also known as the windpipe. Tips To report the tracheostomy, see codes 31600–31610. For excision of tracheal stenosis and anastomosis, see 31780 and 31781. You should not report the development of rotational or advancement flaps or harvesting of cartilage graft separately when performed through the same cricotracheal resection incision. Read Less

short_description: Tracheostomy, planned (separate procedure)
lay_term: The provider performs tracheostomy, which is a surgical procedure in which the provider exposes the trachea, which is the windpipe, and creates an opening in it. This code represents a planned tracheostomy. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider performs a neck incision and divides the overlying muscles. The goal is to expose the tough cartilage rings that make up the outer wall of the trachea. If needed, the provider excises the thyroid isthmus. He then creates an opening into the trachea and inserts a tracheostomy tube. The provider creates an opening in the neck by suturing the skin to the adjacent tissues. This opening connects the neck to the tracheostomy site. This code represents a planned tracheostomy. The provider performs this procedure in patients with an obstructed airway, to assist them in breathing, and to clean and remove secretions from the airway, using a suction tube. Terminology Cartilage: Firm and flexible tissue in the human body. Thyroid isthmus: The band of tissue joining the lobes of the thyroid gland. Tips Code 31600 represents planned tracheostomy. Planned tracheostomy frequently occurs after a patient has been intubated for a long period or requires long–term ventilatory support. On the other hand, providers perform emergency tracheostomies when a patient's airway is so compromised that it may obstruct his breathing at any moment. For example, a patient presents with wheezing, which is quickly progressing to upper–airway obstruction, and the provider performs a tracheostomy. For emergent situations that require an opening of the windpipe, assign 31603 or 31605. Before reporting 31600 or 31601 in addition to another code, you should determine whether the tracheostomy is a separate procedure. You should not report separate procedure codes in addition to the code for the total surgery or service of which it is an integral part. See 31601 for patients under 2 years old. Read Less

short_description: Tracheostomy, fenestration procedure with skin flaps Notes: (For endotracheal intubation, use 31500) (For tracheal aspiration under direct vision, use 31515)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider creates a permanent opening through skin into the trachea by using skin flaps. short_description: Construction of tracheoesophageal fistula and subsequent insertion of an alaryngeal speech prosthesis (eg, voice button, Blom-Singer prosthesis)
lay_term: The provider surgically creates a fistula between the trachea, or wind pipe, and the esophagus, or food pipe. This code also includes subsequent insertion of a speech prosthesis in the passage created. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision on the neck to access the trachea and esophagus. He divides the tissues between the tracheal opening and esophagus, incising the esophagus. The provider thereby creates a fistula, or opening, between the trachea and the esophagus. He then inserts a speech prosthesis in the passage created. The provider closes the incision around the prosthesis with sutures. A Blom–Singer prosthesis is a device that helps the patient to produce sounds or talk. This procedure is performed in patients with paralyzed laryngeal structures. Terminology Fistula: A passage between a hollow organ and the body surface, or between two hollow organs; may be surgically created or result from a natural process. Read Less

short_description: Bronchoscopy, rigid or flexible, including fluoroscopic guidance, when performed; diagnostic, with cell washing, when performed (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs diagnostic rigid or flexible bronchoscopy, a test to view airways and diagnose lung disease. He may or may not use fluoroscopic guidance to perform this test. He may also perform cell washing in which he obtains a sample of suspicious cells. Explanation Bronchoscopy is a procedure in which the provider inserts a flexible or rigid tube, called a bronchoscope, through the nose or mouth to perform visual examination of the airways. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts the scope through the nose or mouth and moves the scope down into the throat. He next advances the scope to the bronchus, the main passageway to the lung. He then, using the eyepiece, examines the mucus lining or covering of these airways and looks for any abnormality that may be present. He may pass saline solution through the tube to wash the airways and to obtain a sample of suspicious cells. He may also use fluoroscopic guidance to perform this procedure. In fluoroscopic guidance, the provider injects a dye and uses X–ray imaging of moving structures to guide the passage of the scope. Terminology Flexible bronchoscopy: Use of a thin, flexible tube to look into airways. Rigid bronchoscopy: Use of a straight, metal tube to look into airways. Tips Use 31623 when the provider performs rigid or flexible bronchoscopy with brushing or protected brushing. He may or may not use fluoroscopic guidance to perform this test. Use 31624 when the provider performs rigid or flexible bronchoscopy with bronchial alveolar lavage. He may or may not use fluoroscopic guidance to perform this test. Code 31622’s descriptor indicates it is a separate procedure, meaning that you cannot report this code separately with a related procedure when performed in an anatomically related region. If the provider performs the 31622 procedure with an unrelated procedure, you may need to append modifier 59 to 31622. Read Less

short_description: Bronchoscopy, rigid or flexible, including fluoroscopic guidance, when performed; with brushing or protected brushings
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses a rigid or flexible bronchoscope for brushing or protected brushing, a procedure using a soft brush to gently wipe the lung tissue or to scrape a lesion. The provider may use fluoroscopic guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts the bronchoscope through the nose or mouth and moves the scope down into the throat. The provider next advances the scope to the bronchus, the main passageway to the lung. The provider examines the mucus lining or covering of the airways and looks for any abnormality that may be present. The provider performs brushing by using either a normal brush or a protected brush. The protected brush is contained in a protective sheath, thus avoiding contamination during passage through the scope channel. The normal brush is not covered by any sheath and is not protected. The provider introduces the brush through the tube of the scope and uses the brush to wipe the lung tissue or to abrade the lung lesion. The provider obtains samples or specimens using the brush and sends the sample to the lab for investigation. The provider may use fluoroscopic guidance, a live X–ray where the images appear on a monitor so the provider can view body structures and instruments during the procedure. The provider removes the scope to complete the procedure. Terminology Bronchoscopy: A procedure in which the provider inserts a flexible or rigid tube (bronchoscope) through the nose or mouth to perform visual examination of the airways. Read Less

short_description: Bronchoscopy, rigid or flexible, including fluoroscopic guidance, when performed; with bronchial alveolar lavage
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses a rigid or flexible bronchoscope for bronchial alveolar lavage, a procedure using saline solution to wash the cells from alveoli, the air sacs at the end of the bronchioles. The provider may use fluoroscopic guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts the bronchoscope through the nose or mouth and moves the scope down into the throat. The provider next advances the scope to the bronchus, the main passageway to the lung. The provider examines the mucus lining or covering of the airways and looks for any abnormality that may be present. The provider passes saline solution through the tube to wash cells from the air sacs at the end of the bronchioles. This may involve repeated instillations. The provider aspirates this fluid for inspection. The provider may use fluoroscopic guidance, a live X–ray where the images appear on a monitor so the provider can view body structures and instruments during the procedure. The provider removes the scope to complete the procedure. Terminology Alveoli: Air sacs that are a continuation of bronchioles (tiny air passages in the lungs) and are responsible for exchange of gases. Aspiration: Removal of fluid, gas, or other material through a tube attached to a suction device, often for laboratory analysis or combined with irrigation, the instillation of fluid to clean a wound or to wash out a cavity such as the abdomen, stomach, lungs, or joints; also, breathing in or sucking in food, fluid, or a foreign object into the airway. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Instillation of a saline solution or water into the bronchi (the two main passageways for air into the lungs) and the alveoli (air sacs that are a continuation of bronchioles, tiny air passages in the lungs) followed by suctioning to remove the fluid, typically performed during a bronchoscopy for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes. short_description: Bronchoscopy, rigid or flexible, including fluoroscopic guidance, when performed; with placement of fiducial markers, single or multiple Notes: (Report supply of device separately)
lay_term: In addition to normal bronchoscopic examination, the provider places one or more markers to create a reference point for future treatment/surgery. Explanation The team brings the patient into the endoscopy suite and administers adequate anesthesia. The provider inserts a rigid or flexible bronchoscope through the nose or mouth to examine the patient's airways for abnormalities such as foreign bodies, bleeding, or tumors. The provider may use fluoroscopic guidance, or live X–ray, which is included in this procedure. In addition to examination of the airway, the provider places one or more radiologically detectable markers, known as fiducial markers, for identification of any suspicious area or lesion. Placing a marker helps the provider to locate problematic areas for treatment in the future, for example, if he plans to perform surgery in a subsequent session. The provider can place as many markers as are required in a single session. After completion of the service, the provider slowly removes the bronchoscope, and the team moves the patient to the recovery room. Terminology Bronchoscopy: A technique to visualize the inside of the airways, using a viewing instrument called a bronchoscope, for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes Fiducial marker: A small object placed near an area of interest in a patient’s anatomy; the marker is easily identifiable using imaging, allowing a provider to locate the area during a procedure Tips The 31626 descriptor covers single or multiple marker placements. For instance, if the provider inserts four fiducial markers bronchoscopically to act as reference points for CyberKnife® radiation delivery, you’ll report the marker placement using only one unit of 31626, not four units. If the provider uses fluoroscopic guidance to place the markers through bronchoscopy, you should not report the guidance used for the procedure separately as this is included in the descriptor of 31626. short_description: Bronchoscopy, rigid or flexible, including fluoroscopic guidance, when performed; with tracheal/bronchial dilation or closed reduction of fracture
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs rigid or flexible bronchoscopy to view airways during a procedure. He may or may not use fluoroscopic guidance. He dilates the stenosis, or narrowing, of the trachea or bronchi using techniques like balloon dilatation. He may treat tracheobronchial fracture, a tear or break that occurs in the airways, leading to obstruction or narrowing. Explanation Bronchoscopy is a procedure in which the provider inserts a flexible or rigid tube, called a bronchoscope, through the nose or mouth to perform visual examination of the airways. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts the scope through the nose or mouth and moves the scope down into the throat. He next advances the scope to the bronchus, the main passageway to the lung. He then, using the eyepiece, examines the mucus lining or covering of these airways and looks for any abnormality or narrowing that may be present. He passes a guide wire through the scope to the site of narrowing. He may introduce a balloon over the guide wire and inflate the balloon at the narrowed site to open the obstruction or treat the fracture. He may also use fluoroscopic guidance to perform this procedure. In fluoroscopic guidance, the provider injects a dye and uses X–ray imaging of moving structures to guide the passage of the scope. Finally, once he completes the procedures, he removes the instrument and scopes and monitors the patient for vital signs. Terminology Flexible bronchoscopy: Use of a thin, flexible tube to look into airways. Rigid bronchoscopy: Use of a straight, hollow, metal tube to look into airways. Read Less

short_description: Bronchoscopy, rigid or flexible, including fluoroscopic guidance, when performed; with transbronchial lung biopsy(s), each additional lobe (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 31632 in conjunction with 31628) (31632 should be reported only once regardless of how many transbronchial lung biopsies are performed in a lobe)
lay_term: In this add–on procedure, the provider uses a rigid or flexible bronchoscope to obtain one or more transbronchial biopsies from an additional lobe of the lung following biopsy of an initial lobe. The provider may use fluoroscopic guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, and at the same session as transbronchial biopsy of an initial lobe, the provider advances the bronchoscope to another lobe. The provider examines the mucus lining or covering of the airways and looks for any abnormality that may be present. The provider then introduces an instrument like tiny forceps through the channel in the scope and takes a transbronchial biopsy of tissue from one lobe of the lung. Transbronchial indicates sampling of tissue beyond the airway directly in view, as opposed to being biopsy of lesions within the airway lumen (tube). The provider may take single or multiple biopsies and sends them for investigation. The provider may use fluoroscopic guidance, a live X–ray where the images appear on a monitor so the provider can view body structures and instruments during the procedure. The provider removes the scope to complete the procedure. Terminology Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, open. Bronchoscopy: A procedure in which the provider inserts a flexible or rigid tube (bronchoscope) through the nose or mouth to perform visual examination of the airways. Forceps: Pincers or tongs used for grasping; also surgical forceps. Lumen: The interior, open area of a vessel or organ; a tubelike cavity, or the interior of a catheter or tube. Tips Because +31632 is an add–on code, payers will not reimburse you if you report it without an appropriate primary code. Use 31628 when the provider obtains a transbronchial biopsy from a single lobe of the lung using bronchoscopy. Read Less

short_description: Tracheoplasty; tracheopharyngeal fistulization, each stage

short_description: Excision tracheal stenosis and anastomosis; cervical
lay_term: The provider excises a narrowing of the trachea and then joins tracheal segments to repair the defect and reestablish the airway. Explanation The patient is anesthetized through an existing tracheostomy, or opening in the trachea. The provider makes a cervical incision down to the trachea, ensuring that he does not damage the thyroid gland, major neck vessels, or the recurrent laryngeal nerves. The provider opens the tracheal lumen, examines the area with the stenosis, and excises it. The provider then inserts a nasotracheal tube through the nose and the throat and advances it into the distal trachea. He then removes the tracheostomy tube. The provider releases the larynx and part of the tracheal segment from the hyoid bone and releases the tracheal segment from the mediastinum. The provider joins the two parts of the trachea with 10 to 15 sutures, called anastomosis. After closing the incision, the provider sutures the patient’s chin to the anterior chest wall to reduce tension on the anastomosis. The provider takes a postoperative chest X–ray to check for a pneumothorax. Terminology Anterior: Closer to the front part of the body. lay_term: The provider removes the entire lung and any visible cancer in the parietal pleural lining of the chest, heart, and diaphragm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses a scalpel to make an incision in the chest, either a sternotomy or thoracotomy. She then may use a rib spreader to separate the ribs, providing more access to the lungs. The provider then collapses the lung and ties off the affected blood vessels, before clamping and cutting the diseased lung's air tube. She then removes the entire lung via the incision. She also removes the parietal pleura lining the ribs, diaphragm, and mediastinum. She then closes the incision with staples or stitches, and ensures that the air tube is not leaking air. This code represents when the service involves removing the lung, areas of the diaphragm, and the covering of the heart or pericardium. If the provider performs sternotomy, she closes the incision by wiring the ribcage halves back together. Terminology Diaphragm: Large flat muscle that separates the lungs from the stomach area; used in breathing. Mediastinum: Space between the lungs which is bounded by the lungs on either side, the sternum in front, the vertebrae in back and the diaphragm at the bottom. Parietal pleura: Membrane lining the inner chest wall. Pericardium: Conical sac membrane that encloses the heart. Pleura: Serous membrane that lines the thorax and walls of the pulmonary cavity and envelops the lungs. Pneumonectomy: Surgical removal of a lung. Rib spreaders: Surgical instrument to separate edges of the ribs. Serous membrane: Thin membrane lining body cavities and secretes a serous fluid, which is clear watery fluid present in the body. Sternotomy: Surgical procedure in which a vertical incision is made along the sternum to split it in two halves. Thoracotomy: Incision into the chest cavity. Tips Use 32440 when the service involves only a total pneumonectomy. Use 32442 when the service involves sleeve pneumonectomy. Use 32445 when the service involves extrapleural pneumonectomy. short_description: Removal of lung, other than pneumonectomy; single lobe (lobectomy)
lay_term: The provider removes a single lobe of the lung. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the pleural space via a wide incision in the chest cavity between two ribs. He spreads the ribs apart with rib spreaders to expose the lung. He clamps, divides, and ligates the lobar vessels and the bronchus, separating them from the lobe to be removed. He excises the lobe is excised and removes it from the surgical field. The remaining lobes are re–expanded. He leaves one or two catheters in the chest cavity for drainage. He closes the chest incisions in layers with sutures. Another method used for access of the lobe is through the sternum which is cut into two halves vertically and spread apart with spreaders. Once the lobectomy is done, the provider ties the two halves of the sternum with wires and closes the chest incision with sutures. Terminology Bronchus (pl. bronchi): One of two main air passageways from the end of the trachea (windpipe) into the lungs; also known as the right and left bronchi. Lobectomy: Removal of all or part of a lobe of the brain, thyroid gland, lung, or liver. Pneumonectomy: The surgical removal of a lung. Segmentectomy: Surgery to remove part of an organ or gland. Tips For removal of two lobes of a lung, see 32482. For removal of an entire lung, see 32440 through 32445. For removal of a single segment of a lung (segmentectomy), see 32484. lay_term: The provider removes a part of the lung and repairs the resected bronchus by connecting the cut ends. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses a scalpel to make an incision in the chest, known as thoracotomy or sternotomy. She then may use a rib spreader to spread the ribs apart, which exposes the lungs. The provider then identifies the segment or lobe to be excised. She clamps, ties, and cuts the lung segment, main bronchial vessels, and bronchial tubes. She then removes part of the lung and resects the bronchus. A typical procedure involves removing an upper lobe and part of the bronchus going to a remaining lower lobe. The provider then reconnects the bronchus of the remaining lobe or lobes of the affected lung to the remaining portion of the cut bronchus. She may use a chest tube for drainage of secretions from the chest cavity. The provider then closes the incision with sutures or stitches. If the provider performed sternotomy, she closes the incision by wiring the ribcage halves back together. Terminology Anastomosis: Surgical connection between two, usually tubular structures. Pneumonectomy: Surgical removal of a lung. Rib spreaders: Surgical instrument to separate edges of the ribs. Sleeve lobectomy: Surgical removal of a lobe of the lung along with a portion of the bronchus that attaches to a remaining lobe. Sternotomy: Surgical procedure in which a vertical incision is made along the sternum to split it in two halves. Thoracotomy: Incision into the chest cavity. lay_term: The provider removes an intact abscess called an empyema from above the pleura (covering) of the lungs along with surrounding pleural lining. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the thorax called thoracotomy. She then uses a rib spreader to split the ribs apart for better access to the lungs. She begins removal of the pleura at the edge of the empyema, peeling the layer off the lung, using instruments as needed. If tears occur in the lung, she closes them, such as by cautery or sutures. Once she frees the layer sufficiently, she lifts the tissue, including the abscess, as a unit and removes it from the patient’s body. The provider then closes the chest incision with staples or stitches. The provider may place one or more chest drains with one end in the thoracic cavity and the other end exiting the body so the tube may be connected to a collection container. The chest tube helps in reexpanding the lungs and allows for drainage of air, blood, or fluid. Terminology Empyema: Accumulation of pus in a body cavity, such as the chest or abdomen, or between membranes such as the dura covering the brain or the pleura covering the lungs. Enucleation: Removal of a mass without cutting into the mass itself. Extrapleural: Outside or around the pleural layer. Pleura: A bi–layer membrane that lines the chest cavity and covers the lungs; the outer layer is the parietal pleura and the inner layer is the visceral pleura. Rib spreaders: Surgical instrument to separate edges of the ribs. Thoracotomy: Incision into the chest cavity. Tips If a pulmonary lobectomy is performed at the same time as this procedure, it may be reported separately with the appropriate modifier, such as modifier 59. Read Less

short_description: Thoracentesis, needle or catheter, aspiration of the pleural space; with imaging guidance
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes the fluid, blood, or air from the space between the lungs and chest wall using a needle or catheter. He performs the procedure using imaging guidance. Explanation The patient is placed in a seated position and slightly leaning forward with the arms resting on small table. lay_term: The provider injects a chest tube or catheter with an agent to dissolve fibrin proteins in the patient’s chest. This code describes all related services on each day of treatment after the first. Explanation On the day after previous fibrinolysis instillation, the provider provides an additional day of instillation services. She ensures the patient is in proper position and checks the indwelling chest tube or the catheter. She clamps the tube or catheter and carefully disconnects it from the drainage hose. She injects the fibrinolytic agent into the tube or catheter after clamp removal to allow the agent to move into the chest cavity. She puts the clamp back on the tube or catheter and moves the patient into various positions over a couple of hours to move the agent within the chest cavity. She removes the clamp and restarts suction. She may repeat this service multiple times during the day. lay_term: Using a video–assisted endoscopic approach, the provider takes one or more samples involving one or more abnormal substances in a single lung. Explanation After the patient is prepped, draped, and anesthetized, the provider may direct an anesthesiologist to collapse one lung and ventilate the other for the procedure. The provider makes a small incision and inserts the thoracoscope with camera so he can examine the lung area. He makes additional small incisions and inserts specialized instruments. He identifies the area of infiltrate for biopsy and uses the instruments, such as special staplers, to remove a small piece of lung for diagnostic examination. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates a small incision on the side of the chest between the ribs. He then, through one of the incisions, introduces an endoscope, a thin tube–like instrument containing a tiny camera. With the help of this camera, he examines the lungs and pleura. He first compresses the lungs to have adequate visualization and then thoroughly examines the lung surface to identify and isolate the bullae. He re–expands the lung to assess for air leak and to identify the culprit bullae. He next excises the offending bullae by blunt dissection, folding and cutting them down using surgical instruments. He then re–expands the lungs. Finally, he withdraws the endoscope and other instruments and closes the surgical wound. He may leave one or more tubes temporarily in the chest cavity to drain the fluid or air. He may also perform other pleural procedures at the same session. Terminology Pleura: Membrane lining the chest cavity and enveloping the lungs. Plication: Folding and suturing the tissue. Resection: Removal of an organ or tissue. Thoracoscopy: Use of an endoscope to examine the lungs, the middle of the chest, and the membranes that line the lungs, which are called pleural layers. Tips See 32601–32674 for other thoracoscopic procedures. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Surgical thoracoscopy (video-assisted thoracic surgery [VATS]) always includes diagnostic thoracoscopy. Section Specific Guideline Pleural cavity or lung biopsy procedures may be accomplished using a percutaneous, thoracoscopic (Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery [VATS]), or thoracotomy approach. They involve the removal of differing amounts of tissue for diagnosis. A biopsy may be performed using different techniques such as incision or wedge. Lung resection procedures include diagnostic and therapeutic procedures, including the removal of blebs, bullae, cysts, and benign or malignant tumors or lesions. These procedures may involve the removal of small portions of the lung or even an entire lung. Additionally, lung resection procedures may require the removal of adjacent structures. Both diagnostic lung biopsies and therapeutic lung resections can be performed utilizing a wedge technique. However, a diagnostic biopsy of a lung nodule using a wedge technique requires only that a tissue sample be obtained without particular attention to resection margins. A therapeutic wedge resection requires attention to margins and complete resection even when the wedge resection is ultimately followed by a more extensive resection. In the case of a wedge resection in which intraoperative pathology consultation determines that a more extensive resection is required in the same anatomic location, it becomes classified as a diagnostic wedge resection (32507, 32668). When no more extensive resection is required, the same procedure is a therapeutic wedge resection (32505, 32666). Pleural or lung biopsies or diagnostic wedge resections should be reported using codes 32096, 32097, 32098, 32400, 32408, 32507, 32607, 32608, 32609, or 32668. The open or thoracoscopic (VATS) therapeutic resection of lung mass or nodules via a wedge resection is reported using codes 32505, 32506, 32666, and 32667. More extensive anatomic lung resection procedures, which can be performed with either thoracotomy or thoracoscopic (VATS) approaches, include: segmentectomy, lobectomy, bilobectomy, and pneumonectomy. When diagnostic biopsy(ies) of the lung are performed, regardless of the approach (ie, open or thoracoscopic [VATS]) or technique (eg, incisional resection, cautery resection, or stapled wedge), and the specimen is sent for intraoperative pathology consultation, and during that same operative session the surgeon uses these results to determine the extent of the necessary surgical resection that includes the anatomical location biopsied, only the most extensive procedure performed (eg, segmentectomy, lobectomy, thoracoscopic [VATS] lobectomy) should be reported. The therapeutic wedge resection codes (32505, 32506, 32666, or 32667) should not be reported in addition to the more extensive lung procedure (eg, lobectomy) unless the therapeutic wedge resection was performed on a different lobe or on the contralateral lung, whether or not an intraoperative pathology consultation is used to determine the extent of lung resection. When a diagnostic wedge resection is followed by a more extensive procedure in the same anatomical location, report add-on codes 32507 or 32668 with the more extensive procedure(s). When a therapeutic wedge resection (32505, 32506, 32666, or 32667) is performed in a different lobe than the more extensive lung resection (eg, lobectomy), report the therapeutic wedge resection with modifier 59.

short_description: Thoracoscopy, surgical; with removal of clot or foreign body from pericardial sac
lay_term: This procedure involves visualizing the pericardial sac with an endoscope and removing a blood clot or foreign body. Explanation A patient may need to have this procedure due to trauma, which causes a clot to form in the pericardium, or has caused a foreign body to enter the pericardium. Clots may also form in the pericardium due to Infection, heart attack, or lung cancer. While the patient is under anesthesia, the provider incises the chest and inserts a trocar, or port, that holds instruments used during the procedure. The provider passes air through the trocar to partially collapse the lung to allow him to visualize the area to be treated. He then inserts either a flexible or rigid endoscope, with a video camera attached, into the trocar to view the pericardial sac. He removes the foreign body with an instrument inserted into another trocar. The provider then removes the trocars and endoscope and inserts a chest tube to drain the wound and re–expand the lung. Terminology Pericardial sac: Also called the pericardium, a sac that contains the heart and the roots of the great vessels, or the vessels that transport blood to and from the heart. Thoracoscopy: To visually examine the chest cavity by using an endoscope. Read Less

short_description: Thoracoscopy, surgical; with creation of pericardial window or partial resection of pericardial sac for drainage
lay_term: This procedure involves visualizing the pericardial sac with an endoscope, incising it, and creating a flap to drain the fluid. Explanation Infection, cancer, or other underlying disorders may cause fluid to build up in the pericardial sac, called pericardial effusion. The excess fluid may place pressure on the heart and cause it to function abnormally. While the patient is under anesthesia, the provider incises the chest and inserts a trocar, or port, that holds instruments used during the procedure. The provider passes air through the trocar to partially collapse the lung to allow him to visualize the area to be treated. He then inserts either a flexible or rigid endoscope, with a video camera attached, into the trocar to view the pericardial sac. The provider inserts an instrument into a trocar or through the endoscope. He then creates an opening, or flap, called a window, in the pericardial sac to drain the fluid. He incises, or resects, the pericardium. The provider then removes the trocars and endoscope and inserts a chest tube to drain the wound and re–expand the lung. Terminology Pericardial sac: Also called the pericardium, a sac that contains the heart and the roots of the great vessels, or the vessels that transport blood to and from the heart. short_description: Thoracoscopy, surgical; with lobectomy (single lobe) Notes: (For thoracoscopic [VATS] segmentectomy, use 32669)
lay_term: This procedure involves visualizing the chest cavity and the lobe of the lung to remove it. Explanation A patient may need to have a lobectomy, or removal of a lobe of the lung, to treat infections, tumors, or lung trauma. While the patient is under anesthesia, the provider incises the chest and inserts a trocar, or port, that holds instruments used during the procedure. The provider passes air through the trocar to partially collapse the lung to allow him to visualize the area to be treated. He then inserts either a flexible or rigid endoscope, with a video camera attached, into the trocar to view the chest cavity and the lobe of the lung to remove. He also inserts other operating instruments through additional trocars placed in the chest cavity to perform the excision. The provider uses these instruments to clamp, or secure, and then cut, bronchial tubes and blood vessels that are connected to the lobe. He then excises the lobe and sutures the area where the lobe was removed. The provider removes the trocars and endoscope and inserts a chest tube to drain the wound and re–expand the lung. Terminology Lobe: A lobe is a section of the lung. The right lung has three lobes, and the left lung has two lobes. Thoracoscopy: To visually examine the chest cavity by using an endoscope. Tips Report 32670 when the provider removes two lobes of the lung. Report 32671 when the provider removes the entire lung. Read Less

short_description: Thoracoscopy, surgical; with thoracic sympathectomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs thoracoscopy, using an endoscope to visually examine the pleura and lungs, to assist with destroying a portion of the sympathetic nerve trunk in the chest area. The provider may perform this procedure to treat hyperhydrosis, a condition characterized by excessive sweating. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates a small incision on the side of the chest between the ribs. She then, through one of the incisions, introduces an endoscope, a thin tube–like instrument containing a tiny camera. With the help of this camera, she examines the lungs and pleura. She compresses the lungs to have adequate visualization. She next identifies the sympathetic nerve trunk passing through the chest area. She then clips or cuts a portion of the nerve trunk that controls the target area, such as the portion that controls sweating. She then re–expands the lungs. Finally, she withdraws the endoscope and other instruments and closes the surgical wound. She may leave one or more tubes temporarily in the chest cavity to drain the fluid or air. Terminology Pleura: Membrane lining the chest cavity and enveloping the lungs. Thoracoscopy: Use of an endoscope to examine the lungs, the middle of the chest, and the membranes that line the lungs, which are called pleural layers.
