short_description: Repair lung hernia through chest wall
lay_term: The provider surgically repairs part of a lung that is pushing through a tear or weak spot in the chest wall, neck passageway, or diaphragm. Explanation The surgical team preps the patient. Once patient sedation takes effect, the provider begins the surgical repair of the hernia via anterolateral or posterolateral thoracotomy, an open incision into the chest wall. The provider makes an incision over the defect, and she dissects the tissue upward pulling back all the abdominal contents above the diaphragm. She returns the lung to its proper position by freeing incarcerated tissue, which may or may not require resection. With the lung in the thoracic cavity, the provider assesses the chest wall defect and repairs the defect with appropriate suturing over the weakened area of the chest. She adds reinforcement by placing a soft synthetic or autologous patch over the hernia defect and securing the patch in place. If needed, she brings additional tissue over to the defect to reinforce the site and support the closure. Finally, she places chest tubes as needed for air leak or bleeding. She then closes the surgical opening. Terminology Anterolateral: Situated in front and to one side. Autologous: Surgical placement of any tissue from one part of the body to another location in the same patient. Diaphragm: The dome–shaped, muscular partition separating the thorax from the abdomen. Incarcerated: An abnormal retention or confinement of a body part. Posterolateral: Situated behind and to one side. Resection: The surgical removal of part of an organ or structure. Thorax: Part of the body between the neck and the abdomen. Tips Lung hernias are classified by their anatomic location and the reason why they occur. There are two anatomic classifications: diaphragmatic or cervical intercostal. A cervical intercostal hernia involves a lung sticking trough the opening at the top of the rib cage. The reasons hernias occur include a rare congenital condition, disease, surgery, or trauma. Read Less

short_description: Open closure of major bronchial fistula
lay_term: The provider performs surgical closure of a fistula, which is a large abnormal passage or communicating tract between a bronchus and another body part such as the pleural surface of the lung or cutaneous surface of the thoracic wall. Explanation The surgical team preps and drapes the patient. Once the patient’s anesthesia takes effect, the provider exposes the fistula through an incision without disturbing the lung to chest wall relation. He dissects a strip from adjacent tissue and fashions it into a pedunculated flap leaving one end of the flap attached at a selected portion of its margin. He then inserts the free end of the flap into the bronchus to block the bronchus, and he sutures the sides to tissues in the adjacent area to prevent dislodgment. The area may require drainage tubes and/or packing prior to the final closure of the operative wound. Terminology Bronchopleural: The joining of a bronchial tube and the pleura. Bronchocutaneous: The joining of the bronchus, pleural space, and subcutaneous tissue. Bronchus: One of the two primary divisions of the trachea that provide the passageway for air into the lungs. Pedunculated flap: A simple or compound mass of tissue, muscle, periosteum, bone, or cartilage in the neighborhood of a defect, raised from its bed but left attached at a selected portion of the surrounding area. Periosteum: The dense layer of vascular connective tissue that envelops the bones. Pleura: The double–folded membrane surrounding each lung or the pulmonary cavity. Tips There are two types of bronchial fistula: bronchopleural and bronchocutaneous. This code applies to the closure of either type. Read Less

short_description: Major reconstruction, chest wall (posttraumatic)

short_description: Donor pneumonectomy(s) (including cold preservation), from cadaver donor
lay_term: The provider removes a lung or lungs from a deceased donor. This code also includes the cold preservation of the lung or lungs for transplantation. Explanation The retrieval team accesses the pleural cavity by performing a median sternotomy, but a clamshell or other suitable approach may be used. The provider assesses the lungs and then cools them to minimize cellular metabolism and function. short_description: Thoracoplasty, Schede type or extrapleural (all stages); with closure of bronchopleural fistula Notes: (For open closure of major bronchial fistula, use 32815) (For resection of first rib for thoracic outlet compression, see 21615, 21616)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs excision of the ribs to remove support around the lungs. This causes lateral collapse of the chest wall and pleural cavity in patients suffering from empyema, cavitary tuberculosis, or a bronchopleural fistula. In addition to rib excision, the provider also closes a bronchopleural fistula. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a chest incision, most commonly a posterolateral one. After gaining access, he excises ribs 2–8 subperiosteally to prevent the regeneration of ribs. In extrapleural thoracoplasty the provider excises only ribs and surrounding tissues; in Schede type thoracoplasty, with ribs and surrounding tissue, he also removes the tough, edematous outer layer of pleura. The provider also resects and sutures a bronchopleural fistula during the procedure. For fistula repair, he can also use a muscle graft taken from outside the chest cavity. After that he covers the treated fistula area with muscles and closes the area with sutures. Finally, he fills the chest cavity with gauze packing and sutures the skin loosely over it. The provider may perform removal of gauze packing in different stages, usually during an interval of a few weeks. This gives time to generate granulation tissue and replace the space previously taken by a pus collection. Terminology Bronchopleural fistula: A condition, also called BPF, involving an abnormal passageway between a bronchus and the pleural cavity, the space between the membranes surrounding the lungs; major causes of this condition are surgery on the lung and bronchus, chemotherapy or radiotherapy for cancers, and tuberculosis. Empyema: Accumulation of pus in the chest cavity. Extrapleural: Outside or around the pleural layer. Fistula: An abnormal passageway between two organs in the body or between an organ and the exterior of the body. Pleural space/cavity: The space between the two layers of membranes that cover the lungs; outer layer is called the parietal pleura and inner layer is called the visceral pleura. Subperiosteal: Situated or occurring beneath the outer tissue layer of the bone. Thoracoplasty: Surgical removal of part of the ribs to cause the collapse of a diseased lung. Read Less

lay_term: In this unilateral procedure, the provider uses a minimally invasive approach to introduce a wandlike needle (cryoprobe) into the chest cavity to destroy (ablate) tumor cells in the lung, pleura, or chest wall by freezing the tissue. Imaging guidance, if used, is included. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates a small incision in the chest wall between the ribs. Through this incision, she introduces a cryoprobe and approaches the tumor area. She may use imaging guidance to position the cryoprobe at the tumor. She may destroy one or more tumors on one side of the body. She then withdraws the cryoprobe and closes the skin incision using an adhesive dressing. short_description: Pericardial drainage with insertion of indwelling catheter, percutaneous, including fluoroscopy and/or ultrasound guidance, when performed; 6 years and older without congenital cardiac anomaly
lay_term: The provider uses a needle inserted through the chest wall to drain fluid from around the heart in a patient without congenital cardiac anomaly who is 6 years old or older; he also inserts a catheter and leaves it indwelling for continued drainage. Fluoroscopy and/or ultrasound guidance is included in this code when performed. Explanation This procedure is performed on a patient who is 6 years old or older and who does not have a congenital cardiac anomaly. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider selects a site typically between the xiphoid process and the left sternocostal margin. The provider may create a small incision to reduce needle resistance and then advances a needle attached to a syringe or suction device into the pericardial space. The provider often uses fluoroscopic or ultrasound imaging guidance to ensure accuracy of the needle placement. The provider identifies the proper location and then aspirates fluid from the pericardial sac into the syringe, after which he withdraws the needle. He then inserts a catheter through the same puncture site, which he leaves indwelling for further drainage in case the fluid builds up again. Pericardial drainage may be performed to relieve pericardial effusion or cardiac tamponade as well as for diagnostic, palliative, or prophylactic purposes. Terminology Anomaly: An organ or body part that is not normal structurally or functionally, is out of place, or is absent; typically describes a congenital deformity. Aspiration: Removal of fluid, gas, or other material through a tube attached to a suction device, often for laboratory analysis or combined with irrigation, the instillation of fluid to clean a wound or to wash out a cavity such as the abdomen, stomach, lungs, or joints; also, breathing in or sucking in food, fluid, or a foreign object into the airway. Cardiac tamponade: Accumulation of fluid within the pericardial sac so severe that it compresses the heart, preventing the ventricle from filling with blood and compromising heart function; it is a medical emergency and must be treated quickly. Computed tomography (CT): An imaging procedure in which an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors rotate around a patient and produce a tomogram, a computer–generated three–dimensional image of the inside of an object from a large series of two–dimensional X–ray images taken around a single axis of rotation; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Congenital: Describes a condition or defect existing from birth; congenital disorders may be inherited or due to other factors such as infection, injury, or environmental factors. Effusion: Accumulation or buildup of fluid within an enclosed space; for example, pericardial effusion is a buildup of fluid and/or blood within the pericardial sac, the membrane that surrounds the heart. Fluoroscopy: A live X–ray where the images appear on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Indwelling catheter or stent: A hollow tube left temporarily or permanently implanted in a body passage or organ, such as the bladder, to promote drainage, administer fluids or gases, provide access by surgical instruments, and other functions. Percutaneous procedure: A minimally invasive procedure performed through the skin. Pericardial sac: A sac that contains the heart and the roots of the great vessels (the vessels that transport blood to and from the heart); also known as the pericardium. Pericardial space: A space between the layers of the sac surrounding the heart. Sternocostal margin: The area where the rib (costal) cartilages meet the sternum (breast bone); also referred to as sternochondral joints or costosternal joints. Ultrasound: The use of high–frequency sound waves to view internal tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Xiphoid: Bony process (protuberance) found at the lowest portion of the sternum (breastbone). Tips Ultrasound or fluoroscopic imaging is included with this procedure, so do not report it separately. short_description: Pericardiectomy, subtotal or complete; with cardiopulmonary bypass
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider excises pericardium, the outer covering of the heart, completely or partially. He places the patient on cardiopulmonary bypass to take over the function of the heart and lungs during the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the sternum, dividing it, and enters into the chest cavity. He gains access to the pericardium, which is the outer most covering of the heart. The provider may excise the layer either completely or partially. During the procedure the provider uses a device called a cardiopulmonary bypass unit, which temporarily takes on the functions of heart and lung so that the heart and lungs are motionless while the provider performs the procedure. After the procedure, the provider restores the natural circulation of blood via the heart , wires the sternum to let it join naturally, and closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): Technique that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs and maintains the circulation of blood and the oxygen content of the body during surgery, giving the provider a motionless operative field; known as a heart–lung machine or pump; "on pump" means the provider performed CPB. Constrictive pericarditis: Long–term inflammation of the sac–like covering of the heart, the pericardium, with thickening, scarring, and muscle tightening. Pericardiectomy: The surgical removal of a portion or all of the pericardium, the outer most layer of the heart; performed in patients with constrictive pericarditis or with calcified pericardium. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline A pacemaker system with lead(s) includes a pulse generator containing electronics, a battery, and one or more leads. A lead consists of one or more electrodes, as well as conductor wires, insulation, and a fixation mechanism. Pulse generators are placed in a subcutaneous "pocket" created in either a subclavicular site or just above the abdominal muscles just below the ribcage. Leads may be inserted through a vein (transvenous) or they may be placed on the surface of the heart (epicardial). The epicardial location of leads requires a thoracotomy for insertion. A single chamber pacemaker system with lead includes a pulse generator and one electrode inserted in either the atrium or ventricle. A dual chamber pacemaker system with two leads includes a pulse generator and one lead inserted in the right atrium and one lead inserted in the right ventricle. In certain circumstances, an additional lead may be required to achieve pacing of the left ventricle (bi-ventricular pacing). In this event, transvenous (cardiac vein) placement of the lead should be separately reported using code 33224 or 33225. For body surface-activation mapping to optimize electrical synchrony of a biventricular pacing or biventricular pacing-defibrillator system at the time of implant, also report 0695T with the appropriate code (ie, 33224, 33225, 33226). Epicardial placement of the lead should be separately reported using 33202, 33203. A leadless cardiac pacemaker system includes a pulse generator with built-in battery and electrode for implantation in a cardiac chamber via a transvenous transcatheter approach. For implantation of a right ventricular leadless pacemaker system, use 33274. Insertion, replacement, or removal of a right ventricular leadless pacemaker system includes insertion of a catheter via transvenous access under fluoroscopic guidance into the right ventricle. For a complete dual-chamber leadless cardiac pacemaker system which is implanted in both the right ventricle and right atrium, or individual components of a dual-chamber leadless pacemaker system, see 0795T, 0796T, 0797T, 0798T, 0799T, 0800T, 0801T, 0802T, 0803T. Device evaluation at the time of leadless pacemaker insertion, replacement, or removal is included in 33274, 33275, 0795T, 0796T, 0797T, 0798T, 0799T, 0800T, 0801T, 0802T, 0803T, 0823T, 0824T, 0825T and is not separately reported. For subsequent leadless pacemaker device evaluation, see 93279, 93286, 93288, 93294, 93296, 0804T, 0826T. For a single-chamber leadless cardiac pacemaker implanted in the right atrium that is not a component of a dual-chamber leadless pacemaker system, see 0823T, 0824T, 0825T. Right heart catheterization (93451, 93453, 93456, 93457, 93460, 93461, 93593, 93594, 93596, 93597) may not be reported in conjunction with leadless pacemaker insertion and removal codes 33274, 33275, 0795T, 0796T, 0797T, 0798T, 0799T, 0800T, 0801T, 0802T, 0803T, 0823T, 0824T, 0825T, unless complete right heart catheterization is performed for an indication distinct from the leadless pacemaker procedure. Like a pacemaker system, an implantable defibrillator system includes a pulse generator and electrodes. Three general categories of implantable defibrillators exist: transvenous implantable pacing cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), subcutaneous implantable defibrillator (S-ICD), and substernal implantable cardioverter-defibrillator. Implantable pacing cardioverter-defibrillator devices use a combination of antitachycardia pacing, low-energy cardioversion or defibrillating shocks to treat ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. The subcutaneous implantable defibrillator uses a single subcutaneous electrode to treat ventricular tachyarrhythmias. The substernal implantable cardioverter-defibrillator uses at least one substernal electrode to perform defibrillation, cardioversion, and antitachycardia pacing. Subcutaneous implantable defibrillators differ from transvenous implantable pacing cardioverter-defibrillators in that subcutaneous defibrillators do not provide antitachycardia pacing or chronic pacing. Substernal implantable defibrillators differ from both subcutaneous and transvenous implantable pacing cardioverter-defibrillators in that they provide antitachycardia pacing, but not chronic pacing. Implantable defibrillator pulse generators may be implanted in a subcutaneous infraclavicular, axillary, or abdominal pocket. Removal of an implantable defibrillator pulse generator requires opening of the existing subcutaneous pocket and disconnection of the pulse generator from its electrode(s). A thoracotomy (or laparotomy in the case of abdominally placed pulse generators) is not required to remove the pulse generator. The electrodes (leads) of an implantable defibrillator system may be positioned within the atrial and/or ventricular chambers of the heart via the venous system (transvenously), or placed on the surface of the heart (epicardial), or positioned under the skin overlying the heart (subcutaneous). Electrode positioning on the epicardial surface of the heart requires a thoracotomy or thoracoscopic placement of the leads. Epicardial placement of electrode(s) may be separately reported using 33202, 33203. The electrode (lead) of a subcutaneous implantable defibrillator system is tunneled under the skin to the left parasternal margin. Subcutaneous placement of electrode may be reported using 33270 or 33271. The electrode (lead) of a substernal implantable defibrillator system is tunneled subcutaneously and placed into the substernal anterior mediastinum without entering the pericardial cavity and may be reported using 0571T, 0572T. In certain circumstances, an additional electrode may be required to achieve pacing of the left ventricle (bi-ventricular pacing). In this event, transvenous (cardiac vein) placement of the electrode may be separately reported using 33224 or 33225. Removal of a transvenous electrode(s) may first be attempted by transvenous extraction (33234, 33235, or 33244). However, if transvenous extraction is unsuccessful, a thoracotomy may be required to remove the electrodes (33238 or 33243). Use 33212, 33213, 33221, 33230, 33231, 33240 as appropriate, in addition to the thoracotomy or endoscopic epicardial lead placement codes (33202 or 33203) to report the insertion of the generator if done by the same physician during the same session. Removal of a subcutaneous implantable defibrillator electrode may be separately reported using 33272. For removal of a leadless pacemaker system without replacement, use 33275. For removal and replacement of a leadless pacemaker system during the same session, use 33274. When the "battery" of a pacemaker system with lead(s) or implantable defibrillator is changed, it is actually the pulse generator that is changed. Removal of only the pacemaker or implantable defibrillator pulse generator is reported with 33233 or 33241. If only a pulse generator is inserted or replaced without any right atrial and/or right ventricular lead(s) inserted or replaced, report the appropriate code for only pulse generator insertion or replacement based on the number of final existing lead(s) (33227, 33228, 33229 and 33262, 33263, 33264). Do not report removal of a pulse generator (33233 or 33241) separately for this service. Insertion of a new pulse generator, when existing lead(s) are already in place and when no prior pulse generator is removed, is reported with 33212, 33213, 33221, 33230, 33231, 33240. When a pulse generator insertion involves the insertion or replacement of one or more right atrial and/or right ventricular lead(s) or subcutaneous lead(s), use system codes 33206, 33207, 33208 for pacemaker, 33249 for implantable pacing cardioverter-defibrillator, or 33270 for subcutaneous implantable defibrillator. When reporting the system insertion or replacement codes, removal of a pulse generator (33233 or 33241) may be reported separately, when performed. In addition, extraction of leads 33234, 33235 or 33244 for transvenous or 33272 for subcutaneous may be reported separately, when performed. An exception involves a pacemaker upgrade from single to dual system that includes removal of pulse generator, replacement of new pulse generator, and insertion of new lead, reported with 33214. For insertion, removal, relocation, and repositioning of cardiac contractility modulation-defibrillation codes, see 0915T-0925T. Revision of a skin pocket is included in 33206-33249, 33262, 33263, 33264, 33270, 33271, 33272, 33273. When revision of a skin pocket involves incision and drainage of a hematoma or complex wound infection, see 10140, 10180, 11042, 11043, 11044, 11045, 11046, 11047, as appropriate. Relocation of a skin pocket for a pacemaker (33222) or implantable defibrillator (33223) is necessary for various clinical situations such as infection or erosion. Relocation of an existing pulse generator may be performed as a stand-alone procedure or at the time of a pulse generator or electrode insertion, replacement, or repositioning. When skin pocket relocation is performed as part of an explant of an existing generator followed by replacement with a new generator, the pocket relocation is reported separately. Skin pocket relocation includes all work associated with the initial pocket (eg, opening the pocket, incision and drainage of hematoma or abscess if performed, and any closure performed), in addition to the creation of a new pocket for the new generator to be placed. Repositioning of a pacemaker electrode, implantable defibrillator electrode(s), or a left ventricular pacing electrode is reported using 33215, 33226, or 33273, as appropriate. Device evaluation codes 93260, 93261, 93279-93298 for pacemaker system with lead(s) may not be reported in conjunction with pulse generator and lead insertion or revision codes 33206-33249, 33262, 33263, 33264, 33270, 33271, 33272, 33273. For leadless pacemaker systems, device evaluation codes 93279, 93286, 93288, 93294, 93296 may not be reported in conjunction with leadless pacemaker insertion and removal codes 33274, 33275. Defibrillator threshold testing (DFT) during transvenous implantable defibrillator insertion or replacement may be separately reported using 93640, 93641. DFT testing during subcutaneous implantable defibrillator system insertion is not separately reportable. DFT testing for transvenous or subcutaneous implantable defibrillator in follow-up or at the time of replacement may be separately reported using 93642 or 93644. Radiological supervision and interpretation related to the pacemaker or implantable defibrillator procedure is included in 33206-33249, 33262, 33263, 33264, 33270, 33271, 33272, 33273, 33274, 33275. Fluoroscopy (76000, 77002), ultrasound guidance for vascular access (76937), right ventriculography (93566), and femoral venography (75820) are included in 33274, 33275, when performed). To report fluoroscopic guidance for diagnostic lead evaluation without lead insertion, replacement, or revision procedures, use 76000. The following definitions apply to 33206-33249, 33262, 33263, 33264, 33270, 33271, 33272, 33273. Single lead: a pacemaker or implantable defibrillator with pacing and sensing function in only one chamber of the heart or a subcutaneous electrode. Dual lead: a pacemaker or implantable defibrillator with pacing and sensing function in only two chambers of the heart. Multiple lead: a pacemaker or implantable defibrillator with pacing and sensing function in three or more chambers of the heart. Section Specific Guideline Selective vascular catheterizations should be coded to include introduction and all lesser order selective catheterizations used in the approach (eg, the description for a selective right middle cerebral artery catheterization includes the introduction and placement catheterization of the right common and internal carotid arteries). Additional second and/or third order arterial catheterizations within the same family of arteries supplied by a single first order artery should be expressed by 36218 or 36248. Additional first order or higher catheterizations in vascular families supplied by a first order vessel different from a previously selected and coded family should be separately coded using the conventions described above. short_description: Insertion of pacemaker pulse generator only; with existing single lead
lay_term: The provider places a new pacemaker pulse generator in the patient in a subcutaneous pocket in front of the chest. The provider performs this procedure primarily for artificial regulation of heart beats by the device in patients with arrhythmia, which is irregular heart rhythm. He performs this procedure for a patient with a lead in a single chamber of the heart. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision on the skin in the subclavicular region, which is the skin below the collarbone, extending to the subpectoral region, which is the skin in the front of the chest near the armpit. He then creates a subcutaneous pocket for lodging the device in the pectoralis fascia, which is the sheath covering the muscle in front of the chest, or just below the pectoral muscle. He then frees the end of the existing lead from the fibrous adhesions surrounding it, taking care to protect the lead from any damage. He cleans the pocket by irrigating it with saline. He then places the new generator for a single lead system into the pocket. He tests the existing lead for proper functionality and attaches it to the new pulse generator. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the skin pocket with sutures. He may alternatively use staples or tissue adhesive for the closure. The provider programs the device for functionality. Terminology Lead: Insulated wires that conduct electrical impulse from one end, attached to the pulse generator, to the other end positioned in the heart chamber. Pacemaker: A device that continuously senses, monitors, and regulates the heart rate. Pulse generator: A device that produces electrical signals that can make the heart beat. Subcutaneous: Just underneath the skin. Tips Use this code for insertion of new battery only, with an already existing single lead. Code 33212 includes radiological supervision and interpretation related to the procedure as well. Read Less

short_description: Repositioning of previously implanted transvenous pacemaker or implantable defibrillator (right atrial or right ventricular) electrode
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repositions an electrode that is already in place within the right atrium or right ventricle of a patient’s heart. This procedure is done for a pacemaker implant or implantable defibrillator that is not functioning properly due to improper electrode placement or lead dislodgement. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the previously created pocket for the cardiac device generator. He then removes the pulse generator and tests that the generator and electrode are functioning correctly. When he determines there is no defect in the equipment, he replaces the generator, reattaches the electrode to the generator, and places the electrode in a new, corrected position. He then tests the device again to ensure it is functioning correctly. Finally, he places the generator back into its previous position and closes the cardiac device pocket. Terminology Atrium: One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Defibrillator: A small battery powered impulse generator that monitors and controls an abnormal heart rhythm. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; also referred to as a lead. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Pacemaker: A small device that the provider places just under the skin of the patient’s chest to control abnormal heart rhythm. Pacemaker electrodes: A device consisting of a flexible insulated electrical conductor with one end connected to an external pulse generator and other end to the heart. Transvenous: Through the vein. Veins: Vessels that carry oxygen poor blood from the body to the heart. Ventricle: One of the two lower chambers of the heart; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood throughout the body; the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider inserts a single electrode transvenously, or through a vein, and connects it to a permanent pacemaker or implantable defibrillator already in place. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider disconnects and repairs two electrodes from an impulse generator, like a pacemaker or an implanted cardiac defibrillator, and then reattaches the electrodes to the generator. He performs this service for a pacemaker implant or implantable defibrillator that is not functioning properly due to a problem with the electrode. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the existing cardiac device pocket. He then removes the pulse generator to gain access to the electrodes. lay_term: In a patient with an existing pacemaker pocket, the physician creates a new pocket in a different location and relocates the pacer Explanation The sites of the existing and planned pockets are prepped. The patient may be sedated and local anesthesia administered. ECG, blood pressure, and pulse oximetry are monitored. The physician cuts any scar tissue away from the pacer and leads. He tests the leads, and inspects the site and pacer. The physician makes an incision in the subcutaneous tissue, such as in the upper abdominal wall, to create a new pocket for the pacer. Additional anesthesia may be administered to allow the physician to place lead extenders to the new pocket. The leads and pacer are connected and placed in the new pocket, which is closed. The old pocket is addressed to prevent infection and ensure healing. Tips Reasons for skin pocket revision and relocation include erosion or the pocket being too small. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider creates a new pocket in a different location and relocates the defibrillator device pocket in a patient with an existing implantable defibrillator. The provider performs this procedure as a result of a complication such as an infection or erosion at the original site. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the scar over the location of the original impulse generator placement. He then removes any scar tissue he finds away from the device and leads, and inspects the site. He chooses an alternate location for implantation of the implantable defibrillator and makes an incision in the subcutaneous tissue, just under the skin to create a new pocket for the device. He disconnects the leads from the device, and passes the electrodes to the new pocket, creating a new subcutaneous tunnel as necessary. He then places the device in the new pocket, attaches the electrodes, and tests the device. He then closes the pocket by suturing. Next, he addresses the old pocket to prevent infection and ensure healing. When the procedure is complete, he closes the wound in layers. Terminology Defibrillator: A small battery powered impulse generator that monitors and controls an abnormal heart rhythm. Erosion: The gradual destruction or wearing a way of an area of tissue due to pressure, friction, ulceration, or trauma. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Infection: A disease condition that bacteria, viruses, or other microorganisms cause. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider introduces an additional pacing electrode for left ventricular pacing through a vein and advances it to the left ventricle. He attaches the electrode to an existing pacemaker or implantable defibrillator. He may also revise, remove and insert, or replace the existing impulse generator. The provider performs this procedure in patients with a high risk of heart failure who need biventricular pacing to help keep the heart beat in balance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider introduces a pacing electrode lead through a vein, usually the internal jugular or subclavian vein, and advances it under fluoroscopic guidance to the left ventricle. He ensures that the pacing electrode is in the correct position over the left ventricle. Next, the provider may open the existing cardiac device pocket, remove the generator in place, and revise the skin pocket as necessary. He may then place a new generator, or use the existing unit and attach the left ventricular lead to the generator. Finally, he closes the cardiac device pocket. Terminology Biventricular pacing: Contraction of both the ventricles in synchronization and together that improves the symptoms of heart failure. Cardiac venous system: Consists of cardiac veins which are grouped into; coronary sinus and its branches, the anterior cardiac veins and the thebesian veins. Defibrillator: A small battery powered impulse generator that monitors and controls an abnormal heart rhythm. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Internal jugular vein: Deeper of the two jugular veins in the neck that drains the blood from brain, face, and neck to the heart. Left Ventricle: Left of the two lower chambers of the heart. Pacemaker: A small device that the provider places just under the skin of a patient’s chest to control an abnormal heart rhythm. Pacemaker electrodes: A device consisting of a flexible insulated electrical conductor with one end connected to an external pulse generator and other end to the heart. Subclavian vein: One of the two veins on either side of the body that drains blood from the arm to the heart. Thesbesian vein: The smallest cardiac veins consisting of valveless veins in the walls of all four chambers of the heart that drain directly into the heart chambers. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repositions the electrode already in place in the left ventricular chamber of the heart. He also revises the skin pocket and removes, inserts, and or replaces the existing generator. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the cardiac device skin pocket. He removes the pulse generator and tests the electrodes for their pacing function. Next, he revises the cardiac device skin pocket as necessary. Using fluoroscopic guidance, he then gains transvenous access through the subclavian or internal jugular vein and repositions the electrode into a different position in the left ventricle, and retests the electrode functioning. Finally, he reconnects the electrode to a new or the existing generator, places the generator into the pocket, and closes the cardiac device pocket. Terminology Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Internal jugular vein: Deeper of the two jugular veins in the neck that drains the blood from brain, face, and neck to the heart. Left Ventricle: Left of the two lower chambers of the heart. Pacemaker: A small device that the provider places just under the skin of patient’s chest to control abnormal heart rhythm. Pacemaker electrodes: A device consisting of flexible insulated electrical conductor with one end connected to an external pulse generator and other end to the heart. Subclavian vein: One of the two veins on either side of the body that drains blood from the arm to the heart. Read Less

short_description: Insertion of implantable defibrillator pulse generator only; with existing dual leads
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider places a new implantable defibrillator pulse generator in a subcutaneous pocket in the front of a patient’s chest. The provider performs this procedure for a patient with a lead in two chambers of the heart. This service is primarily done for artificial regulation of a patient’s heart rate by the device in patients with arrhythmia, which is an irregular heart rhythm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises an existing pocket in the patient’s skin, or he makes an incision on the skin in the subclavicular region, which is the skin below the collarbone. He extends the incision to the subpectoral region, which is the skin in the front of the chest near the armpit. He then creates a subcutaneous pocket for the device in the pectoralis fascia, or the sheath covering the muscle in the front of the chest, or just below the pectoral muscle. Next, he frees the existing leads from the fibrous adhesions surrounding them, taking care to protect the leads from any damage. He cleans the pocket by irrigating it with saline. He then places the new generator for the dual lead system into the pocket. He tests the existing leads for proper functionality and attaches the leads to the new pulse generator. After achieving hemostasis, or the stoppage of bleeding, he closes the skin pocket with sutures. He may alternatively use staples or tissue adhesive for the closure. Finally, the provider programs the device for functionality. Terminology Atrium: One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Defibrillator: A small battery powered impulse generator that monitors and controls an abnormal heart rhythm. Dual lead: A device that attaches to a pulse generator and can transmit and receive electrical impulses; in a dual lead, the pacing and sensing function are in two chambers of the heart, usually one in the right atrium and one in the right ventricle; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes, or reference may be to an electrode at the end of a lead. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Irrigation: A flushing or washout procedure. Pulse generator: A device that produces electrical signals that can make the heart beat. Subcutaneous: Just underneath the skin. Ventricle: One of the two lower chambers of the heart; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood throughout the body; the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Tips When the provider places a new defibrillator pulse generator with existing multiple leads having the pacing and sensing function in three or more chambers of the heart, use 33231, Insertion of implantable defibrillator pulse generator only; with existing multiple leads. When the provider places a new defibrillator pulse generator with an existing single lead in one of the chambers of the heart, use 33240, Insertion of implantable defibrillator pulse generator only; with existing single lead. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider places a new implantable defibrillator pulse generator in a patient in a subcutaneous pocket in the front of a patient’s chest. The provider performs this procedure for a patient with a lead in at least three chambers of the heart. This service is primarily done for artificial regulation of a patient’s heart rate by the device in patients with arrhythmia, which is an irregular heart rhythm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises an existing pocket in the patient’s skin, or he makes an incision on the skin in the subclavicular region, which is the skin below the collarbone. He extends the incision to the subpectoral region, which is the skin in the front of the chest near the armpit. He then creates a subcutaneous pocket for the device in the pectoralis fascia, or the sheath covering the muscle in front of the chest, or just below the pectoral muscle. Next, he frees the existing leads from the fibrous adhesions surrounding them, taking care to protect the leads from any damage. He cleans the pocket by irrigating it with saline. He then places the new generator for the multiple lead device into the pocket. He tests the existing leads for proper functionality and attaches the multiple leads to the new pulse generator. After achieving hemostasis, or the stoppage of bleeding, he closes the skin pocket with sutures. He may alternatively use staples or tissue adhesive for the closure. Finally, the provider programs the device for functionality. Terminology Defibrillator: A small battery powered impulse generator that monitors and controls an abnormal heart rhythm. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Irrigation: A flushing or washout procedure. Multiple leads: A device that attaches to a pulse generator and can transmit and receive electrical impulses; in a multiple lead, the pacing and sensing function are in three or more chambers of the heart; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes, or reference may be to an electrode at the end of a lead. Pulse generator: A device that produces electrical signals that can make the heart beat. Subcutaneous: Just underneath the skin. Tips When the provider places a new defibrillator pulse generator with existing dual leads having the pacing and sensing function in two chambers of the heart, use 33230, Insertion of implantable defibrillator pulse generator only; with existing dual leads. When the provider places a new defibrillator pulse generator with an existing single lead in one of the chambers of the heart, use 33240, Insertion of implantable defibrillator pulse generator only; with existing single lead. short_description: Removal of permanent transvenous electrode(s) by thoracotomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a thoracotomy, to open the chest wall and remove the permanent transvenous electrode from the heart surface. This procedure usually occurs after the removal of the generator and the cutting only of the leads in a prior procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest wall and exposes a small area of the heart where the electrodes attach to the heart. He then removes the scar tissue surrounding the lead and electrode attachment to the surface of the heart. Next, he may place a tourniquet above and below the vein where the lead attaches. He then separates the electrode from the heart and repairs the defect that occurs from removal of the electrode. Finally, he stops all bleeding at the surgical site and closes the chest wall wound by suturing the tissues in layers. Terminology Pacemaker electrodes: A device consisting of a flexible insulated electrical conductor with one end connected to an external pulse generator and the other end to the heart. Thoracotomy: Incision into the chest wall. Transvenous: Through the vein. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider places a new implantable defibrillator pulse generator in a patient in a subcutaneous pocket in the front of the patient’s chest. The provider performs this procedure for a patient with a lead in one chamber of the heart. The service is primarily done for artificial regulation of a patient’s heart rate by the device in patients with arrhythmia, which is an irregular heart rhythm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises an existing pocket in the patient’s skin, or he makes an incision on the skin in the subclavicular region, which is the skin below the collarbone. He extends the incision to the subpectoral region, which is the skin in the front of the chest near the armpit. He then creates a subcutaneous pocket for the device in the pectoralis fascia, or the sheath covering the muscle in front of the chest, or just below the pectoral muscle. Next, he frees the existing lead from the fibrous adhesions surrounding it, taking care to protect the lead from any damage. He cleans the pocket by irrigating it with saline. He then places the new generator for the single lead device into the pocket. He tests the existing lead for proper functionality and attaches the lead to the new pulse generator. After achieving hemostasis, or stoppage of bleeding, he closes the skin pocket with sutures. He may alternatively use staples or tissue adhesive for the closure. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Irrigation: A flushing or washout procedure. lay_term: The provider opens the surgically created pocket in the chest wall and removes an implantable defibrillator pulse generator. Defibrillators sense and regulate the heart rate by delivering a mild electric shock when the patient requires it. Components need to be removed when they no longer function properly or when an infection occurs. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the scar over the cardiac device pocket and opens the pocket. She then frees the leads from the fibrous tissue and disconnects them from the generator. Next, she removes the pulse generator and leaves the leads in place in the pocket. Finally, she closes the pocket and skin with sutures. Terminology Defibrillator: A device that continuously senses, monitors, and regulates the heart rate; it can deliver a mild electrical shock to regulate an abnormal rhythm when needed or restart the heart if it stops beating; the device consists of electrodes or leads placed on or in the heart that do the sensing and a pulse generator that delivers the shock; defibrillators can be implanted or placed within a surgically created pocket in the chest or abdomen or worn externally on the chest or in a clothes pocket. Dual chamber leads: Insulated wires that can transmit and receive electrical impulses attached to a pulse generator; in a dual lead system, the provider places leads on or in two chambers of the heart, usually one in the right atrium and one in the right ventricle; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Single chamber implantable electrode: Insulated wires that can transmit and receive electrical impulses attached to a pulse generator; in single lead system, the provider places a lead in or on a single chamber of the heart, either the atrium or ventricle. Tips When the provider removes and replaces an implantable defibrillator pulse generator with single lead system, use 33262, Removal of implantable defibrillator pulse generator with replacement of implantable defibrillator pulse generator; single lead system. When the provider removes and replaces an implantable defibrillator pulse generator with dual lead system, use 33264, Removal of implantable defibrillator pulse generator with replacement of implantable defibrillator pulse generator; multiple lead system. short_description: Removal of single or dual chamber implantable defibrillator electrode(s); by thoracotomy
lay_term: The provider performs a thoracotomy, an incision in the chest wall, and opens the chest cavity to remove a single or dual chamber implantable defibrillator electrode. Defibrillators sense and regulate the heart rate by delivering a mild electric shock when the patient requires it. Components need to be removed when they no longer function properly or when an infection occurs. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the scar over the cardiac device pocket and opens the pocket. He then frees the lead or leads from the fibrous tissue and disconnects them from the generator. Next, he incises the chest wall and exposes the heart where the electrodes attach to the heart. He then removes the scar tissue surrounding the lead and electrode. He separates the electrode from the heart and repairs the defect that occurs from removal of the electrode. short_description: Removal of single or dual chamber implantable defibrillator electrode(s); by transvenous extraction

Components need to be removed when they no longer function properly or when an infection occurs. When she frees the lead from the scar tissue, she twists the lead counterclockwise and gently pulls on it. She then withdraws the lead through the vein by inserting a sheath and wire through the femoral or internal jugular vein and threading it to the lead. lay_term: The provider either replaces or implants a new permanent defibrillator system with single or dual chamber transvenous leads or electrodes. Defibrillators sense and regulate the heart rate by delivering a mild electric shock when the patient requires it. Components need to be removed when they no longer function properly or when an infection occurs. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates an incision at the selected site. If a previously implanted defibrillator system is present, he opens the pocket and disconnects the leads so that he may replace the generator. If he is not replacing a defibrillator, he places a generator in a newly created pocket. He then threads a catheter through a vein. He may use fluoroscopy to guide the electrode catheter to the appropriate chambers of the heart. Next, he inserts the leads through the catheter and places the electrode leads in the desired heart chambers. For a single chamber system, he places a lead in the right ventricle. For a dual chamber system, he places a lead in the right ventricle and atrium. Once the leads are placed in the chambers of the heart, he attaches the leads to the pulse generator in the prepared pocket, and evaluates the function of the system. Finally, he checks for bleeding, removes all instruments, and closes the incision in the chest. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider inserts or replaces a permanent subcutaneous implantable cardioverter defibrillator system. When necessary, he evaluates the device functionality by performing a defibrillation threshold evaluation, induction of arrhythmia, evaluation of sensing for arrhythmia termination, and he programs or reprograms the sensing or therapeutic parameters as the patient requires. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider marks anatomical landmarks for incisions. The provider makes an initial incision to create a device pocket, typically in the left upper thorax near the fifth and sixth intercostal space. He makes an incision near the lower part of the sternum, or breastbone, to assist with electrode placement. He threads the electrode subcutaneously from the device pocket through to the sternal incision. Next, he makes an incision higher up on the sternum and threads the electrode up to this incision. The provider then connects the device to the electrode, and performs an intraoperative interrogation. He then places the device in the pocket. The provider may also perform a defibrillation threshold evaluation, he may induce arrhythmia, to evaluate the device sensing for arrhythmia termination, and he may program or reprogram the sensing or therapeutic parameters of the system. Finally, the provider closes the incisions. Removal of a previously placed pulse generator and electrode may be separately reported. Terminology Arrhythmia: An abnormal beating of the heart with an irregular or abnormal rhythm. Defibrillator system: Defibrillator system consists of a device that delivers a therapeutic dose of electrical energy to the heart; it is commonly given in patients to treat life threatening cardiac diseases. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses. Intercostal space: The space between two ribs. Interrogation: Assessment or examination. Intraoperative: Occurring during a surgical procedure. Thorax: Chest. Read Less

lay_term: The provider removes a permanent leadless pacemaker (LP) from the right ventricle via a steerable catheter placed through the femoral vein. This code includes imaging guidance and testing/programming of the leadless pacemaker when performed, so those services cannot be reported separately. Explanation A leadless pacemaker is a cylindrical device usually implanted in the endocardium (inner wall) of a ventricle that can both sense heart rate and rhythm and stimulate contractions; it consists of a generator with a built–in battery and electrode inserted via a catheter with no wires to connect it to a monitor but communicates via magnetic, ultrasound, or electrical waves for device evaluation and programming. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized or sedated in the catheterization lab, the provider punctures the skin over the femoral vein. The provider selects an appropriate retrieval catheter depending on the type of leadless pacemaker being removed. For an LP with a helix (coil) affixing it to the endocardium, he chooses a dedicated steerable retrieval catheter manufactured to remove the LP. He inserts it into the femoral vein through an 18F sheath. The retrieval catheter, which has a single– or triple–loop snare at its end and an integrated protective sleeve, is advanced under imaging guidance to the vena cava and then right ventricle. The provider positions it near the LP, retracts the protective sleeve, and engages or captures the cap of the LP with the snare. He closes the snare over the proximal docking feature of the LP after which he turns it counter–clockwise for two full rotations to disengage the LP from the endocardium. He advances the protective sleeve over the entire device and withdraws it from the body. For a different type of LP with tines affixing it to the endocardium, he selects an appropriately sized nondedicated steerable catheter through which he inserts a gooseneck snare. He uses the snare to engage a retrieval feature at the proximal end of the LP device, applies counter–traction, and removes the device. After removal of the device, he applies pressure over the femoral vein to control bleeding. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that a provider inserts into a vessel through which he can pass instruments, blood can be withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a provider can insert this flexible tube into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Endocardium: The inner lining of the chambers of the heart. Femoral vein: Large vein in the upper thighs and groin area that returns blood to the inferior vena cava from the leg and pelvic region. Imaging guidance: Use of fluoroscopy (a live, real–time, X–ray where the image appears on a television monitor), ultrasound (high–frequency sound waves), or other forms of imaging to view tissues during surgical procedures. Pacemaker interrogation: The analysis of pacemaker function by placing a sensing device (such as a wand) on the chest over the device; the wand senses data stored in the device (such as battery life, lead function, and when and how often the pacemaker has stimulated the heart) and sends that data to a computer for analysis by the provider; the provider can also reprogram the pacemaker with the device. Venography: Radiographic imaging of veins following the administration of a radiopaque substance; also known as phlebography; providers perform the X–ray to diagnose deep vein thrombosis, a condition causing blood to move slowly due to blood clots in the vessel, and to assess if veins are functioning properly. Ventricles: Lower chambers of the heart that receive blood from a corresponding upper chamber atrium and from which blood is forced into the arteries. Ventriculography: Placement of a catheter into the lower heart chamber (left ventricle) and injection of contrast medium to visualize the left ventricle and its contractions. Tips For transcatheter insertion or replacement of a permanent leadless pacemaker, right ventricular, including imaging guidance (e.g., fluoroscopy, venous ultrasound, ventriculography, femoral venography) and device evaluation (e.g., interrogation or programming), when performed, see 33274. lay_term: The provider permanently implants a wireless sensor into the pulmonary artery (PA) during catheterization to monitor pulmonary artery pressures and calibrates the sensor; this code covers both right heart and pulmonary artery catheterization and pulmonary arteriography with radiological supervision and interpretation (RS&I) when performed. Explanation With the patient appropriate prepped and anesthetized or sedated and after cleaning the skin with an antiseptic solution, the provider makes a small incision in the femoral vein and inserts an introducer sheath over a flexible guidewire under fluoroscopic guidance. Through the sheath, she passes a balloon–tipped pulmonary artery catheter with the balloon inflated through the chambers of the heart and across the valve until it reaches a wedge position in the left or right pulmonary artery in the lower lobe of either lung. She measures the pulmonary artery and pulmonary wedge pressures and may measure cardiac output. At this point she performs a pulmonary artery angiogram to identify the target implant site. With the balloon inflated, she injects contrast material through the distal lumen of the pulmonary artery catheter. She identifies the target site in the pulmonary artery, which is in the lower lobe of either lung and directed distally (downward) and posteriorly (toward the back). She measures the diameter and angulation of the area of the vessel where the body of the sensor will be placed and diameter of the vessel where the distal loop of the sensor will be positioned, making sure the target site meets manufacturer’s specifications. She inserts the sensor delivery guidewire through the PA catheter and across the target site for the implant, after which she withdraws and removes the PA catheter, keeping the guidewire in place. She flushes the guidewire lumen (interior channel) with saline and swirls the distal end of the sensor delivery catheter in saline to activate the hydrophilic coating. She guides the delivery catheter through the sheath over the guidewire and into position at the implant target site. She releases the sensor and slowly removes the delivery catheter under fluoroscopic guidance while maintaining the guidewire and sensor positions. She reinserts the PA catheter over the guidewire and carefully removes the guidewire through the PA catheter, maintaining the sensor position. She positions the PA catheter tip proximal to the sensor or in the opposite lung and measures the PA pressure. After placing the provided antenna that comes with the sensor under the patient’s back, centered under the sensor position, she acquires the sensor signal. Using both the PA catheter pressure display and the sensor display, she programs the mean PA pressure and cardiac output baselines and takes baseline readings. She removes the antenna from under the patient’s back and removes the PA catheter and introducer sheath. She closes the incision and applies pressure for a few minutes to prevent bleeding. The wireless pulmonary artery pressure sensor provides long–term monitoring capability of the heart’s pumping capacity, heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressures, and other heart functions to monitor whether the patient is developing worsening congestive heart failure. Cardiac catheterization: The insertion of a catheter (tube) into a major vessel in the groin or another location with advancement to the heart to perform diagnostic tests, such as dye studies and therapeutic procedures. Femoral vein: Large vein in the upper thighs and groin area that returns blood to the inferior vena cava from the leg and pelvic region. Fluoroscopy: A live X–ray where the images appear on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Hemodynamic monitoring: Measurement of blood flow, blood pressure, and oxygen via insertion of a catheter tipped with a monitoring device into a vein, a ventricle of the heart, or an artery. short_description: Suture repair of aorta or great vessels; with shunt bypass
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses sutures to repair the great vessels of the heart, or the large vessels that bring blood to and from the heart, including the aorta, the pulmonary arteries and veins, or the vena cava. The provider uses a shunt bypass to perform this procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision, such as a sternotomy or thoracotomy to access the area of the aorta or other great vessels requiring repair. Next, he inserts a shunt to bypass the portion of the aorta being worked on. He may clamp the vessel and use sutures to repair the injury that results from a penetrating chest wound. He then removes the shunt before closing the incision site. Then the provider closes the wound, and may leave a chest or drainage tube in place. Finally, he applies a sterile dressing. Terminology Aorta: The largest artery in the body responsible for carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle of the heart to the entire body except the lungs. Cardiopulmonary bypass, or CPB: Technique used during surgery that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs to maintain the circulation of blood and the oxygen content of the body; it allows the patient's blood to bypass the heart and lungs, and gives the provider a still operative field; a pump, oxygenator, cannula, and tubing together are often called a heart lung machine or pump; the use of CPB may be called on bypass or on the pump. Shunt: A small hollow tube that allows movement of fluid from one part of the body to another. Sternotomy: An incision in the sternum, or breastbone. Thoracotomy: Surgical incision of the chest wall to expose organs such as the heart, lungs, esophagus or food pipe, or anterior spine, to diagnose a condition, disease or injury. Vena cava: The large vein that carries deoxygenated blood into the heart; the superior vena cava carries blood from the upper parts of the body, and the inferior vena cava carries blood from the lower parts of the body; these two empty into the right atrium of the heart. Tips You may see documentation of aortorrhaphy, which is suture of the aorta. lay_term: The provider implants a device that he delivers through a catheter placed through the skin under fluoroscopic guidance and across the septum to close off the left atrial appendage, uses angiography to visualize and define the left atrium (upper chamber of the heart) and appendage if necessary, and interprets the angiography if performed. Explanation The patient is appropriately prepped, which includes antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent postoperative infection, and placed under general anesthesia. He incises the skin over the femoral vein and introduces a catheter into the vein to obtain vascular access. He threads the catheter up through the vein and into the heart using fluoroscopic guidance. He uses a standard transseptal needle and sheath to pierce the septum (the wall between the chambers of the heart) to introduce the delivery system and access the left atrial appendage (LAA), a small ear–shaped sac in the wall of the atrium where blood can collect and clots form when the patient's heart does not contract properly. He may administer a large dose (bolus) of heparin to help prevent clots during the procedure. He may also use contrast angiography to visualize the left atrium and measure LAA dimensions (opening, width of neck, and depth), which he uses to choose the size of the implant device. There are several devices that he can choose to use; two are the Watchman® and Amplatzer™ cardiac plug (ACP) devices. Exact technique varies with the different devices, but the basic steps are the same. He again uses fluoroscopy to position the device properly in the LAA cavity. He withdraws the sheath over the device and deploys the device in position. He performs a ‘tug test’ to confirm stability and verifies seating of the device. He releases the device from the delivery cable and rules out possible complications, such as bleeding, clot, and pericardial effusion. Upon completion of the procedure, the provider withdraws the catheter and closes the incision. Terminology Angiography: A medical imaging technique in which the provider injects a dye into blood vessels and uses plain X–rays, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging to visualize the inside, or lumen, of the vessels; more specific terms include arteriography when performed on the arteries or venography when performed on the veins; angiography can also be used to study blood supply to organs such as the heart, kidneys, and liver. Endocardial: Within the heart. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Pericardial effusion: An abnormal collection of fluid in the lining (pericardium) around the heart. Tips This code includes imaging and supervision and interpretation when performed, so the coder should typically not separately code for the radiology service. Refer to CPT® and payer–specific guidelines to review requirements. In addition, heart catheterization is included in this procedure unless performed for distinctly different indications than the left atrial appendage closure. Check with payer to ascertain their policies. Read Less

short_description: Repair of non-structural prosthetic valve dysfunction with cardiopulmonary bypass (separate procedure) Notes: (For reoperation, use 33530 in addition to 33496)
lay_term: With the patient on cardiopulmonary bypass, the provider repairs a dysfunctional or leaking prosthetic valve that is not working properly due to overgrowth of vascular structures or exudate. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision into the area of the previous sternotomy, typically excising the scar. He initiates cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). He visualizes the area requiring repair, generally by making an incision in the aorta to access the valve. He performs the necessary repair by removing clots, thrombus, or exudate or by inserting new sutures to treat leaks. He closes the incision in the aorta and takes the patient off CPB. The provider then removes any instruments, checks for bleeding, and closes the chest incision. Terminology Aorta: The main artery that comes out of the top of the left ventricle of the heart and carries oxygenated blood to the body; it consists of an ascending and descending aorta which serve the upper and lower parts of the body respectively. Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): Technique that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs and maintains the circulation of blood and the oxygen content of the body during surgery, giving the provider a motionless operative field; known as a heart–lung machine or pump; on pump means the provider performed CPB. Dysfunction: Impairment; inability to function as designed. Exudate: Cellular material that leaks out of blood vessels and gets deposited in tissue, typically a result of inflammation. Nonstructural prosthetic valve dysfunction: Functional impairment of a prosthetic, or artificial, valve due to causes unrelated to the actual prosthesis, such as thrombus, blood clot, pannus, or anatomical changes in the area of the valve. Pannus: Overgrowth of vascular structures or cellular debris, i.e., exudate, deposited in tissues in reaction to inflammation, a response to injury or destruction of tissue often accompanied by increased blood flow. Prosthesis (pl. prostheses): An artificial or man–made replacement for a body part; also known as a prosthetic or prosthetic device. Sternotomy: Cutting into the bone plate in the middle front of the chest to which the ribs are attached by cartilage. Thrombus: A blood clot. Valve: A structure in an organ that can open and close to control the passage of fluid, blood, or other materials; the heart has four valves, the mitral, aortic, pulmonary, and tricuspid. short_description: Repair of coronary arteriovenous or arteriocardiac chamber fistula; with cardiopulmonary bypass
lay_term: With the patient on cardiopulmonary bypass, the provider closes a fistula, either from outside the heart or from inside a cardiac chamber. He performs this procedure to close off the abnormal passageway that allows blood to flow where it should not. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider opens the chest, typically by median sternotomy. He opens the pericardium and inspects the coronary anatomy. He establishes cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). The technique depends on the fistula location. The provider may use pledgeted sutures on the vessels outside of the heart or may create an incision into the heart to close a fistula from within the chamber in which it terminates. He then closes off the fistula and repairs the incision in the chamber. He takes the patient off CPB. The provider then removes any instruments, checks for bleeding, and closes the incision in the chest. short_description: Repair of anomalous coronary artery from pulmonary artery origin; by ligation

He incises the pericardium and examines the anatomy of the heart. If an anomalous left coronary artery arising from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA) is present, he performs simple ligation of the coronary artery close to its origin from the pulmonary artery. short_description: Repair of anomalous coronary artery from pulmonary artery origin; with construction of intrapulmonary artery tunnel (Takeuchi procedure)
lay_term: The provider creates a tunnel inside the pulmonary artery to access the opening of the anomalous coronary artery. He then anastomoses, or joins, the coronary artery to the aorta. He then closes or patches the pulmonary artery with tissue from the pericardium or with a polytetrafluoroethylene (PTF), graft. To report combined arterial-venous grafts it is necessary to report two codes: (1) the appropriate combined arterial-venous graft code (33517-33523); and (2) the appropriate arterial graft code (33533-33536). Procurement of the saphenous vein graft is included in the description of the work for 33517-33523 and should not be reported as a separate service or co-surgery. Procurement of the artery for grafting is included in the description of the work for 33533-33536 and should not be reported as a separate service or co-surgery, except when an upper extremity artery (eg, radial artery) is procured. To report harvesting of an upper extremity artery, use 33509 or 35600. To report harvesting of an upper extremity vein, use 35500 in addition to the bypass procedure. To report harvesting of a femoropopliteal vein segment, report 35572 in addition to the bypass procedure. When surgical assistant performs arterial and/or venous graft procurement, add modifier 80 to 33517-33523, 33533-33536, as appropriate. For percutaneous ventricular assist device insertion, removal, repositioning, see 33990, 33991, 33992, 33993, 33995, 33997. Section Specific Guideline Selective vascular catheterizations should be coded to include introduction and all lesser order selective catheterizations used in the approach (eg, the description for a selective right middle cerebral artery catheterization includes the introduction and placement catheterization of the right common and internal carotid arteries). Additional second and/or third order arterial catheterizations within the same family of arteries supplied by a single first order artery should be expressed by 36218 or 36248. Additional first order or higher catheterizations in vascular families supplied by a first order vessel different from a previously selected and coded family should be separately coded using the conventions described above. short_description: Coronary artery bypass, using venous graft(s) and arterial graft(s); 3 venous grafts (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 33519 in conjunction with 33533-33536)
lay_term: The provider diverts blood flow from damaged vessels in the heart by grafting three vein segments taken from another location, such as the leg, while the patient is undergoing a coronary artery bypass grafting procedure that includes both venous and arterial grafting. He performs the procedure to restore circulation, improve the function of the heart, and decrease symptoms like angina. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, and while undergoing a coronary artery bypass grafting procedure that includes arterial grafting as well as venous grafting, the provider harvests three vein segments suitable for coronary artery bypass grafting, typically from the saphenous vein in the leg. After completing arterial grafting, he attaches the distal end of the prepared saphenous veins to appropriate locations on the side of the diseased target vessels and the proximal ends to holes punched in the aorta. He then continues with the primary procedure, reversing cardioplegia and weaning the patient from cardiopulmonary bypass. He then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Angina pectoris: Episodes of severe chest pain due to insufficient blood supply within the heart. Aorta: The main artery that comes out of the top of the left ventricle and carries oxygenated blood to the body; it consists of an ascending and descending aorta which serve the upper and lower parts of the body respectively. Cardioplegia: A chemical solution used to stop the heart from beating so that surgery can be performed without excessive blood loss; cold cardioplegia lowers the temperature of the body as well as stops the heart. Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): Technique that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs and maintains the circulation of blood and the oxygen content of the body during surgery, giving the provider a motionless operative field; known as a heart–lung machine or pump; on pump means the provider performed CPB. Coronary artery bypass graft (CABG): Placement of a vein graft between the aorta and one or more obstructed main arteries of the heart to reestablish blood flow to the portion of the heart served by that artery; an arterial graft anastomosis may also be performed. Saphenous vessels: Veins of the lower extremities frequently harvested and used for anastomosis. Tips When you read the operative report, underline or highlight the number and type of grafts the provider completes as a reference when selecting a code, from the range +33517 through 33530, Combined arterial and venous grafting for coronary bypass. Note that +33517 is an add–on code and must be reported with an appropriate primary procedure for a venous or arterial grafting procedure. Read Less

short_description: Coronary artery bypass, using arterial graft(s); single arterial graft
lay_term: The provider diverts blood flow from a damaged vessel in the heart by grafting in a single segment of an artery from another location, such as in the chest or abdomen, to restore circulation, improve the function of the heart, and decrease symptoms like angina. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a midline sternotomy, an incision through the breastbone. He inserts aortic and venous cannulas to establish cardiopulmonary bypass, or machine circulation. He injects a cardioplegia solution to stop the heart for the procedure. He harvests a single arterial graft, typically from the internal mammary artery in the chest, leaving the end of the graft attached to its blood supply. He grafts the artery to an appropriate location on side of the diseased vessel. He weans the patient off the bypass pump. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Angina pectoris: Episodes of severe chest pain due to insufficient blood supply within the heart. Coronary artery bypass graft (CABG): Placement of a vein graft between the aorta and one or more obstructed main arteries of the heart to reestablish blood flow to the portion of the heart served by that artery; an arterial graft anastomosis may also be performed. Internal mammary artery: The blood vessel on either side of the breastbone that is often used as a replacement artery in coronary bypass surgery; supplies the thoracic (chest) wall, mediastinum, the organs and structures in the chest, and diaphragm, the membrane dividing the abdominal and chest cavities; also known as the internal thoracic artery. short_description: Myocardial resection (eg, ventricular aneurysmectomy)
lay_term: The provider opens and removes an aneurysm sac from the wall of a ventricle of the heart and sutures the defect closed to strengthen the heart wall and prevent rupture of the aneurysm, typically during a coronary artery bypass graft procedure.
