He makes an incision to open the left ventricle to access the aortic semilunar valve or to open the right ventricle to access the pulmonary semilunar valve. He cleans the leaflets and then uses either sutures or a patch to repair the defect. He closes the incisions in the ventricle and removes the patient from cardiopulmonary bypass. Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): Technique that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs and maintains the circulation of blood and the oxygen content of the body during surgery, giving the provider a motionless operative field; known as a heart–lung machine or pump; on pump means the provider performed CPB. Leaflets: Leaf–shaped flaps of tissue; two or three leaflets come together in the center of a heart valve, opening to allow blood to flow from one heart chamber to another and closing to stop the flow of blood between chambers; also called cusps. Median sternotomy: Cutting into the bone plate in the middle front of the chest to which the ribs are attached by cartilage. Patch graft: Artificial, autologous tissue (from the patient's own body), or preserved tissue from a donor; the provider uses the tissue to cover a defect or replace removed tissue or a portion of a structure. Semilunar valve: A valve, or by extension, a cusp of a valve, shaped like a crescent moon; the pulmonary semilunar valve controls blood flow from the right ventricle to the lungs, and the aortic semilunar valve controls blood from the left ventricle to the body. Ventricle: One of the two lower chambers of the heart; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood throughout the body; the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Read Less

short_description: Anastomosis of pulmonary artery to aorta (Damus-Kaye-Stansel procedure)

short_description: Application of right and left pulmonary artery bands (eg, hybrid approach stage 1) Notes: (For banding of the main pulmonary artery related to septal defect, use 33690)
lay_term: The provider places a band, typically of umbilical tape, around both the right and left pulmonary arteries. The procedure reduces the left to right blood flow and relieves or prevents congestive heart failure and pulmonary hypertension. This procedure is part of other staged procedures. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the chest, typically a left anterior thoracotomy or a left lateral thoracotomy, sparing the sternum for subsequent procedures. The provider exposes the main pulmonary artery (MPA), and aorta and prepares the bands for placement. The provider dissects the tissue connecting the aorta and main pulmonary artery. He passes the band through the transverse sinus to surround both the aorta and MPA. He carefully advances the aortic end of the band through the previous site of dissection and places it between the aorta and the MPA. The provider places both left and right pulmonary artery bands. The provider closes the incisions in the heart, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision in the chest. Terminology Atrium (pl. atria): One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Congestive heart failure: Excessive fluid collects in the tissues of the lungs, trunk, or extremities due to heart disease; it results in difficulty breathing and increased blood pressure; too much salt intake contributes to this condition. Gusset: Material, natural or artificial, placed to make a structure stronger. Hybrid approach: When more than one provider, typically two different cardiac specialists, perform a procedure together due to the difficulty of the patient’s case; the hybrid approach is used to repair complex cardiac anomalies, typically in infants. Left anterior thoracotomy: Incision through the left front portion of the thorax; it preserves the sternum for later procedures that require median sternotomy. Left lateral thoracotomy: Incision through the left side of the thorax; it preserves the sternum for later procedures that require median sternotomy. Median sternotomy: Cutting into the bone plate in the middle front of the chest to which the ribs are attached by cartilage. Pulmonary artery: The major artery that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Pulmonary artery band: A preferably adjustable band, typically umbilical tape that the provider places around the aortopulmonary trunk, aorta, and pulmonary artery to restrict pulmonary blood flow and prevent enlargement of the ventricle and elevated blood pressure in the pulmonary artery; typically part of staged procedures to correct or modify multiple congenital cardiac anomalies. Pulmonary hypertension: Elevated blood pressure in the pulmonary artery circulation, typically due to excessive blood flow or obstruction. Septal defect: A defect, present at birth, in which the wall (septum) fails to close completely between the atria, the upper chambers of the heart, or the ventricles, the lower chambers of the heart. Staged, staged procedure: Complex anomalies often require several procedures spread out over time to correct the associated deformities. Transverse sinus: A wide passage behind the aorta, the main artery coming off the left ventricle, and the base of the pulmonary artery and passing across and in front of the atria, the upper chambers of the heart. Additional Info Code 33620 describes pulmonary artery banding (PAB), a surgical technique providers may use as an initial step toward an operative correction of congenital heart defects. The operation is usually performed through the patient's sternum, although your provider's notes may indicate the approach was via a lateral thoracotomy. The narrowing of the main pulmonary artery and the aorta is made by wrapping a piece of surgical tape around the artery and drawing it tight. Providers may find it difficult to achieve the optimal degree of narrowing on the first surgical attempt, so additional operations may be necessary. Read Less

short_description: Repair atrial septal defect, secundum, with cardiopulmonary bypass, with or without patch
lay_term: The provider performs surgical closure of an atrial septal defect by opening up the atrium and closing the defect with a patch under direct visualization of the area. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and under general anesthesia, the provider opens the pericardium and places the patient on cardiopulmonary bypass (the heart–lung machine), which diverts blood away from the right atrium. Cardioplegia (a mixture of medications and nutrients) with high potassium is administered after the aorta is clamped, thus stopping the heart from beating (cardiac arrest). The right atrium is then opened to allow access to the atrial septum below. Smaller defects are closed with sutures, and larger defects are closed with a patch. Patches may be comprised of the patient's own pericardium, commercially available bovine pericardium, or synthetic material (Gore–Tex® and Dacron®). Once the defect is closed, the atrial incision is closed as well, and the provider removes the aortic cross–clamp. After normal ventilation is restored, the patient is warmed and a stable rhythm is achieved. Once that is achieved, the patient may be removed from cardiopulmonary bypass. A single drainage tube is placed and the chest is closed. Terminology Atrial septal defect (ASD): A hole between the upper heart chambers, present from birth, that causes blood flow between the left and right atria via the interatrial septum; it is a congenital defect resulting from the failure of the normal opening between the atria in the fetus to close after birth; ostium secundum atrial septal defect is the most common type of atrial septal defect. Median sternotomy: Incision into the bone plate in the middle front of the chest to which the ribs are attached by cartilage. Thoracotomy: Surgical incision to open the chest wall. Tips There are multiple procedures for repair of an atrial septal defect; study the documentation and choose the correct code from codes 33641 through 33697. Read Less

short_description: Repair of atrial septal defect and ventricular septal defect, with direct or patch closure Notes: (Do not report modifier 63 in conjunction with 33647) (For repair of tricuspid atresia (eg, Fontan, Gago procedures), use 33615)
lay_term: The provider closes a hole or defect in the atrial and ventricular septa (walls) using stitches or a patch of Dacron® or pericardium to prevent the mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood into different chambers of the heart. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepared and under general anesthesia, the surgeon makes an incision in the chest wall (median sternotomy) and cardiopulmonary bypass (heart–lung machine) is also utilized to do the work of circulation during the procedure. Depending on the location of the defect, an incision will be made in either the right atrium, the pulmonary artery, or the outflow tract of the right ventricle (infundibulum). In a small ventricular septal defect (VSD), simple stitching of the hole with thread made of polypropylene or similar material is enough. When the defect is large, a synthetic "patch" created from the patient's own pericardial tissue or made of a fabric–like Dacron® or Gore–Tex® is used. The patch is then sutured into place to close the defect. The "hole" in the atrium or ventricle is thus closed. The atrial, pulmonary artery or infundibular incision is then closed with sutures. Once the surgical procedure is completed, the patient is weaned gradually off the heart–lung bypass machine until the newly repaired heart is capable of managing all the blood flow again. Chest tubes are then placed to drain the surgical area. Eventually, the tissue of the heart heals over the patch or stitches, and by six months after the surgery, the hole is completely covered with tissue. Terminology Atrial septal defect (ASD): A form of congenital heart defect (a hole between the chambers) that causes blood flow between the left and right atria via the interatrial septum. Ventricular septal defect (VSD): A defect in the ventricular septum, the wall dividing the left and right ventricles of the heart. Congenital VSDs are collectively the most common congenital heart defects. Tips There are multiple procedures for repair of an atrial septal defect; study the documentation and choose the correct code from codes 33641 through 33697. Read Less

short_description: Repair of incomplete or partial atrioventricular canal (ostium primum atrial septal defect), with or without atrioventricular valve repair
lay_term: The provider closes a "hole" in the wall between the atria and ventricles by suturing the area or by using a patch made of Dacron® material or pericardium. Based on the severity of valve defect, the tricuspid and mitral valves are also repaired while making sure that the valve leaflets are properly placed. Explanation Under general anesthesia, an incision is made in the middle of the chest and the heart is exposed. A heart–lung machine (cardiopulmonary bypass) is used to maintain the body as the heart would as the heart itself is cooled, stopped, emptied and opened, usually through the right atrium. A division in the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve is closed with interrupted sutures and the valve is closed with adequate sutures. The ventricular septal defect is closed by sewing to it a patch of Dacron® cloth or a patch of pericardium. The atrial septal defect is also closed using a patch of Dacron® or pericardium. The affected tricuspid and mitral valves may be reconstructed based on the severity of the defect and supported by the rebuilt septum. The heart is then closed and restarted as the heart–lung machine is removed. Terminology Atrium (pl. atria): One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Atrioventricular (AV) canal defect: A large hole in the center of the heart where the wall (septum) between the two atria joins the wall between the two ventricles involving both upper and lower chambers; the tricuspid and mitral valves that normally separate the heart's upper and lower chambers aren't formed as individual valves; there are two common types of atrioventricular canal defects — partial (involving only the two upper chambers of the heart) and complete, which allows blood to travel freely among all four chambers of the heart. Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): Technique that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs and maintains the circulation of blood and the oxygen content of the body during surgery, giving the provider a motionless operative field; known as a heart–lung machine or pump; on pump means the provider performed CPB. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers in the heart that receive blood from a corresponding upper chamber (atrium) and from which blood is forced into the arteries. Read Less

short_description: Repair of complete atrioventricular canal, with or without prosthetic valve Notes: (Do not report modifier 63 in conjunction with 33670)
lay_term: Cardiac surgery is used to repair defects of the septa and valves of the heart. This is usually performed by using sutures and patches of Dacron® or pericardium. A prosthetic valve may also be used to replace the defective valve. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and under general anesthesia, the provider makes an incision in the middle of the chest and exposes the heart. Cardiopulmonary bypass is started, and the right atrium is emptied and opened. The cleft of the faulty mitral valve that is the cause of the leak is sutured and closed. This has to be done carefully so that valve closes properly. Similarly, the ventricular septal defect is closed with a patch or multiple patches. Then the atrial septal defect is similarly closed. He also repairs a ventricular septal defect, or a hole in the tissue wall separating the two ventricles. The provider places the patient on cardiopulmonary bypass during the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest wall to access the heart. He usually opens the chest through a median sternotomy incision, an approach in which he incises the sternum (breastbone) in the midline to open the chest. When appropriate, the provider places the patient on cardiopulmonary bypass. He exposes the sinus of Valsalva fistula by making an incision in the heart, and then he assesses the patient's anatomy to decide how to repair. He uses a patch or graft to repair the abnormal connection. He next assesses the ventricular septal defect and uses another patch or graft to repair the hole. short_description: Repair sinus of Valsalva aneurysm, with cardiopulmonary bypass

short_description: Repair of isolated partial anomalous pulmonary venous return (eg, Scimitar Syndrome) Notes: (Do not report 33724 in conjunction with 32551, 33210, 33211)
lay_term: The provider incises the chest wall and repairs an isolated partial anomalous pulmonary venous return (PAPVC), a congenital condition in which one or more of the pulmonary veins fail to reach the left atrium of the heart, instead it drains oxygenated blood from the lungs into the right atrium of the heart by way of an abnormal, or anomalous, connection. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest wall to access the heart. He usually opens the chest through a median sternotomy incision, an approach in which he incises the sternum (breastbone) in the midline to open the chest. Next, he incises the right atrium and opens the atrial septum, near the pulmonary veins that are draining abnormally into the right atrium. He creates a baffle, or an alternate pathway, to direct the veins to drain to the left atrium across the opening he creates in the atrial septum. Next, he incises the pulmonary veins to disconnect them from their right atrium attachments. He then reattaches them to the back of the left atrium. He ties off any abnormal veins that are carrying pulmonary or oxygenated blood to the heart, and he closes the atrial septal defect. He then discontinues the cardiopulmonary bypass and restarts the heart. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the chest wall by suturing the tissues in layers. short_description: Atrial septectomy or septostomy; closed heart (Blalock-Hanlon type operation)
lay_term: The provider removes the atrial septum or intentionally creates an opening in the atrial septum, the wall of tissue separating the right and left atrium of the heart. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest wall to access the heart. The provider usually opens the chest by median sternotomy incision, an approach in which the provider incises the sternum (breastbone) in the midline to open the chest. The provider does not place the patient on cardiopulmonary bypass to perform this procedure. The provider occludes portions of the left and right atria with a clamp and occludes the pulmonary veins. The provider makes incisions in both the left and right atria to access and excise the atrial septum, or they may only create a hole in the atrial septum to allow the flow of oxygenated blood from the left to the right atrium. Finally, the provider stops all bleeding and closes the chest wall, such as by suturing the tissues in layers. short_description: Shunt; subclavian to pulmonary artery (Blalock-Taussig type operation)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically creates a shunt between the subclavian and the pulmonary artery. A shunt forms the bypass channel or passageway in the blood circulation connecting two blood vessels and diverts blood from one region to the other. The aim of this procedure is to improve oxygenation of the blood in a patient with cyanosis from insufficient pulmonary, or lung, blood flow due to a congenital heart defect. The provider performs this procedure as a temporary measure until he can perform another procedure to correct the actual heart defect. This procedure is also known as a Blalock Taussig operation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest wall to open the chest. The provider identifies and ligates the end of the subclavian artery going to the arm and creates a connection between the subclavian artery and the right or left pulmonary artery. He attaches the subclavian artery to the pulmonary artery using a synthetic material or graft creating a shunt from the subclavian to the pulmonary. This shunt improves the amount of blood that flows to the lung effectively treating the cyanosis. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the chest wall by suturing the soft tissues in layers. Terminology Congenital: A condition existing at or dating from birth. Cyanosis: Bluish colour in the skin and the mucus membranes due to lack of the oxygen in the blood. Pulmonary artery: A blood vessel that carries the deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs for purification. Blalock–Taussig (BT) shunt: A technique in which the provider uses a graft to connect the left subclavian to the pulmonary artery to divert some of the blood into the pulmonary artery in a patient with a double inlet left ventricle, a congenital condition where the left and right atria of the heart connects to the same ventricle. Subclavian artery: Paired arteries in the upper thorax that supply blood to some areas of the brain, neck, chest, and upper limb. short_description: Shunt; ascending aorta to pulmonary artery (Waterston type operation)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically creates a shunt between the ascending aorta and the pulmonary artery. A shunt forms the bypass channel or passageway in the blood circulation connecting two blood vessels and diverts blood from one region to the other. The aim of this procedure is to improve oxygenation of the blood in a patient with cyanosis from insufficient pulmonar blood flow due to a congenital heart defect. This procedure is also known as Waterston type operation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest wall to open the chest. He next places the patient on cardiopulmonary bypass. The provider then creates side to side connections between the ascending aorta and the pulmonary artery. He tries to ensure that diameter of the connection is accurate so as to have adequate blood flow to the lungs. He also ligates (ties off) a ductus arteriosus that did not close. He then discontinues the cardiopulmonary bypass and restarts the heart. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the chest wall by suturing the soft tissues in layers. Terminology Ascending aorta: First section of the aorta, the largest artery in the body arising from the left ventricle. Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): Technique that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs and maintains the circulation of blood and the oxygen content of the body during surgery, giving the provider a motionless operative field; known as a heart–lung machine or pump; on pump means the provider performed CPB. Congenital: A condition existing at or dating from birth. Cyanosis: Bluish colour in the skin and the mucus membranes due to lack of the oxygen in the blood. Patent ductus arteriosus: A persistent opening between two major blood vessels leading from the heart; this normal connection, known as a ductus arteriosus, is a necessary part of a fetus’s circulatory system in vitro; the ductus usually closes shortly after birth, however, in some individuals it remains open, or patent, which is why it is called a patent ductus arteriosus. Pulmonary artery: A blood vessel that carries the deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs for purification. short_description: Shunt; superior vena cava to pulmonary artery for flow to 1 lung (classical Glenn procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically creates a shunt between the superior vena cava and the right pulmonary artery. A shunt forms the bypass channel or passageway in the blood circulation connecting two blood vessels and diverts blood from one region to the other. short_description: Repair of transposition of the great arteries with ventricular septal defect and subpulmonary stenosis; without surgical enlargement of ventricular septal defect
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs a cardiac defect present from birth, in which the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle. This causes problems in circulation of oxygenated blood in the body. The provider switches the aorta and the pulmonary artery to their normal positions without the need to enlarge the hole in the ventricular septum. The provider also removes an obstructive band of fibrous muscle present at the tip of pulmonary artery. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest wall to access the heart. He usually opens the chest by median sternotomy incision, an approach in which he incises the sternum, or the breastbone in the midline to open the chest. He then places the patient on cardiopulmonary bypass to perform this service. Next, he opens the right atrium and locates the ventricular septal defect. He sutures a patch, or graft, in place to repair the defect and to divert the oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the aorta. He then ligates the main pulmonary artery and places a fabric or cadaver graft, or conduit, so that one end connects to the branched pulmonary arteries and the other end connects to the right ventricle. This way he directs the deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the pulmonary circulation. If there is an elevation in the pulmonary vascular resistance, the provider may place a bioprosthetic valve in the pulmonary outflow conduit to help control blood flow from the heart to the lungs. He stops any bleeding and weans the patient off bypass, closing incisions made to establish the bypass. He then closes the chest wall by suturing the layers of tissue together and may place chest or drainage tubes before dressing the chest incision. Congenital: A condition existing at or dating from birth. Graft: A tissue a provider transfers from one part of the body to other. Midline: Meaning middle. Pulmonary artery: A blood vessel that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle of the heart to the lungs. Pulmonary vascular resistance: The resistance, or opposing force to the flow of blood that the heart must overcome to push blood through the circulatory system. Subpulmonary stenosis: The narrowing of the pulmonary artery, a blood vessel that carries the deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs to be oxygenated. Transposition of great vessels, or TGV: A congenital anomaly in which major blood vessels of the heart, such as the pulmonary veins or pulmonary arteries, are abnormally arranged or attached in the heart; typically the two main vessels leaving the heart are reversed; the aorta, which normally carries oxygen rich blood from the left side of the heart to the body, arises instead from the right ventricle and carries oxygen poor blood to the body; the pulmonary artery, which normally carries oxygen poor blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs, arises instead from the left ventricle and carries oxygenated blood returning from the lungs back to the lungs; also called an arterial switch, or TGA for transposition of the great arteries. short_description: Repair of transposition of the great arteries, aortic pulmonary artery reconstruction (eg, Jatene type); with repair of subpulmonic obstruction
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs a cardiac defect present from birth, in which the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle. This causes problems in circulation of oxygenated blood in the body. The provider switches the aorta and the pulmonary artery to their normal positions and moves the coronary arteries to the new aorta. The provider also removes an obstructive band of fibrous muscle present at the tip of the pulmonary artery. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the chest, to repair the subpulmonic, or obstruction, at the base of the lung. The provider initiates cardiopulmonary bypass and then infuses a solution in the coronary circulation that keeps the heart paralyzed during the procedure. He then moves through the atrium to remove an obstructive band of fibrous muscle where the main right ventricular cavity meets the pulmonary outlet. Next, the provider detaches the aorta and pulmonary artery from their roots. He then positions the pulmonary artery over the right ventricle and the aorta over the left ventricle. The provider basically interchanges the pulmonary trunk and the aorta, so that the blood flows from the pulmonary veins through the left ventricle to the aorta. This makes the pulmonary artery root the new aorta and the aortic root the new pulmonary artery. The provider then detaches the coronary arteries from the aortic root and attaches them to the new aorta. He creates a connection between the aorta and the new aorta. He then attaches the pulmonary artery to the aortic root and closes the ductal arch, which is an extension of the aorta. The provider closes the incision with sutures and may place chest or drainage tubes. short_description: Obliteration of aortopulmonary septal defect, with cardiopulmonary bypass
lay_term: The provider obliterates, or corrects, an aortopulmonary defect in a patient. This heart anomaly involves an abnormal communication between the ascending aorta and the pulmonary artery. The provider performs this procedure using cardiopulmonary bypass. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest. A typical approach is a median sternotomy, which is a surgical incision through the center of the breastbone (sternum) to access the heart and chest organs. The provider visualizes the ascending aorta (the first section of the aorta, the largest artery in the body) and the pulmonary artery (which carries blood from the heart to the lungs). The provider initiates cardiopulmonary bypass, which uses a machine to temporarily take over the function of the heart and lungs during surgery. The provider connects the patient to the cardiopulmonary bypass system by inserting tubes (cannulation) to connect the patient to the machine. Once the bypass machine starts working, the provider uses medication (cardioplegia solution) to stop the heart from beating temporarily. The provider identifies the aortopulmonary defect, which involves an abnormal communication between the ascending aorta and pulmonary artery. The provider separates the aorta and pulmonary artery and may use sutures to correct the septal defect. The septum is the structure that divides the aorta and the pulmonary artery. The provider may use a patch to close the defect. Examples include a pericardial patch (made from the patient’s pericardium, the sac that surrounds the heart) or a synthetic material patch. When the procedure is complete, the provider restarts the heart and discontinues the cardiopulmonary bypass, disconnecting the patient from the machine. The provider removes surgical tubes and instruments, closes tissues, including the sternum, and closes the incision, placing drainage tubes, as needed. Read Less

short_description: Repair of hypoplastic or interrupted aortic arch using autogenous or prosthetic material; without cardiopulmonary bypass

lay_term: During a primary vascular procedure, the provider places a graft in a part of the aortic arch that extends under one or more of the vessels that take off from the arch including isolating and controlling blood flow of the arch vessels with the patient under total circulatory arrest and/or isolated cerebral perfusion. Report this code in addition to the code for the primary procedure. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized for a primary vascular procedure and after exposing the heart and great vessels through a previously made median sternotomy incision, the provider cannulates the aorta and the superior and inferior venae cavae. He frees up the aorta and examines the aortic arch and identifies landmarks. He identifies an intimal tear of the ascending aorta or lesser curvature of the arch and determines that a hemiarch graft is the appropriate treatment. He initiates cardiopulmonary bypass and establishes hypothermia. He cross–clamps the aorta, administers cardioplegia, and the heart stops. He may establish isolated cerebral perfusion. He places clamps on the three brachiocephalic branches that take off from the arch. He transects the aortic arch obliquely and removes part of the lesser curvature of the arch. He prepares a graft with a beveled (slanted) end to match the angle of the transected arch and sews the graft to the distal aspect of the lesser curvature of the arch in a curvilinear fashion, sparing the ostia (openings) of the brachiocephalic vessels that take off from the arch. He cannulates the side arm of the graft, and de–airs the arch and graft as pump flow resumes. He completes the proximal anastomosis while rewarming the patient. The provider then continues with the primary vascular procedure. Aortic arch: The aorta, the largest artery in the body, rises out of the heart as the ascending aorta and then curves down forming an arch; three arteries — the left subclavian, left common carotid, and brachiocephalic (innominate), which divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian — arise from the arch; the descending part of the aorta divides into the thoracic and abdominal aorta. Aortic dissection: Blood coursing between the layers of the inner lining (intima) of the aorta due to an intimal tear which causes separation of the layers (dissection). Brachiocephalic artery: Short artery that arises from the arch of the aorta and divides into the carotid and subclavian arteries of the right side, also known as the innominate artery. lay_term: The provider repairs a defect, such as an aneurysm, in the aortic arch with a synthetic graft with the patient under intermittent cardiopulmonary bypass or deep hypothermic circulatory arrest while isolating the circulation to the brain from the systemic circulation. The arch vessels are individually reimplanted in the aortic arch graft or reimplanted as a two–vessel or three–vessel island, also called a 2– or 3–vessel Carrel patch graft. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider opens the chest, through an approach such as a median sternotomy. She initiates cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), which she may discontinue and restart as appropriate during the procedure. The provider also induces deep hypothermia using heat exchanger or cooling circuits in the CPB machine. The body is cooled to a temperature of 18 degrees centigrade, which stops circulation (total circulatory arrest) and creates a bloodless field. Before that, she establishes circulation to the brain (isolated cerebral perfusion) through the carotid arteries via extracorporeal circulation through the axillary arteries. She resects (removes) the aneurysmal sac from the aortic arch, preserving the ostia of the arch vessels. She prepares a Dacron® graft to match the transected arch and anastomoses the distal end of the graft to the proximal descending aorta. She attaches the arch vessels to the graft, individually or as islands of two or three vessels using patch grafts. If the left common carotid and brachiocephalic are attached as a 2–vessel island patch graft, the left subclavian may be attached to the arch graft during rewarming of the patient. CPB, which had been stopped earlier, is resumed while the patient is still hypothermic. The provider cannulates the side arm of the graft, and de–airs the arch and graft as pump flow resumes. She completes the proximal anastomosis while slowly rewarming the patient. Once the patient is rewarmed, CPB and extracorporeal circulation to the brain are discontinued, hemostasis assured, and the two halves of the sternum are rejoined with wires. She closes the incision in layers. lay_term: The provider creates a graft from the soft tissues behind the pharynx. He also makes a neck incision and repairs the descending thoracic aorta. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the left and right sides of the neck to reach the common carotid arteries. He identifies, isolates, and dissects the common carotid artery from surrounding structures. She then creates a tunnel from one side of the neck to the other, cutting into the soft tissue behind the pharynx, or retropharyngeal. She places a tube in the tunnel and opens one of the carotid arteries and attaches one end of the tube to the artery. She makes an opening in the other carotid artery and connects the free end of the tube to this artery opening. Alternatively, she clamps the vessel on either side of the problem area in the carotid artery and incises the artery above the damage or blockage. She then sutures the synthetic vein graft to this open end and then sutures the graft to the side of the artery on the other side of the neck. In either approach, the provider leaves the problem area there but effectively bypasses it. When the procedure is complete, she closes the incision with sutures. short_description: Endovascular stent repair of coarctation of the ascending, transverse, or descending thoracic or abdominal aorta, involving stent placement; across major side branches
lay_term: The provider uses a minimally invasive approach to place a stent (tube) across one or more major side branches of the aorta to treat coarctation (narrowing, generally present at birth). Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision to access the target blood vessel, makes an opening in the vessel, and introduces items for the endovascular procedure, such as a sheath, guidewire, and catheter. The provider uses imaging guidance to navigate the catheter to the heart. The provider may insert a temporary pacemaker, inserting a lead into a heart chamber and attaching the lead to an external temporary generator box, for pacing to facilitate stent placement. The provider also may perform diagnostic congenital left heart catheterization, navigating a catheter into the left side of the heart and using imaging such as fluoroscopy to examine and assess the heart, including congenital defects. The provider then navigates to the coarctation (narrowing) in the aorta. It may be in the thoracic aorta (ascending, transverse, or descending) or in the abdominal aorta. The provider may use angiography to visualize the target lesion and may perform balloon angioplasty in the target zone to widen it before or after stent deployment. The provider places the tubelike stent, which crosses one or more major side branches. The major side branches of the thoracic aorta (above the diaphragm) are the brachiocephalic, carotid, and subclavian arteries. The major side branches of the abdominal aorta (below the diaphragm) are the celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric, and renal arteries. The provider may place one or more additional stents for extension. The provider confirms stent placement and then removes all instruments and closes the access site. Terminology Angiography: A medical imaging technique in which the provider injects a dye into blood vessels and uses plain X–rays, computed tomography (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to visualize the inside (lumen) of the vessels; more specific terms include arteriography when performed on the arteries or venography when performed on the veins; angiography can also be used to study blood supply to organs such as the heart, kidneys, and liver. Aorta: The largest artery in the body, which arises from the left ventricle of the heart and supplies oxygenated blood to the rest of the body; it consists of an ascending and descending aorta that serve the upper and lower parts of the body respectively. Brachiocephalic artery: A small artery arising from the aorta that supplies blood to the right arm and head; also known as the innominate. Carotid artery: One of two large main arteries in the neck that supply the head and neck with oxygenated blood. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel or other hollow structure through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure for drainage or to instill fluids. Celiac artery: An artery that has its origin in the abdominal aorta, and which supplies many major internal organs, such as the stomach, spleen, liver, and esophagus. Congenital: Describes a condition or defect existing from birth; congenital disorders may be inherited or due to other factors such as infection, injury, or environmental factors. Diaphragm: Large flat muscular membrane that separates the lungs from the stomach area; used in breathing. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the images appear on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Guidewire: A device used to position a catheter, tube, or other devices into a tubular structure. Inferior mesenteric artery: Branching from the abdominal aorta around the level of the third lumbar vertebra, this artery supplies oxygenated blood to the descending colon, sigmoid colon, and parts of the rectum. Renal artery: Either of two branches of the abdominal aorta, each of which supplies one of the kidneys. Stent: A thin, plastic or metal tubelike device that is inserted into a tubular structure, such as a vessel or duct, to open or widen a narrowed area or support a weakened part of the structure. Subclavian artery: Major arteries of the upper extremities that pass beneath the clavicle and carry oxygen rich blood to the arm. Superior mesenteric artery (SMA): A large artery that originates from the upper part of the aorta just below the celiac artery, around the level of the first lumbar vertebra, the SMA supplies oxygenated blood to the greater part of the small intestine, the cecum, ascending colon, and right half of the transverse colon. Transluminal balloon angioplasty: A procedure to open up or widen the lumen (the interior, open area) of a blood vessel by passing and inflating a balloon across a narrowed part of the vessel. short_description: Pulmonary artery embolectomy; with cardiopulmonary bypass
lay_term: The provider performs an urgent surgical procedure to remove an embolus or blockage from the pulmonary artery. This life–threatening blockage commonly occurs due to a blood clot in the leg that travels to the heart where it is obstructing blood flow to the lungs. This service includes cardiopulmonary bypass. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest, through an approach such as median sternotomy, and initiates cardiopulmonary bypass. He makes an incision over the main pulmonary artery to visualize the clot. He may attempt mechanical manipulation to mobilize the clot and remove it through the hole, or he uses forceps to remove the clot, trying to remove it in one piece. The provider then repairs the artery. The provider then closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): Technique that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs and maintains the circulation of blood and the oxygen content of the body during surgery, giving the provider a motionless operative field; known as a heart–lung machine or pump; on pump means the provider performed CPB. Forceps: A two–bladed instrument used to compress or grasp. Median sternotomy: A surgical procedure in which the provider makes a vertical inline incision along the sternum, or the breastbone. Pulmonary artery: Blood vessel which receives blood form from the right ventricle and delivers it to the lungs. short_description: Repair of pulmonary artery arborization anomalies by unifocalization; without cardiopulmonary bypass
lay_term: The provider performs repairs of the pulmonary arteries and creates a unifocal, or single, pulmonary blood supply, thereby resulting in complete repair of the arborization (branching) anomalies. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest, through an approach such as thoracotomy or sternotomy. He accesses the major aortopulmonary collateral arteries (MAPCAs) and divides them from the aorta and other vessels as appropriate. He sews and closes the stumps on the aorta. He then sutures the free ends of the collateral arteries to the appropriate pulmonary artery segments. Alternatively, he may ligate, or tie off these side branches at their origin to control perfusion. Either approach results in the provider effectively rerouting misdirected blood vessels into a single vessel or into the pulmonary artery. The provider closes the incision with sutures. short_description: Implantation of a total replacement heart system (artificial heart) with recipient cardiectomy Notes: (For implantation of ventricular assist device, see 33975, 33976, 33979, 33990, 33991, 33995)
lay_term: The provider removes the patient’s heart and implants an artificial heart as a temporary measure until a donor heart is found or for patients who are not eligible for a heart transplant and require permanent mechanical cardiac support. Explanation A total artificial heart (TAH) is a device that replaces the two lower chambers, or ventricles, of the heart and the four heart valves due to end–stage heart failure. In end–stage heart failure, the patient has no treatment option, other than a heart transplant, to pump enough blood to meet the body's needs. There are two types of heart systems. One connects to an outside power source through tubes running through a hole in the abdomen to the outside source. The other type of system consists of a pump and a battery contained in the patient’s chest. The internal battery receives wirelessly transmitted power through the skin from an external primary device. This code is for implantation of the latter type of TAH. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the center of the chest from just below the Adam's apple to just above the navel, then divides the breastbone, or sternum, in half and spreads the rib cage to access the heart. He then creates a subcutaneous pocket in the muscle in the patient’s abdomen and places the control unit with the internal battery. Next, he administers medication to stop the patient’s heart and places the patient on a heart and lung bypass machine, transferring the patient to total cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). He cross–clamps the aorta and sections the aorta and pulmonary artery close to the valves. He removes the heart's ventricles and connects the TAH to the upper chambers of the heart, checking carefully for leaks. After he makes all the attachments, he removes any air from the system, removes the aortic clamp, and weans the patient off CPB onto the TAH. He repairs the sternum, sewing it together with small wires, and closes the skin incision over the sternum with sutures or surgical staples. He inserts tubes in the chest and connects them to a suction device to drain blood and fluid away from the heart. He also inserts a tube through the patient’s mouth or nose into the stomach to drain stomach fluids. He then applies a sterile bandage or dressing. Terminology Adam’s apple: The lump that sticks out in the front of a person's neck formed by the large cartilage of the throat. Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): Technique that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs and maintains the circulation of blood and the oxygen content of the body during surgery, giving the provider a motionless operative field, often called a heart–lung machine or pump. Subcutaneous: Under the skin. Skin staples: A type of U–shaped fastener used to close skin wounds in place of sutures. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers in the human heart that receive blood from a corresponding upper chamber, or atrium, and from which blood is forced into the arteries. Tips Providers may document a heart–lung machine or pump or that the patient is on pump to indicate CPB use. For removal and replacement of a total artificial heart (TAH), see 33928. For removal of a previously placed TAH in order to implant a donor heart, see 33929 (list separately in addition to the code for implantation of the donor heart). Read Less

short_description: Donor cardiectomy-pneumonectomy (including cold preservation)
lay_term: The provider surgically removes a donor heart in a procedure known as a cardiectomy. He also removes the lungs, which is called a pneumonectomy, from the donor and preserves the organs in cold storage for future transplantation in a recipient patient who needs them. Explanation When the donor is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the procurement provider performs a bronchoscopy and takes cultures to assess for lung disease. Multiple teams may be present, to harvest other organs such as the kidney and liver, including an anesthesia team to provide muscle relaxants or maintain hemodynamics prior to heart removal. The procurement provider performs a sternotomy in which he extends the incision down to the abdomen. He inspects the organs to determine if they're viable. He removes the heart and lungs often en bloc, or as one, and places them in a sterile container with a preserving solution and on ice for transport. Hemodynamics: Study of blood flow or circulation in the body. Pulmonary artery: A blood vessel carrying blood from the heart to the lungs for purification. Sternotomy: A surgical procedure in which the provider makes an incision along the sternum, or the breastbone. short_description: Heart-lung transplant with recipient cardiectomy-pneumonectomy
lay_term: The provider surgically removes the patient’s heart and lung and transplants a donor heart and lung into the patient’s body. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest, typically through a midline sternotomy approach. He prepares the heart and lungs for removal and initiates cardiopulmonary bypass. He removes the patient's heart and lungs. Next, he transplants the donor heart and lungs into the recipient, making connections as necessary. He begins by connecting a portion of the native heart to the donor heart such as the left atrium, atrial septum, and right atrium. He continues by trimming to size and connecting the patient's trachea and aorta to the allograft trachea and aorta. Similarly, he makes necessary connections between the donor lung allograft and the patient. When the donor heart starts functioning, he removes the patient from cardiopulmonary bypass. The provider closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Allograft: A graft between members of the same species; the graft material is obtained from a cadaver, often a tissue bank, or living human donor other than the patient. Aorta: The largest artery in the body, which arises from the left ventricle of the heart and supplies oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. Cardiectomy: Excision or surgical removal of the heart. Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): A technique which allows the patient's blood to bypass the heart and lungs, giving the provider a still operative field; a pump, oxygenator, cannula, and tubing together are often called a heart lung machine or pump; documentation of on pump means CPB was done during the procedure. Pneumonectomy: Excision or surgical removal of a lung or a part of a lung. Trachea: The windpipe. Tips To report a heart transplant, with or without recipient cardiectomy, see 33945. Read Less

short_description: Donor cardiectomy (including cold preservation)
lay_term: The provider performs a cardiectomy, or surgical removal of the heart, for transplant. He places the heart in a cold preservation solution for a later transplant. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the procurement provider performs a sternotomy and carries the incision down to the abdomen. Multiple teams may be present, to harvest other organs such as the kidney and liver, including an anesthesia team to provide muscle relaxants or maintain hemodynamics, or proper blood flow, prior to the heart removal. The procurement provider inspects the heart to determine its suitability. He places cannula into the aorta and pulmonary artery, clamps the aorta, and uses the cannula for cold saline perfusion. He removes the heart and places it in a sterile container with a preserving solution and ice for transport or transplantation. Terminology Aorta: The largest artery in the body, which arises from the left ventricle of the heart and supplies oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. Cannula: A thin tube that the provider inserts into the blood vessel or body cavity to administer medication, drain fluid, or insert a surgical instrument. Pulmonary artery: A blood vessel carrying blood from the heart to the lungs for purification. Sternotomy: A surgical procedure in which the provider makes an incision along the sternum or the breastbone. Tips Cold preservation is an inclusive component of the donor organ resection service and not the backbench preparation service; therefore, cold preservation of a donor heart allograft is included in 33940. lay_term: The provider prepares the donor heart that he receives in a cold solution for transplantation to a recipient’s body. He inspects the heart, excises, or sutures the blood vessels if they need repair, and removes any blood clots. He also excises the pulmonary artery and aorta as necessary. Explanation The provider receives the cold preserved heart allograft. He places it on a sterile table keeping the allograft on ice with a cold preservation solution bath. He inspects the organs for suitability. He repairs and trims the vessels as necessary, excising, or suturing defects in the coronary arteries, aorta, superior vena cava, and inferior vena cava. He removes any clots. He separates the pulmonary artery from the aorta and inspects the pulmonary valve. He creates an opening in the left atrium. The provider then inspects the mitral valve and atrial septum. He trims the left atrium, pulmonary artery, and aorta as necessary. He inspects the aortic valve. He oversews or sutures closed the left atrial appendage, or atrium as necessary. He places the heart in ice and cold solution until ready for transplantation. Terminology Allograft: A graft between members of the same species; the graft material is obtained from a cadaver, often a tissue bank, or living human donor other than the patient. Aorta: The largest artery in the body, which arises from the left ventricle of the heart and supplies oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. Atrial septum: The wall between the atria, which are the upper chambers of the heart. Atrium or auricle of heart: There are four chambers in human heart; two upper auricles or atria and two lower ventricles; auricles supply blood to the ventricles and the ventricles pump blood to the organs of the body through blood vessels called arteries. Cadaver donation: Organ donation, in which organs such as the heart, lungs, kidneys, liver, pancreas are taken from dead people, as well as tissue donation, such as the skin and bone. Coronary artery: Blood vessel supplying blood to the heart. Inferior vena cava: Vein which returns blood to the from the lower part of the body, Mitral valve: Valve between the left auricle and left ventricle of the heart. Pulmonary artery: A blood vessel carrying blood from the heart to the lungs for purification. Pulmonary valve: Valve that lets the blood flow out from the heart to the pulmonary artery. Superior vena cava: Vein which returns blood to the heart from the head, neck and both upper limbs. Read Less

short_description: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO)/extracorporeal life support (ECLS) provided by physician; initiation, veno-venous Notes: (Do not report modifier 63 in conjunction with 33946, 33947, 33948, 33949) (For insertion of cannula[e] for extracorporeal circulation, see 33951, 33952, 33953, 33954, 33955, 33956)
lay_term: The provider initiates extracorporeal circulation by inserting a cannula through a venovenous (VV) route where the blood that drains from the venous system is returned to the venous system. This method is useful in patients experiencing lung failure such as cardiopulmonary insufficiency, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), or in lung transplantation situations as a bridge to transplantation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the right jugular vein. He then cleans the area around the vein to insert a cannula into the open end of the vein. The provider then slowly inserts the cannula, through the right jugular vein into the heart's right atrium. This tube acts as an exit point for the oxygen–depleted blood from the body into an external device that acts as an artificial lung, or oxygenator. Depending upon the type of cannula the provider uses, the blood may return through the same cannula as with a double lumen catheter. If the provider uses a single lumen catheter, he must then create a means for insertion of the returning oxygenated blood. The provider uses the extracorporeal circulation device to actively pump the blood through the oxygenator in the external device, where the gas exchange occurs. A heat exchanger acts to warms the blood to body temperature before returning the blood to the patient through the cannula. Once all cannula are appropriately in position and secure, and flows are optimal, the provider then closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Acute respiratory distress syndrome, or ARDS: A buildup of fluid, or inflammation, in the lungs due to trauma or disease. Atrium: One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Cannula: A tube, not as flexible perhaps as a catheter, through which a trocar, a hollow pointed puncturing device, can be inserted to enable the placement of other instruments. Cardiopulmonary insufficiency: Interrupted blood circulation in the heart and pulmonary vessels that leads to decreased oxygen saturation in the blood. Extracorporeal circulation: Use of a heart–lung machine to circulate the blood, providing oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange, and bypassing the heart and lungs; also, use of an artificial kidney to remove substances typically excreted in the urine. Jugular vein: The blood vessel that drains blood from the neck, brain, and a part of the face to the heart. Venous system: The part of the cardiovascular system, the veins, responsible for carrying deoxygenated blood back to the heart. Tips If the provider uses a veno–arterial (VA) route, see 33947. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Prolonged extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) or extracorporeal life support (ECLS) is a procedure that provides cardiac and/or respiratory support to the heart and/or lungs, which allows them to rest and recover when sick or injured. ECMO/ECLS supports the function of the heart and/or lungs by continuously pumping some of the patient's blood out of the body to an oxygenator (membrane lung) where oxygen is added to the blood, carbon dioxide (CO2) is removed, and the blood is warmed before it is returned to the patient. There are two methods that can be used to accomplish ECMO/ECLS. One method is veno-arterial extracorporeal life support, which will support both the heart and lungs. Veno-arterial ECMO/ECLS requires that two cannula(e) are placed-one in a large vein and one in a large artery. The other method is veno-venous extracorporeal life support. Veno-venous ECMO/ECLS is used for lung support only and requires one or two cannula(e), which are placed in a vein. Services directly related to the cannulation, initiation, management, and discontinuation of the ECMO/ECLS circuit and parameters (33946, 33947, 33948, 33949) are distinct from the daily overall management of the patient. The daily overall management of the patient is a factor that will vary greatly depending on the patient's age, disease process, and condition. Daily overall management of the patient may be separately reported using the relevant hospital inpatient or observation care services (99221, 99222, 99223, 99231, 99232, 99233, 99234, 99235, 99236) or critical care or intensive care evaluation and management codes (99291, 99292, 99468, 99469, 99471, 99472, 99475, 99476, 99477, 99478, 99479, 99480). Services directly related to the ECMO/ECLS involve the initial cannulation and repositioning, removing, or adding cannula(e) while the patient is being supported by the ECMO/ECLS. Initiation of the ECMO/ECLS circuit and setting parameters (33946, 33947) is performed by the physician and involves determining the necessary ECMO/ECLS device components, blood flow, gas exchange, and other necessary parameters to manage the circuit. The daily management of the ECMO/ECLS circuit and monitoring parameters (33948, 33949) requires physician oversight to ensure that specific features of the interaction of the circuit with the patient are met. Daily management of the circuit and parameters includes management of blood flow, oxygenation, CO2 clearance by the membrane lung, systemic response, anticoagulation and treatment of bleeding, and cannula(e) positioning, alarms and safety. Once the patient's heart and/or lung function has sufficiently recovered, the physician will wean the patient from the ECMO/ECLS circuit and finally decannulate the patient. The basic management of the ECMO/ECLS circuit and parameters are similar, regardless of the patient's condition. ECMO/ECLS commonly involves multiple physicians and supporting nonphysician personnel to manage each patient. Different physicians may insert the cannula(e) and initiate ECMO/ECLS, manage the ECMO/ECLS circuit, and decannulate the patient. In addition, it would be common for one physician to manage the ECMO/ECLS circuit and patient-related issues (eg, anticoagulation, complications related to the ECMO/ECLS devices), while another physician manages the overall patient medical condition and underlying disorders, all on a daily basis. The physicians involved in the patient's care are commonly of different specialties, and significant physician team interaction may be required. Depending on the type of circuit and the patient's condition, there is substantial nonphysician work by ECMO/ECLS specialists, cardiac perfusionists, respiratory therapists, and specially trained nurses who provide long periods of constant attention. If the same physician provides any or all of the services for placing a patient on an ECMO/ECLS circuit, they may report the appropriate codes for the services they performed, which may include codes for the cannula(e) insertion (33951, 33952, 33953, 33954, 33955, 33956), ECMO/ECLS initiation (33946 or 33947), and overall patient management (99221, 99222, 99223, 99231, 99232, 99233, 99234, 99235, 99236, 99291, 99292, 99468, 99469, 99471, 99472, 99475, 99476, 99477, 99478, 99479, 99480). ECMO/ECLS daily management (33948, 33949) and repositioning services (33957, 33958, 33959, 33962, 33963, 33964) may not be reported on the same day as initiation services (33946, 33947) by the same or different individuals. If different physicians provide parts of the service, each physician may report the correct code(s) for the service(s) they provided, except as noted. Repositioning of the ECMO/ECLS cannula(e) (33957, 33958, 33959, 33962, 33963, 33964) at the same session as insertion (33951, 33952, 33953, 33954, 33955, 33956) is not separately reportable. Replacement of ECMO/ECLS cannula(e) in the same vessel should only be reported using the insertion code (33951, 33952, 33953, 33954, 33955, 33956). If cannula(e) are removed from one vessel and new cannula(e) are placed in a different vessel, report the appropriate cannula(e) removal (33965, 33966, 33969, 33984, 33985, 33986) and insertion (33951, 33952, 33953, 33954, 33955, 33956) codes. Extensive repair or replacement of an artery may be additionally reported (eg, 35266, 35286, 35371, and 35665). Fluoroscopic guidance used for cannula(e) repositioning (33957, 33958, 33959, 33962, 33963, 33964) is included in the procedure when performed and should not be separately reported. Daily management codes (33948 and 33949) should not be reported on the same day as initiation of ECMO (33946 or 33947). Initiation codes (33946 or 33947) should not be reported on the same day as repositioning codes (33957, 33958, 33959, 33962, 33963, 33964). See the CPT® codes for ECMO/ECLS Procedure Chart. lay_term: The provider initiates extracorporeal circulation, by inserting a cannula through a veno–arterial (VA) route, where the blood that drains from the venous system is returned to the arterial system. This method is useful in patients experiencing severe heart failure, or in post cardiac or heart transplant surgeries. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin typically over the right jugular vein or common femoral vein. He then cleans the area around the vein to insert a cannula into the open end of the vein. The provider then slowly inserts a venous cannula, placing the tip of the femoral venous cannula in the inferior vena cava or right atrium. This cannula acts as an exit point, for the oxygen–depleted blood from the body into an external device that acts as an artificial lung, or oxygenator. Next, he places an arterial cannula into the right femoral artery, often placing the tip into the iliac artery, for infusion of the oxygenated blood back into the patient. Depending upon the type of cannula the provider uses, the blood may return through the same cannula. If he uses a double–lumen catheter, this type of tube allows for the blood to return through the same cannula. If he uses a single–lumen catheter, he must create a means for the return of oxygenated blood. The provider uses the extracorporeal circulation device to actively pump the blood through the oxygenator in the external device, where the gas exchange occurs. A heat exchanger acts to warm the blood to body temperature before returning the blood to the patient through the cannula. Once all cannula are appropriately in position and secure, and flows are optimal, the provider closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Aorta: The largest artery in the body, which arises from the left ventricle of the heart and supplies oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. Atrium: One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Cannula: A tube, not as flexible perhaps as a catheter, through which a trocar, a hollow pointed puncturing device, can be inserted to enable the placement of other instruments. Double lumen tube: A tube with two channels, typically a large one for suctioning fluid and a smaller one for instilling fluid. Extracorporeal circulation: Use of a heart–lung machine to circulate the blood, providing oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange, and bypassing the heart and lungs; also, can use of an artificial kidney to remove substances typically excreted in the urine. Femoral artery: Largest blood vessel passing through the thigh. Femoral vein: The main blood vessel that carries deoxygenated blood from the legs to the heart. Iliac artery: A major vessel supplying oxygenated blood to abdominal and pelvic organs, also known as the common iliac artery. Jugular vein: The blood vessel that drains blood from the neck, brain, and a part of the face to the heart. Venae cavae: The major trunks of the venous circulatory system; the superior vena cava brings blood back to the heart from the upper body circulation while the inferior vena cava brings it back from the lower body circulation. Tips If the provider uses a venovenous (VV), route, see 33946. Read Less

lay_term: The provider handles the daily management of a venovenous (VV) ECMO or ECLS circulation for a patient who was previously placed on extracorporeal circulation where the blood that drains from the venous system is returned to the venous system. As the service progresses, the provider checks physical signs of perfusion and intravascular volume, including urine output, and blood pressures. She also checks head ultrasounds and uses neurologic exams. She closely watches hemoglobin, platelet levels, and clotting times. Electrolytes: Substance that dissociate in a solution and acquire the capacity to conduct electricity. Endotracheal: Inside the trachea or windpipe. short_description: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO)/extracorporeal life support (ECLS) provided by physician; insertion of peripheral (arterial and/or venous) cannula(e), percutaneous, birth through 5 years of age (includes fluoroscopic guidance, when performed) Notes: (For initiation and daily management of extracorporeal circulation, see 33946, 33947, 33948, 33949)
lay_term: The provider inserts a peripheral cannula through a percutaneous incision to perform extracorporeal circulation in a child from birth through five years of age. This procedure is commonly done for a child with cardiopulmonary insufficiency, a condition of the heart and lungs where an interruption in the blood circulation in the heart and pulmonary vessels leads to decreased oxygen saturation in the blood and may result in pulmonic regurgitation and heart failure. The procedure includes the use of fluoroscopic guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the peripheral artery or vein percutaneously (through the skin). He then cleans the area around the femoral or other vein or artery to insert a peripheral cannula into the open end of the vessel. The provider then slowly inserts the cannula, through the femoral or another vessel. This tube acts as an exit point for the oxygen–depleted blood from the body into an external device that acts as an artificial lung, or oxygenator. The provider may use fluoroscopic guidance while performing this procedure. If he uses a single–lumen catheter, he must next create a means for insertion of the returning oxygenated blood. In the same manner as the exit tube, he places the return cannula through the femoral or another vessel. A double– lumen catheter allows for the blood to return through the same cannula. The provider uses the extracorporeal circulation device to actively pump blood through the oxygenator in the external device, where the gas exchange occurs. A heat exchanger acts to warm the blood to body temperature before returning the blood to the patient through the cannula. The procedure includes the use of fluoroscopic guidance. The provider closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Aorta: The largest artery in the body, which arises from the left ventricle of the heart and supplies oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. Atrium (pl. atria): One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Cannula: A tube, not as flexible perhaps as a catheter, through which a trocar, a hollow pointed puncturing device, can be inserted to enable the placement of other instruments. Extracorporeal circulation: Use of a heart–lung machine to circulate the blood, providing oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange, and bypassing the heart and lungs; also, can use of an artificial kidney to remove substances typically excreted in the urine. Femoral artery: Main artery in the groin and thigh that provides oxygenated blood to the tissues of the leg. Femoral vein: Main blood vessel that carries deoxygenated blood from the legs to the heart. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Jugular vein: The blood vessel that drains blood from the neck, brain, and a part of the face to the heart. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Peripheral: Along the outside boundary or edges. Tips See 33952 for the same procedure in patients six years and older. Read Less

lay_term: The provider inserts a peripheral cannula through a percutaneous incision to perform extracorporeal circulation in a child six years and older. This procedure is commonly done for a child with cardiopulmonary insufficiency, a condition of the heart and lungs where an interruption in the blood circulation in the heart and pulmonary vessels leads to decreased oxygen saturation in the blood and may result in pulmonic regurgitation and heart failure. The procedure includes the use of fluoroscopic guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the peripheral artery or vein percutaneously, or through the skin. He then cleans the area around the femoral or other vein or artery to insert a peripheral cannula into the open end of the vessel. The provider then slowly inserts the cannula, through the femoral or another vessel. This tube acts as an exit point for the oxygen–depleted blood from the body into an external device that acts as an artificial lung, or oxygenator. The provider may use fluoroscopic guidance when he requires the guidance of a live X–ray image of the body structures while performing this procedure. Depending upon the type of cannula the provider uses, the blood may return through the same cannula. A double–lumen catheter allows for the blood to return through the same cannula. If he uses a single–lumen catheter, he must create a means for return of the oxygenated blood. In the same manner as the exit tube, he places the return cannula through the femoral or another vessel. The provider uses the extracorporeal circulation device to actively pump the blood through the oxygenator in the external device, where the gas exchange occurs. A heat exchanger acts to warm the blood to body temperature before returning the blood to the patient through the cannula. The procedure includes the use of fluoroscopic guidance. The provider closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Aorta: The largest artery in the body, which arises from the left ventricle of the heart and supplies oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. Atrium (pl. atria): One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Cannula: A tube, not as flexible perhaps as a catheter, through which a trocar, a hollow pointed puncturing device, can be inserted to enable the placement of other instruments. Extracorporeal circulation: Use of a heart–lung machine to circulate the blood, providing oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange, and bypassing the heart and lungs; also, can use of an artificial kidney to remove substances typically excreted in the urine. Femoral artery: The main artery in the groin and thigh that provides oxygenated blood to the tissues of the leg. Femoral vein: The main blood vessel that carries deoxygenated blood from the legs to the heart. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Jugular vein: The blood vessel that drains blood from the neck, brain, and a part of the face to the heart. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Peripheral: Along the outside boundary or edges. short_description: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO)/extracorporeal life support (ECLS) provided by physician; removal of peripheral (arterial and/or venous) cannula(e), percutaneous, birth through 5 years of age
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes a peripheral cannula for extracorporeal circulation, percutaneously, or through an incision through the skin, in a child from birth through five years of age. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the peripheral arterial and or venous cannula. He then cleans the area around the femoral or other vein or artery to remove the previously placed cannula from the open end of the vessel. The provider then slowly removes the cannula. For this service, the patient no longer needs the extracorporeal circulation device. The provider closes the incision with sutures. This code represents the percutaneous removal of a peripheral cannula for extracorporeal circulation, in a child from birth through five years of age. Terminology Aorta: The main artery that comes out of the top of the left ventricle and carries oxygenated blood to the body; it consists of an ascending and descending aorta which serve the upper and lower parts of the body respectively. Atrium: One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Cannula: A tube, not as flexible perhaps as a catheter, through which a trocar, a hollow pointed puncturing device, can be inserted to enable the placement of other instruments. Extracorporeal circulation: Use of a heart lung machine to circulate the blood, providing oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange, and bypassing the heart and lungs; also, can use of an artificial kidney to remove substances typically excreted in the urine. Femoral artery: Largest blood vessel passing through the thigh. Jugular vein: The blood vessel that drains blood from the neck, brain, and a part of the face to the heart. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Tips For the same procedure in patients six years and older, see 33966, Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, ECMO or extracorporeal life support, ECLS provided by physician; removal of peripheral, arterial and or venous cannula, percutaneous, six years and older.
