lay_term: The provider places an ilio–iliac tube endograft to repair a ruptured iliac artery on one side of the body. This code covers pre–procedure sizing and device selection, any nonselective catheterization, angioplasty/stenting, any endograft extensions performed up to the aortic bifurcation and down to the iliac bifurcation and all radiological supervision and interpretation. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the groin and dissects down to expose the aorta and iliac arteries. If necessary, he may occlude (close off) the iliac artery by expanding a balloon inserted through a catheter to beyond the ruptured area. He may perform angioplasty or place a stent to open up or widen the lumen (interior channel) of the iliac artery. Then, under imaging guidance, he inserts a catheter into the iliac artery. The provider then guides the tube endograft through the catheter and into the iliac artery so that the tube extends across the ruptured area and beyond into healthy areas on both sides of the defect. If the tube endograft isn’t long enough, the provider may place extensions up to as far as the aortic bifurcation (the take–off of the iliac arteries) and down to the iliac bifurcation where the common iliac arteries branch into the smaller internal and external iliac arteries. When expanded, the prosthesis reinforces the artery walls and restores blood flow. The provider withdraws the catheter, checks for bleeding, and closes all incisions. Terminology Aneurysm: Weakness in the wall of a blood vessel, such as the aorta, or the wall of heart chamber, typically the left ventricle, causing the wall to balloon out; sometimes requiring surgical excision or repair to prevent rupture. Angioplasty: A surgical procedure to widen a narrowed or blocked artery. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Nonselective catheterization: Refers to a catheter that remains in the accessed vessel or that the provider advanced to the aorta, which is still considered nonselective. Endovascular: Within a blood vessel, as in a surgical procedure in which the provider places a catheter into the blood vessel. Endovascular aneurysm repair, or EVAR: Surgical repair of an aneurysm, or weakening, in the aorta through a catheter passed through the femoral artery. Endovascular prosthesis: A tubelike structure placed within a vessel to repair the vessel; for instance, blood can flow through the prosthesis rather than placing pressure on an aneurysm; the prosthesis may have multiple connected tubes to allow for placement in multiple vessels as a unit. Endovascular surgery: A minimally invasive procedure allowing diagnostic and surgical access to blood vessels via catheter introduction. Iliac artery: The main blood vessels that supply oxygenated blood to the pelvic area; iliac arteries bifurcate from the aorta. Image guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a television monitor; ultrasound, high–frequency sound waves to view tissues; or other forms of imaging during surgical procedures. Prosthesis: An artificial or manmade replacement for a body part; also known as a prosthetic or prosthetic device; plural prostheses. Pseudoaneurysm: A collection of blood, or a hematoma contained by the periarterial fibrous tissue and formed due to a leaking hole in an artery; also known as a false aneurysm. Stent: A tubelike device used to maintain the opening of a tubular structure. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Codes 34701, 34702, 34703, 34704, 34705, 34706 describe introduction, positioning, and deployment of an endograft for treatment of abdominal aortic pathology (with or without rupture), such as aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, dissection, penetrating ulcer, or traumatic disruption in the infrarenal abdominal aorta with or without extension into the iliac artery(ies). The terms, endovascular graft, endoprosthesis, endograft, and stentgraft, refer to a covered stent. The infrarenal aortic endograft may be an aortic tube device, a bifurcated unibody device, a modular bifurcated docking system with docking limb(s), or an aorto-uni-iliac device. Codes 34707 and 34708 describe introduction, positioning, and deployment of an ilio-iliac endograft for treatment of isolated arterial pathology (with or without rupture), such as aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous malformation, or trauma involving the iliac artery. For treatment of atherosclerotic occlusive disease in the iliac artery(ies) with a covered stent(s), see 37221, 37223. For covered stent placement for atherosclerotic occlusive disease in the aorta, see 37236, 37237. Add-on code 34717 is reported at the time of aorto-iliac artery endograft placement (34703, 34704, 34705, 34706) for deployment of a bifurcated endograft in the common iliac artery with extension(s) into both the internal iliac and external iliac arteries, when performed, to maintain perfusion in both vessels for treatment of iliac artery pathology (with or without rupture), such as aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, dissection, penetrating ulcer, arteriovenous malformation, or traumatic disruption. The iliac branched endograft is a multi-piece system consisting of a bifurcated device that is placed in the common iliac artery and then additional extension(s) are placed into both the internal iliac artery and external iliac/common femoral arteries as needed, as well as a proximal extension that overlaps with an aorto-iliac endograft, when performed. All additional extensions proximally into the common iliac artery or distally into the external iliac and/or common femoral arteries are inherent to these codes. Report 34705 or 34706 for simultaneous bilateral iliac artery aneurysm repairs with aorto-bi-iliac endograft. For isolated bilateral iliac artery repair using iliac artery tube endografts, report 34707 or 34708 with modifier 50 appended. Decompressive laparotomy for abdominal compartment syndrome after ruptured abdominal aortic and/or iliac artery aneurysm repair may be separately reported with 49000 in addition to 34702, 34704, 34706, or 34708. The treatment zone for endograft procedures is defined by those vessels that contain an endograft(s) (main body, docking limb[s], and/or extension[s]) deployed during that operative session. Adjunctive procedures outside the treatment zone may be separately reported (eg, angioplasty, endovascular stent placement, embolization). For example, when an endograft terminates in the common iliac artery, any additional treatment performed in the external and/or internal iliac artery may be separately reportable. Placement of a docking limb is inherent to a modular endograft(s), and, therefore, 34709 may not be reported separately if the docking limb extends into the external iliac artery. In addition, any interventions (eg, angioplasty, stenting, additional stent graft extension[s]) in the external iliac artery where the docking limb terminates may not be reported separately. Any catheterization or treatment of the internal iliac artery, such as embolization, may be separately reported. For 34701 and 34702, the abdominal aortic treatment zone is defined as the infrarenal aorta. For 34703 and 34704, the abdominal aortic treatment zone is typically defined as the infrarenal aorta and ipsilateral common iliac artery. For 34705 and 34706, the abdominal aortic treatment zone is typically defined as the infrarenal aorta and both common iliac arteries. For 34707, 34708, 34717, 34718, the treatment zone is defined as the portion of the iliac artery(ies) (eg, common, internal, external iliac arteries) that contains the endograft. Codes 34702, 34704, 34706, 34708 are reported when endovascular repair is performed on ruptured aneurysm in the aorta or iliac artery(ies). Rupture is defined as clinical and/or radiographic evidence of acute hemorrhage for purposes of reporting these codes. A chronic, contained rupture is considered a pseudoaneurysm, and endovascular treatment of a chronic, contained rupture is reported with 34701, 34703, 34705, or 34707. Code 34709 is reported for placement of extension prosthesis(es) that terminate(s) either in the internal iliac, external iliac, or common femoral artery(ies) or in the abdominal aorta proximal to the renal artery(ies) in conjunction with 34701, 34702, 34703, 34704, 34705, 34706, 34707, 34708. Code 34709 may only be reported once per vessel treated (ie, multiple endograft extensions placed in a single vessel may only be reported once). Endograft extension(s) that terminate(s) in the common iliac arteries are included in 34703, 34704, 34705, 34706, 34707, 34708 and are not separately reported. Treatment zone angioplasty/stenting, when performed, is included in 34709. In addition, proximal infrarenal abdominal aortic extension prosthesis(es) that terminate(s) in the aorta below the renal artery(ies) are also included in 34701, 34702, 34703, 34704, 34705, 34706 and are not separately reportable. Codes 34710, 34711 are reported for delayed placement of distal or proximal extension prosthesis(es) for endovascular repair of infrarenal abdominal aortic or iliac aneurysm, false aneurysm, dissection, endoleak, or endograft migration. Pre-procedure sizing and device selection, all nonselective catheterization(s), all associated radiological supervision and interpretation, and treatment zone angioplasty/stenting, when performed, are included in 34710 and 34711. Codes 34710 and 34711 may only be reported once per vessel treated (ie, multiple endograft extensions placed in a single vessel may only be reported once). If an aorto-iliac artery endograft (34703, 34704, 34705, 34706) is not being placed during the same operative session, 34718 may be reported for placement of a bifurcated endograft in the common iliac artery with extension(s) into both the internal iliac and external iliac arteries, to maintain perfusion in both vessels for treatment of iliac artery pathology (without rupture), such as aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, dissection, arteriovenous malformation. The iliac branched endograft is a multi-piece system consisting of a bifurcated device that is placed in the common iliac artery and then additional extension(s) are placed into both the internal iliac artery and external iliac/common femoral arteries as needed as well as a proximal extension that overlaps with an aorto-iliac endograft, when performed. All additional extensions placed proximally into the common iliac artery or distally into the external iliac and/or common femoral arteries are inherent to these codes. For isolated bilateral iliac artery repair using iliac artery branched endografts, use 34718 with modifier 50 appended. Codes 34709, 34710, 34711 may not be separately reported with 34717, 34718 for ipsilateral extension prosthesis(es). However, 34709, 34710, 34711 may be reported separately for extension prosthesis(es) in the iliac/femoral arteries contralateral to the iliac branched endograft. Nonselective catheterization is included in 34701, 34702, 34703, 34704, 34705, 34706, 34707, 34708 and is not separately reported. However, selective catheterization of the hypogastric artery(ies), renal artery(ies), and/or arterial families outside the treatment zone of the endograft may be separately reported. Intravascular ultrasound (37252, 37253) performed during endovascular aneurysm repair may be separately reported. Balloon angioplasty and/or stenting within the treatment zone of the endograft, either before or after endograft deployment, is not separately reported. Fluoroscopic guidance and radiological supervision and interpretation in conjunction with endograft repair is not separately reported, and includes all intraprocedural imaging (eg, angiography, rotational CT) of the aorta and its branches prior to deployment of the endovascular device, fluoroscopic guidance and roadmapping used in the delivery of the endovascular components, and intraprocedural and completion angiography (eg, confirm position, detect endoleak, evaluate runoff) performed at the time of the endovascular infrarenal aorta and/or iliac repair. Selective arterial catheterization of the internal and external iliac arteries (eg, 36245, 36246, 36247, 36248) ipsilateral to an iliac branched endograft is included in 34717, 34718 and not separately reported. However, selective catheterization of the renal artery(ies), the contralateral hypogastric artery, and/or arterial families outside the treatment zone of the graft may be separately reported. Intravascular ultrasound (37252, 37253) performed during endovascular aneurysm repair may be separately reported. Balloon angioplasty within the target treatment zone of the endograft, either before or after endograft deployment, is not separately reported. Fluoroscopic guidance and radiological supervision and interpretation performed in conjunction with endovascular iliac branched repair is not separately reported. Endovascular iliac branched repair includes all intraprocedural imaging (eg, angiography, rotational CT) of the aorta and its branches prior to deployment of the endovascular device, fluoroscopic guidance in the delivery of the endovascular components, and intraprocedural arterial angiography (eg, confirm position, detect endoleak, evaluate runoff) performed at the time of the endovascular aorto-iliac repair). Codes 34709, 34710, 34711 include nonselective introduction of guidewires and catheters into the treatment zone from peripheral artery access(es). However, selective catheterization of the hypogastric artery(ies), renal artery(ies), and/or arterial families outside the treatment zone may be separately reported. Codes 34709, 34710, 34711 also include balloon angioplasty and/or stenting within the treatment zone of the endograft extension, either before or after deployment of the endograft, fluoroscopic guidance, and all associated radiological supervision and interpretation performed in conjunction with endovascular endograft extension (eg, angiographic diagnostic imaging of the aorta and its branches prior to deployment of the endovascular device, fluoroscopic guidance in the delivery of the endovascular components, and intraprocedural and completion angiography to confirm endograft position, detect endoleak, and evaluate runoff). Code 34712 describes transcatheter delivery of accessory-enhanced fixation devices to the endograft (eg, anchor, screw, tack), including all associated radiological supervision and interpretation. Code 34712 may only be reported once per operative session. Vascular access requiring use of closure devices for large sheaths (ie, 12 French or larger) or access requiring open surgical arterial exposure may be separately reported (eg, 34713, 34714, 34715, 34716, 34812, 34820, 34833, 34834). Code 34713 describes percutaneous access and closure of a femoral arteriotomy for delivery of endovascular prosthesis through a large arterial sheath (ie, 12 French or larger). Ultrasound guidance (ie, 76937), when performed, is included in 34713. (Percutaneous access using a sheath smaller than 12 French is included in 34701-34712 and is not separately reported.) Code 34812 describes open repair and closure of the femoral artery. Extensive repair of an artery (eg, 35226, 35286, 35371) may also be reported separately. Iliac exposure for device delivery through a retroperitoneal incision, open brachial exposure, or axillary or subclavian exposure through an infraclavicular, or supraclavicular or sternotomy incision during endovascular aneurysm repair may be separately reported (eg, 34715, 34812, 34820, 34834). Endovascular device delivery or establishment of cardiopulmonary bypass that requires creation of a prosthetic conduit utilizing a femoral artery, iliac artery with a retroperitoneal incision, or axillary or subclavian artery exposure through an infraclavicular, supraclavicular, or sternotomy incision (34714, 34716, 34833) and oversewing of the conduit at the time of procedure completion may be separately reported during endovascular aneurysm repair or cardiac procedures requiring cardiopulmonary bypass. If a conduit is converted to a bypass, report the bypass (eg, 35665) and not the arterial exposure with conduit (34714, 34716, 34833). Arterial embolization(s) of renal, lumbar, inferior mesenteric, hypogastric or external iliac arteries to facilitate complete endovascular aneurysm exclusion may be separately reported (eg, 37242). Balloon angioplasty and/or stenting at the sealing zone(s) of an endograft is an integral part of the procedure and is not separately reported. However, balloon angioplasty and/or stent deployment in vessels that do not contain endograft (outside the treatment zone for the endograft), either before or after endograft deployment, may be separately reported (eg, 37220, 37221, 37222, 37223). Other interventional procedures performed at the time of endovascular abdominal aortic aneurysm repair may be additionally reported (eg, renal transluminal angioplasty, arterial embolization, intravascular ultrasound, balloon angioplasty or stenting of native artery[s] outside the endograft treatment zone, when done before or after deployment of endograft). (For fenestrated endovascular repair of the visceral aorta, see 34841-34844. For fenestrated endovascular repair of the visceral aorta and concomitant infrarenal abdominal aorta, see 34845-34848) Section Specific Guideline Selective vascular catheterizations should be coded to include introduction and all lesser order selective catheterizations used in the approach (eg, the description for a selective right middle cerebral artery catheterization includes the introduction and placement catheterization of the right common and internal carotid arteries). Additional second and/or third order arterial catheterizations within the same family of arteries supplied by a single first order artery should be expressed by 36218 or 36248. Additional first order or higher catheterizations in vascular families supplied by a first order vessel different from a previously selected and coded family should be separately coded using the conventions described above. (For monitoring, operation of pump and other nonsurgical services, see 99190-99192, 99291, 99292, 99358, 99359, 99360) (For other medical or laboratory related services, see appropriate section) (For radiological supervision and interpretation, see 75600-75970) (For anatomic guidance of arterial and venous anatomy, see Appendix L) Primary vascular procedure listings include establishing both inflow and outflow by whatever procedures necessary. Also included is that portion of the operative arteriogram performed by the surgeon, as indicated. Sympathectomy, when done, is included in the listed aortic procedures. For unlisted vascular procedure, use 37799.

short_description: Endovascular repair of iliac artery at the time of aorto-iliac artery endograft placement by deployment of an iliac branched endograft including pre-procedure sizing and device selection, all ipsilateral selective iliac artery catheterization(s), all associated radiological supervision and interpretation, and all endograft extension(s) proximally to the aortic bifurcation and distally in the internal iliac, external iliac, and common femoral artery(ies), and treatment zone angioplasty/stenting, when performed, for rupture or other than rupture (eg, for aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, dissection, arteriovenous malformation, penetrating ulcer, traumatic disruption), unilateral (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Do not report 34717 in conjunction with 34710, 34711) (For placement of an iliac branched endograft at a separate setting than aorto-iliac endograft placement, use 34718) (Use 34717 in conjunction with 34703, 34704, 34705, 34706) (34717 may only be reported once per side. For bilateral procedure, report 34717 twice. Do not report modifier 50 in conjunction with 34717) (Do not report 34717 in conjunction with 34709 on the same side)
lay_term: During a procedure to place an endograft in the aortoiliac artery, the provider also places a branched endograft in the main iliac artery and its major branches on one side of the body to repair a rupture or other defect. The procedure includes sizing and device selection, selective catheterization on the same side, all endograft extensions, angioplasty or stenting, and all RS&I, when performed. Report this code in conjunction with the code for the primary procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized for aortoiliac artery endograft placement, the provider identifies the right or left femoral artery, depending on which side of the body he is operating on. He introduces a guidewire into the femoral artery and moves it forward to the diseased portion of the common iliac artery where it divides into the external and internal iliac arteries. He may use imaging guidance while advancing the guidewire. The provider introduces a sheath containing a bifurcated tube device (endograft), that is, a device shaped like a Y, over the guidewire and positions it with the main stem in the iliac artery and one branch in the external and one in the internal iliac artery, which bypasses the aneurysm, stenosis, or other defect that restricts blood flow. He may need to add extensions to reach past the defects in the internal and external iliac arteries and to the femoral artery. In addition, he may insert a stent across another part of the artery or perform an angioplasty by inserting a balloon through a catheter sheath and expanding it to flatten atherosclerotic plaques. He may perform selective or nonselective catheterization of the iliac artery. He performs intraoperative angiography to check for restoration of blood flow from the common iliac artery into the external and internal arteries. The provider then continues with placement of the aortoiliac artery endograft and finally removes all instruments, controls any bleeding, and closes the wound in layers. All pre–procedure sizing and device selection and RS&I is included with this code. Terminology Aneurysm: Weakness in the wall of a blood vessel or the wall of a heart chamber causing the wall to balloon out; sometimes requiring surgical excision, stent, or other type of repair to prevent rupture. Angioplasty: A surgical procedure to widen a narrowed or blocked artery. Aortoiliac artery: The aorta near the umbilicus splits into iliac arteries that run through the pelvis and further divide into arteries supplying blood to the lower limbs. Arteriovenous malformation (AVM): Abnormal connection of the arteries and veins along with absence of capillaries that may cause intense pain and bleeding. Atherosclerosis: Buildup of plaque (fatty deposits) on the walls of an artery; hardening and thickening the artery walls, which can lead to coronary artery disease; sometimes used interchangeably with arteriosclerosis (thickening and hardening of the walls of the arteries). Bifurcation: Division into two branches. Common femoral artery: Largest artery found in the femoral (thigh) region of the body. Dissection (of a vessel): Tearing of the intimal layer (lining) of a vessel allowing blood to flow between the layers of the vessel wall. Endograft: A mesh tube, somewhat like a stent, that can be placed within a vessel and expanded to provide support for a weakened artery wall; endografts can sometimes be inserted using minimally invasive techniques and placed across an aneurysmal section of the vessel, basically bypassing the aneurysm; also called a stent–graft or endoluminal graft. Endovascular: Within a blood vessel, as in a surgical procedure in which the provider places a catheter into the blood vessel. External and internal iliac arteries: Blood vessels that provide blood supply to the lower limbs. Ipsilateral: Situated on same side of the body. Penetrating ulcer: A condition that occurs in blood vessels when atherosclerotic plaque forms an ulcer that penetrates (goes through) the vessel wall; penetrating ulcers are rare and usually are found in the aorta; also called penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer. Pseudoaneurysm: A collection of blood (hematoma) contained by periarterial fibrous tissue and formed due to a leaking hole in an artery; also known as a false aneurysm. Radiologic supervision and interpretation (RS&I): Refers to when a provider oversees an imaging procedure and interprets the results; it may be included as part of a procedure code or be reported separately (if not included in the procedure) using a radiologic procedure code. Selective catheterization: Advancing a catheter into a main branch, or vascular family, off of the aorta or vena cava, or off the vessel initially entered; various vessels may be catheterized in order to reach the aorta or vena cava; in nonselective catheterization, the catheter is placed directly into a vessel and is not advanced any farther. Stent: A thin, plastic or metal tubelike device that is inserted into a tubular structure, such as a vessel or duct, to open or widen a narrowed area or support a weakened part of the structure. Unilateral: On one side only, generally applied to structures situated symmetrically on both the right and the left halves of the body. Tips Report +34717 in conjunction with an appropriate primary code. For the same procedure NOT performed in conjunction with aortoiliac artery endograft placement, see 34718. For other endovascular repair procedures of the aorta and/or iliac arteries, see 34701 through 34843. Read Less

short_description: Placement of extension prosthesis(es) distal to the common iliac artery(ies) or proximal to the renal artery(ies) for endovascular repair of infrarenal abdominal aortic or iliac aneurysm, false aneurysm, dissection, penetrating ulcer, including pre-procedure sizing and device selection, all nonselective catheterization(s), all associated radiological supervision and interpretation, and treatment zone angioplasty/stenting, when performed, per vessel treated (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 34709 in conjunction with 34701, 34702, 34703, 34704, 34705, 34706, 34707, 34708, 34845, 34846, 34847, 34848) (34709 may only be reported once per vessel treated [ie, multiple endograft extensions placed in a single vessel may only be reported once]) (Do not report 34709 for placement of a docking limb that extends into the external iliac artery) (For placement of an iliac branched endograft, see 34717, 34718) (For endograft placement into a renal artery that is being covered by a proximal extension, see 37236, 37237)
lay_term: Report this add–on code for each vessel treated when the provider places an extension prosthesis (tube graft) to repair an infrarenal abdominal aortic or iliac vessel during the performance of a primary vascular procedure. The procedure includes nonselective catheterization, angioplasty or stenting, device selection, and radiological supervision and interpretation when performed. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider initiates the procedure by performing separately reportable services such as artery exposure, guidewire and catheter placement in the vascular system, and angiography to detect the target site of an aneurysm, false aneurysm, dissection, or penetrating ulcer. The provider uses imaging guidance to guide and insert the extension prosthesis into the target area of the infrarenal abdominal aorta or iliac artery. She adjusts the extension prosthesis to ensure its correct position. The extension prosthesis expands, securing itself to the artery walls, thereby allowing blood to flow through the graft without causing further pressure on the aneurysm or penetrating ulcer. In certain instances, if the prosthesis fails to expand, then the provider inserts a balloon catheter to inflate the endoprosthesis to gain full expansion. The provider repeats angiography after the procedure, to ensure the correct position of the prosthesis. At the end of the procedure, the provider removes the instruments and checks for bleeding at the access site. Terminology Aneurysm: Weakness in the wall of a blood vessel, such as the aorta, or the wall of heart chamber, typically the left ventricle, causing the wall to balloon out; sometimes requiring surgical excision or repair to prevent rupture. Angiography: A medical imaging technique in which the provider injects a dye into blood vessels and uses plain X–rays, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging to visualize the inside, or lumen, of the vessels; more specific terms include arteriography when performed on the arteries or venography when performed on the veins; angiography can also be used to study blood supply to organs such as the heart, kidneys, and liver. Angioplasty: A surgical procedure to widen a narrowed or blocked artery. Aorta: Largest artery originating from heart, which supplies oxygenated blood to the body. Balloon catheter: A type of catheter that has a balloon at its tip, which the provider inflates to dilate, or open up, narrow passages in a vessel or tubular structure like the colon. Endovascular: Within a blood vessel, as in a surgical procedure in which the provider places a catheter into the blood vessel. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. Image guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a television monitor; ultrasound, high–frequency sound waves to view tissues; or other forms of imaging during surgical procedures. Infrarenal abdominal aorta aneurysm: An abnormal balloon–like lump present below the kidney in the abdominal aorta. Nonselective catheterization: Refers to a catheter that remains in the accessed vessel or that the provider advanced to the aorta, which is still considered nonselective. Pseudoaneurysm: Leakage of blood from the wall of an artery and then contained by surrounding tissue; also called false aneurysm. Stent: A tubelike device used to maintain the opening of a tubular structure. Ulcer: An open sore on the skin or on a mucous membrane, generally accompanied by loss of tissue and inflammation. short_description: Endovascular repair of iliac artery, not associated with placement of an aorto-iliac artery endograft at the same session, by deployment of an iliac branched endograft, including pre-procedure sizing and device selection, all ipsilateral selective iliac artery catheterization(s), all associated radiological supervision and interpretation, and all endograft extension(s) proximally to the aortic bifurcation and distally in the internal iliac, external iliac, and common femoral artery(ies), and treatment zone angioplasty/stenting, when performed, for other than rupture (eg, for aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, dissection, arteriovenous malformation, penetrating ulcer), unilateral Notes: (For bilateral placement of an iliac branched endograft, report modifier 50) (Do not report 34718 in conjunction with 34701, 34702, 34703, 34704, 34705, 34706, 34707, 34708, 34709, 34717) (Do not report 34718 in conjunction with 34710, 34711 on the same side) (For placement of an iliac branched endograft in the same setting as aorto-iliac endograft placement, use 34717) (For placement of an isolated iliac branched endograft for rupture, use 37799)
lay_term: The provider places a branched endograft in the main iliac artery and its major branches on one side of the body to repair a rupture or other defect. The procedure includes sizing and device selection, selective catheterization on the same side, all endograft extensions, angioplasty or stenting, and all RS&I, when performed. Report this code in conjunction with the code for the primary procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin of the groin over the femoral artery on one side and identifies the femoral artery. He introduces a guidewire into the femoral artery and moves it forward to the diseased portion of the common iliac artery where it divides into the external and internal iliac arteries. He may use imaging guidance while advancing the guidewire. The provider introduces a sheath containing a bifurcated tube device (endograft), that is, a device shaped like a Y, over the guidewire and positions it with the main stem in the iliac artery and one branch in the external and one in the internal iliac artery, which bypasses the aneurysm, stenosis, or other defect that restricts blood flow. He may need to add extensions to reach past the defects in the internal and external iliac arteries and to the femoral artery. In addition, he may insert a stent across another part of the artery or perform an angioplasty by inserting a balloon through a catheter sheath and expanding it to flatten atherosclerotic plaques. He may perform selective or nonselective catheterization of the iliac artery. He performs intraoperative angiography to check for restoration of blood flow from the common iliac artery into the external and internal arteries. The provider finally removes all instruments, controls any bleeding, and closes the wound in layers. All pre–procedure sizing and device selection and RS&I is included with this code. Terminology Aneurysm: Weakness in the wall of a blood vessel or the wall of a heart chamber causing the wall to balloon out; sometimes requiring surgical excision, stent, or other type of repair to prevent rupture. Angioplasty: A surgical procedure to widen a narrowed or blocked artery. Aortoiliac artery: The aorta near the umbilicus splits into iliac arteries that run through the pelvis and further divide into arteries supplying blood to the lower limbs. Arteriovenous malformation (AVM): Abnormal connection of the arteries and veins along with absence of capillaries that may cause intense pain and bleeding. Atherosclerosis: Buildup of plaque (fatty deposits) on the walls of an artery; hardening and thickening the artery walls, which can lead to coronary artery disease; sometimes used interchangeably with arteriosclerosis (thickening and hardening of the walls of the arteries). Bifurcation: Division into two branches. Common femoral artery: Largest artery found in the femoral (thigh) region of the body. Dissection (of a vessel): Tearing of the intimal layer (lining) of a vessel allowing blood to flow between the layers of the vessel wall. Endograft: A mesh tube, somewhat like a stent, that can be placed within a vessel and expanded to provide support for a weakened artery wall; endografts can sometimes be inserted using minimally invasive techniques and placed across an aneurysmal section of the vessel, basically bypassing the aneurysm; also called a stent–graft or endoluminal graft. Endovascular: Within a blood vessel, as in a surgical procedure in which the provider places a catheter into the blood vessel. External and internal iliac arteries: Blood vessels that provide blood supply to the lower limbs. Ipsilateral: Situated on same side of the body. Penetrating ulcer: A condition that occurs in blood vessels when atherosclerotic plaque forms an ulcer that penetrates (goes through) the vessel wall; penetrating ulcers are rare and usually are found in the aorta; also called penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer. Pseudoaneurysm: A collection of blood (hematoma) contained by periarterial fibrous tissue and formed due to a leaking hole in an artery; also known as a false aneurysm. Radiologic supervision and interpretation (RS&I): Refers to when a provider oversees an imaging procedure and interprets the results; it may be included as part of a procedure code or be reported separately (if not included in the procedure) using a radiologic procedure code. Selective catheterization: Advancing a catheter into a main branch, or vascular family, off of the aorta or vena cava, or off the vessel initially entered; various vessels may be catheterized in order to reach the aorta or vena cava; in nonselective catheterization, the catheter is placed directly into a vessel and is not advanced any farther. Stent: A thin, plastic or metal tubelike device that is inserted into a tubular structure, such as a vessel or duct, to open or widen a narrowed area or support a weakened part of the structure. Unilateral: On one side only, generally applied to structures situated symmetrically on both the right and the left halves of the body. Tips For the same procedure performed in conjunction with aortoiliac artery endograft placement, see +34717. For other endovascular repair procedures of the aorta and/or iliac arteries, see 34701 through 34843. Read Less

The provider makes an incision through the skin and inserts a catheter to the targeted area. The provider uses imaging guidance to guide and insert the extension prosthesis into the target area of the infrarenal abdominal aorta or iliac artery. She adjusts the extension prosthesis to ensure its correct position. The extension prosthesis expands, securing itself to the artery walls, thereby allowing blood to flow through the graft without causing further pressure on the aneurysm or penetrating ulcer. In certain instances, if the prosthesis fails to expand, then the provider inserts a balloon catheter to inflate the endoprosthesis to gain full expansion. The provider repeats angiography after the procedure, to ensure the correct position of the prosthesis. At the end of the procedure, the provider removes the instruments, checks for bleeding at the access site, and closes the incision. Angioplasty: A surgical procedure to widen a narrowed or blocked artery. Aorta: Largest artery originating from heart, which supplies oxygenated blood to the body. Balloon catheter: A type of catheter that has a balloon at its tip, which the provider inflates to dilate, or open up, narrow passages in a vessel or tubular structure like the colon. Endovascular: Within a blood vessel, as in a surgical procedure in which the provider places a catheter into the blood vessel. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. lay_term: While performing a primary procedure, the provider makes an incision in the groin down to the femoral artery in order to insert an endovascular prosthesis, a tubelike device placed within a vessel. She then continues with the primary procedure. Report this procedure separately in conjunction with the primary procedure code. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the groin over the femoral artery. She dissects tissue, ties off vessels, and retracts ligaments as necessary to expose the femoral artery. She may introduce a large sheath to provide better access for the separately reportable placement of the endovascular prosthesis. After the placement of the graft, the provider closes the arterial incision and the groin incision in layers with sutures. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Endovascular prosthesis: A tubelike device placed within a vessel to repair the vessel; for instance, blood can flow through the prosthesis rather than placing pressure on an aneurysm; the prosthesis may have multiple connected tubes to allow for placement in multiple vessels as a unit. Femoral artery: Vessel that originates as a continuation of the external iliac artery and supplies blood to the groin and lower limb. Groin: The area between the abdomen and upper thigh. Tips This code represents a unilateral service, meaning performed on one side. Append modifier 50 or RT/LT, depending on payer preference, if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally. lay_term: While performing a primary procedure, the provider makes an incision in the abdominal or retroperitoneal area to locate the iliac artery for placement of an endovascular prosthesis (a tubelike device to improve blood flow) or an occlusion device to obstruct blood flow. She then continues with the primary procedure. Report this procedure separately in conjunction with the primary procedure code. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an abdominal or retroperitoneal incision, such as 2 to 3 cm below and to the side of the umbilicus, to locate the iliac artery. The provider detaches the structures that surround the iliac artery. He creates an opening in the iliac artery large enough for introduction of the guidewires and sheaths used in deploying endovascular devices. He may insert a tube into the artery to keep it open and improve blood flow or, conversely, insert an occlusive device such as a balloon to temporarily stop blood flow when the balloon or occlusive device is expanded. After the separately reportable procedure involving placement of endovascular prosthesis or an occlusion device for endovascular therapy, the provider closes the arterial incision and the tissue incisions in layers with sutures. During the procedure, he takes care not to injure the ureters. Terminology Endovascular prosthesis: A tubelike device placed within a vessel to repair the vessel; for instance, blood can flow through the prosthesis rather than placing pressure on an aneurysm; the prosthesis may have multiple connected tubes to allow for placement in multiple vessels as a unit. Ureters: The tubes by which urine passes from the kidneys to the bladder. lay_term: While performing a primary procedure, the provider makes an abdominal or retroperitoneal incision to access the iliac artery and creates a conduit for endovascular prosthesis placement or cardiopulmonary bypass. This code cannot be billed alone; it must be reported in conjunction with the code for the primary procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an abdominal or retroperitoneal incision. He dissects the structures like the ureters that surround the iliac artery. He places loops proximal and distal to the iliac artery. He then makes a long opening in the lumen of the artery and attaches a conduit, a large diameter tube typically made of graft material, to the iliac artery opening. The provider continues with the primary procedure, placing either an endovascular prosthesis or cardiopulmonary bypass in the conduit. After completing the primary procedure, the provider either removes the conduit or cuts it near the base, repairing the site with sutures, or stitches the conduit to the distal iliac artery for a bypass graft. The provider then closes the incision site with sutures in layers to achieve hemostasis. Terminology Bypass graft: A procedure to alter the blood flow around the area of blockage taking a graft from the patient’s healthy vein or a using a synthetic material. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure’s point of attachment. Endovascular prosthesis: A tubelike device placed within a vessel to repair the vessel; for instance, blood can flow through the prosthesis rather than placing pressure on an aneurysm; the prosthesis may have multiple connected tubes to allow for placement in multiple vessels as a unit. Hemostasis: Stopping of bleeding from incisions and suture lines. Iliac artery: Large artery that supplies blood to the lower limbs and originates from the division of the aorta. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure’s point of attachment. Retroperitoneal incision: Incision behind the peritoneum, a serous cavity lining and covering the abdominal organs. Tips Do not append modifier 50 to add–on codes when a procedure is performed bilaterally; instead, you should report the add–on code twice. Read Less

lay_term: While performing a primary procedure, the provider makes an incision over the brachial artery to expose it for access for endovascular prosthesis placement. Once the primary procedure is completed, she checks for bleeding and closes the brachial artery and the surgical incision with sutures in layers. Report this code separately in addition to the code for the primary procedure. Endovascular prosthesis: A tubelike device placed within a vessel to repair the vessel; for instance, blood can flow through the prosthesis rather than placing pressure on an aneurysm; the prosthesis may have multiple connected tubes to allow for placement in multiple vessels as a unit. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure’s point of attachment. Tips This code represents a unilateral service, meaning performed on one side. lay_term: The provider makes an incision below or above the right or left clavicle down to the axillary or subclavian artery and creates a conduit in the artery for insertion of an endovascular prosthesis (tube graft). Report this code in addition to the code for the primary endovascular repair procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized and during a primary endovascular repair procedure, the provider makes an incision in the clavicular region. She dissects tissue, ties off vessels, and retracts ligaments as necessary to expose the axillary or subclavian artery. She opens the artery and creates a conduit for placement of an endovascular prosthesis. After the placement of the endograft, the provider closes the arterial incision and the clavicular incision in layers with sutures. Terminology Axillary artery: A large blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood to the thorax, the axilla or armpit, and the upper limb. Endovascular: Within a blood vessel, as in a surgical procedure in which the provider places a catheter into the blood vessel. Ligaments: Fibrous bands of tissue that connect bones and joints as well as hold organs in place. Subclavian artery: Major arteries of the upper extremities that pass beneath the clavicle and carry oxygen rich blood to the arm. Read Less

lay_term: In this add–on procedure, the provider places a graft going from one femoral artery to the other at the same session as a separately reportable endovascular repair of an aortic aneurysm. Explanation At the same session as a separately reportable endovascular repair of an aortic aneurysm, the provider exposes and prepares the femoral arteries for the placement of a femoral–to–femoral graft. She closes the incision with sutures in layers. short_description: Open repair of infrarenal aortic aneurysm or dissection, plus repair of associated arterial trauma, following unsuccessful endovascular repair; tube prosthesis
lay_term: After an unsuccessful endovascular repair, the provider uses an abdominal or retroperitoneal incision to repair an aneurysm or dissection in the infrarenal aorta using a tube prosthesis. He also repairs the associated trauma from the unsuccessful repair. Explanation After unsuccessful endovascular repair, when the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the abdomen or retroperitoneum. The provider dissects the structures surrounding the infrarenal aorta. He then explores the aorta below the kidneys to locate the exact site of the aneurysm or dissection. The provider places clamps above and below the site. Under direct visualization, he repairs the aneurysm or dissection, opening it and removing any clots. He incises the aorta to assist with placing a tube prosthesis in the aorta. He sutures the aortic incisions and also repairs any trauma due to the unsuccessful endovascular repair. The provider removes the clamps and closes the incision with sutures in layers. Terminology Aneurysm: Weakness in the wall of a blood vessel or wall of a ventricle of the heart, typically the left ventricle, causing the wall to balloon out; sometimes requiring surgical excision or repair to prevent rupture. Aorta: The main artery that comes out of the top of the left ventricle and carries oxygenated blood to the body; consists of an ascending and descending aorta which serve the upper and lower parts of the body respectively. Aortic dissection: Blood coursing within the layers of the aorta’s walls. Endovascular prosthesis: A tubelike structure placed within a vessel to repair the vessel; for instance, blood can flow through the prosthesis rather than placing pressure on an aneurysm; the prosthesis may have multiple connected tubes to allow for placement in multiple vessels as a unit. Hemostasis: Stopping of bleeding from incisions and suture lines. Infrarenal abdominal aorta: The area below the kidney in the abdominal aorta. Retroperitoneal incision: Incision behind the peritoneum, a serous cavity lining and covering the abdominal organs. Documentation should track all time the physician spends on planning. Use the date the physician completes planning as the date of service. For this code, do not include time the physician spends on planning on the day before or the day of the FEVAR procedure. You also should not use the day before or the day of the FEVAR procedure as the date of service. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline The upper abdominal aorta that contains the celiac, superior mesenteric, and renal arteries is termed the visceral aorta. The planning includes review of high-resolution cross-sectional images (eg, CT, CTA, MRI) and utilization of 3D software for iterative modeling of the aorta and device in multiplanar views and center line of flow analysis. Code 34839 may only be reported when the physician spends a minimum of 90 total minutes performing patient-specific fenestrated endograft planning. Physician planning time does not need to be continuous and should be clearly documented in the patient record. Code 34839 is reported on the date that planning work is complete and may not include time spent on the day before or the day of the fenestrated endovascular repair procedure (34841, 34842, 34843, 34844, 34845, 34846, 34847, 34848) nor be reported on the day before or the day of the fenestrated endovascular repair procedure. Codes 34841, 34842, 34843, 34844, 34845, 34846, 34847, 34848 are used to report placement of a fenestrated endovascular graft in the visceral aorta, either alone or in combination with the infrarenal aorta for aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, dissection, penetrating ulcer, intramural hematoma, or traumatic disruption. The fenestrated main body endoprosthesis is deployed within the visceral aorta. Fenestrations within the fabric allow for selective catheterization of the visceral and/or renal arteries and subsequent placement of an endoprosthesis (ie, bare metal or covered stent) to maintain flow to the visceral artery. The infrarenal component may be a bifurcated unibody device, a modular bifurcated docking system with docking limb(s), or an aorto-uniiliac device. short_description: Endovascular repair of visceral aorta (eg, aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, dissection, penetrating ulcer, intramural hematoma, or traumatic disruption) by deployment of a fenestrated visceral aortic endograft and all associated radiological supervision and interpretation, including target zone angioplasty, when performed; including one visceral artery endoprosthesis (superior mesenteric, celiac or renal artery)
lay_term: Under radiological guidance, the provider places a fenestrated endograft (with holes) to repair the visceral aorta (upper abdominal aorta with the celiac, superior mesenteric, and renal arteries). He also places a single visceral artery prosthesis. Explanation The patient is positioned and prepped, and anesthesia is administered. The provider then makes a small surgical incision near the groin area to access a femoral artery, introduces an endovascular device, and advances a guidewire from the femoral artery into the ascending aorta. Under imaging guidance, the provider identifies the location of the aneurysm (or other vascular problem to be treated) and guides the wire through the site to a point above the renal arteries. The provider cuts into the opposite femoral artery, places a sheath, and moves forward another guidewire toward the ascending aorta. Aortography may be performed to view the treatment site. The provider then introduces a special device, moves the fenestrated endoprosthesis into place, and fixates it to achieve the desired repair of the aorta. Under imaging guidance, the visceral artery prosthesis is then inserted through a fenestration and fixed in place. Angioplasty of the target area may be performed during the encounter. The provider then performs a complete examination of the blood vessels to analyze the accurate fixation of the endografts, presence or absence of any persistent blood flow, or any stricture or blood clot in between the arteries. Once everything is inspected, the provider withdraws the instruments and finally closes the incision in layers. Terminology Aneurysm: Weakness in the wall of a blood vessel or the wall of a heart chamber causing the wall to balloon out; sometimes requiring surgical excision, stent, or other types of repair to prevent rupture. Angioplasty: A surgical procedure to widen a narrowed or blocked artery. Ascending aorta: Part of the aorta that rises up from the heart from which the coronary arteries branch off to supply the heart with blood. Celiac artery: An artery that has its origin in the abdominal aorta, and which supplies many major internal organs, such as the stomach, spleen, liver, and esophagus. Dissection (of a vessel): Tearing of the intimal layer (lining) of a vessel allowing blood to flow between the layers of the vessel wall. Endoprosthesis: An intravascular device like a hollow stent that is placed into a duct to allow drainage through a blockage area or to act as a replacement for damaged ductal or vessel walls. Endograft: A mesh tube, somewhat like a stent, that can be placed within a vessel and expanded to provide support for a weakened artery wall; endografts can sometimes be inserted using minimally invasive techniques and placed across an aneurysmal section of the vessel, basically bypassing the aneurysm; also called a stent–graft or endoluminal graft. Endovascular: Within a blood vessel, as in a surgical procedure in which the provider places a catheter into the blood vessel. Femoral artery: The main artery in the groin and thigh that provides oxygenated blood to the tissues of the leg. Fenestration: A surgically created opening or cutting of a small hole in a surface such as a membrane, typically to allow fluid to drain; also, perforations, windows, or holes in a structure like a vessel, cannula, or tube. Guidewire: A device used to position a catheter, tube, or other devices into a tubular structure. Intramural hematoma: Leakage of blood within the aortic wall. Penetrating ulcer: A condition that occurs in blood vessels when atherosclerotic plaque forms an ulcer that penetrates (goes through) the vessel wall; penetrating ulcers are rare and usually are found in the aorta; also called penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer. Prosthesis (pl. prostheses): An artificial/synthetic or man–made replacement for a body part; also known as a prosthetic or prosthetic device. Pseudoaneurysm: A collection of blood (hematoma) contained by periarterial fibrous tissue and formed due to a leaking hole in an artery; also known as a false aneurysm. Renal artery: Either of two branches of the abdominal aorta, each of which supplies one of the kidneys. Superior mesenteric artery (SMA): A large artery that originates from the upper part of the aorta just below the celiac artery, around the level of the first lumbar vertebra, the SMA supplies oxygenated blood to the greater part of the small intestine, the cecum, ascending colon, and right half of the transverse colon. Tips There are multiple codes for endovascular repair of the visceral aorta; study the documentation and the descriptors for codes 34841 to 34848 to choose the best code. For example, codes 34841, 34842, 34843, and 34844 are for endovascular repair of the visceral aorta, and the difference is whether one, two, three, or four or more visceral artery endoprostheses were used, respectively. Codes 34845, 34846, 34847, and 34848 are also for endovascular repair of the visceral aorta but differ from the above four in that they include repair of the infrarenal abdominal aorta, with concomitant unibody or modular infrarenal aortic endograft and again, the difference in these four codes is whether one, two, three, or four or more visceral artery endoprostheses were used. The provider then makes a small surgical incision near the groin area to access a femoral artery, introduces an endovascular device, and advances a guidewire from the femoral artery into the ascending aorta. The provider cuts into the opposite femoral artery, places a sheath, and moves forward another guidewire toward the ascending aorta. Aortography may be performed to view the treatment site. The provider then introduces a special device, moves the fenestrated endoprosthesis into place, and fixates it to achieve the desired repair of the aorta. Under imaging guidance, the three additional visceral artery prostheses are then inserted through the fenestrations and fixed in place. Angioplasty of the target area may be performed during the encounter. The provider then performs a complete examination of the blood vessels to analyze the accurate fixation of the endografts, presence or absence of any persistent blood flow, or any stricture or blood clot in between the arteries. Celiac artery: An artery that has its origin in the abdominal aorta, and which supplies many major internal organs, such as the stomach, spleen, liver, and esophagus. Endoprosthesis: An intravascular device like a hollow stent that is placed into a duct to allow drainage through a blockage area or to act as a replacement for damaged ductal or vessel walls. lay_term: Under radiological guidance, the provider places a fenestrated endograft (with holes) to repair the visceral aorta (upper abdominal aorta with the celiac, superior mesenteric, and renal arteries). He places either a one piece or multiple piece endograft in the infrarenal aorta (abdominal aorta below the kidneys). He also places two additional visceral artery endoprostheses. Explanation The patient is positioned and prepped, and anesthesia is administered. The provider then makes a small surgical incision near the groin area to access a femoral artery, introduces an endovascular device, and advances a guidewire from the femoral artery into the ascending aorta. Under imaging guidance, the provider identifies the location of the aneurysm (or other vascular problem to be treated) and guides the wire through the site to a point above the renal arteries. The provider cuts into the opposite femoral artery, places a sheath, and moves forward another guidewire toward the ascending aorta. The provider then introduces a special device, moves the fenestrated endoprosthesis into place, and fixates it to achieve the desired repair of the aorta. Under imaging guidance, the two additional visceral artery prostheses are then moved through the fenestrations and fixed in place. Aortography may be performed to view the treatment site. He also places either a unibody (one–piece) or modular (multi–piece) endograft to repair the aorta below the kidneys. This endograft could be bifurcated unibody, modular bifurcated with docking limb(s), aorto–uni–iliac, or aorto–uni–femoral. Angioplasty of the target area may be performed during the encounter. The provider then performs a complete examination of the blood vessels to analyze the accurate fixation of the endografts, presence or absence of any persistent blood flow, or any stricture or blood clot in between the arteries. Once everything is inspected, the provider withdraws the instruments and finally closes the incision in layers. Angioplasty: A surgical procedure to widen a narrowed or blocked artery. Ascending aorta: Part of the aorta that rises up from the heart from which the coronary arteries branch off to supply the heart with blood. Celiac artery: An artery that has its origin in the abdominal aorta, and which supplies many major internal organs, such as the stomach, spleen, liver, and esophagus. Dissection (of a vessel): Tearing of the intimal layer (lining) of a vessel allowing blood to flow between the layers of the vessel wall. Endoprosthesis: An intravascular device like a hollow stent that is placed into a duct to allow drainage through a blockage area or to act as a replacement for damaged ductal or vessel walls. Endograft: A mesh tube, somewhat like a stent, that can be placed within a vessel and expanded to provide support for a weakened artery wall; endografts can sometimes be inserted using minimally invasive techniques and placed across an aneurysmal section of the vessel, basically bypassing the aneurysm; also called a stent–graft or endoluminal graft. Endovascular: Within a blood vessel, as in a surgical procedure in which the provider places a catheter into the blood vessel. Femoral artery: The main artery in the groin and thigh that provides oxygenated blood to the tissues of the leg. Fenestration: A surgically created opening or cutting of a small hole in a surface such as a membrane, typically to allow fluid to drain; also, perforations, windows, or holes in a structure like a vessel, cannula, or tube. Guidewire: A device used to position a catheter, tube, or other devices into a tubular structure. Infrarenal abdominal aortic: The part of the abdominal aorta below the kidney. Intramural hematoma: Leakage of blood within the aortic wall. Penetrating ulcer: A condition that occurs in blood vessels when atherosclerotic plaque forms an ulcer that penetrates (goes through) the vessel wall; penetrating ulcers are rare and usually are found in the aorta; also called penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer. Prosthesis (pl. prostheses): An artificial/synthetic or man–made replacement for a body part; also known as a prosthetic or prosthetic device. Pseudoaneurysm: A collection of blood (hematoma) contained by periarterial fibrous tissue and formed due to a leaking hole in an artery; also known as a false aneurysm. Renal artery: Either of two branches of the abdominal aorta, each of which supplies one of the kidneys. For example, codes 34841, 34842, 34843, and 34844 are for endovascular repair of the visceral aorta, and the difference is whether one, two, three, or four or more visceral artery endoprostheses were used, respectively. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline The upper abdominal aorta that contains the celiac, superior mesenteric, and renal arteries is termed the visceral aorta. For reporting purposes, the thoracic aorta extends from the aortic valve to the aortic segment just proximal to the celiac artery. Code 34839 is used to report the physician planning and sizing for a patient-specific fenestrated visceral aortic endograft. The planning includes review of high-resolution cross-sectional images (eg, CT, CTA, MRI) and utilization of 3D software for iterative modeling of the aorta and device in multiplanar views and center line of flow analysis. Code 34839 may only be reported when the physician spends a minimum of 90 total minutes performing patient-specific fenestrated endograft planning. Physician planning time does not need to be continuous and should be clearly documented in the patient record. Code 34839 is reported on the date that planning work is complete and may not include time spent on the day before or the day of the fenestrated endovascular repair procedure (34841, 34842, 34843, 34844, 34845, 34846, 34847, 34848) nor be reported on the day before or the day of the fenestrated endovascular repair procedure. Codes 34841, 34842, 34843, 34844, 34845, 34846, 34847, 34848 are used to report placement of a fenestrated endovascular graft in the visceral aorta, either alone or in combination with the infrarenal aorta for aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, dissection, penetrating ulcer, intramural hematoma, or traumatic disruption. The fenestrated main body endoprosthesis is deployed within the visceral aorta. Fenestrations within the fabric allow for selective catheterization of the visceral and/or renal arteries and subsequent placement of an endoprosthesis (ie, bare metal or covered stent) to maintain flow to the visceral artery. Patient variation in the location and relative orientation of the renal and visceral artery origins requires use of a patient-specific fenestrated endograft for endovascular repair that preserves flow to essential visceral arteries and allows proximal seal and fixation to be achieved above the renal level as well as in the distal aorta or iliac vessel(s). Fenestrated aortic repair is reported based on the extent of aorta treated. Codes 34841, 34842, 34843, 34844 describe repair using proximal endoprostheses that span from the visceral aortic component to one, two, three, or four visceral artery origins and distal extent limited to the infrarenal aorta. These devices do not extend into the common iliac arteries. Codes 34845, 34846, 34847, 34848 are used to report deployment of a fenestrated endograft that spans from the visceral aorta (including one, two, three, or four visceral artery origins) through the infrarenal aorta into the common iliac arteries. The infrarenal component may be a bifurcated unibody device, a modular bifurcated docking system with docking limb(s), or an aorto-uniiliac device. Codes 34845, 34846, 34847, 34848 include placement of unilateral or bilateral docking limbs (depending on the device). Any additional endograft extensions that terminate in the common iliac arteries are included in 34845, 34846, 34847, 34848. Codes 34709, 34710, 34711 may not be separately reported for proximal abdominal aortic extension prosthesis(es) or for distal extension prosthesis(es) that terminate(s) in the aorta or the common iliac arteries. However, 34709, 34710, 34711 may be reported for distal extension prosthesis(es) that terminate(s) in the internal iliac, external iliac, or common femoral artery(ies). short_description: Direct repair of aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, or excision (partial or total) and graft insertion, with or without patch graft; for aneurysm and associated occlusive disease, carotid, subclavian artery, by neck incision
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes an incision in the neck. He then advances to the target area of the carotid or subclavian artery to treat an aneurysm and related occlusive disease. The provider then performs direct repair or places a graft over the site of repair. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the front of the neck, on the outer one–third of the clavicle through the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The provider dissects the structures surrounding the target site in the carotid or subclavian artery and applies clamps on either side. She then removes the aneurysm and the other obstructions present. Following the removal of the aneurysm and obstruction, she neatly sutures the remaining ends of the artery together, or the provider places a graft to fill in the gap created in the artery. The provider also may place a patch graft, for instance, suturing a piece of tissue like a patch over an open area on one side of the vessel to cover the area or help widen the artery and ease blood flow. She closes the incision with sutures in layers. Terminology Aneurysm: Weakness in the wall of a blood vessel or wall of a ventricle of the heart, typically the left ventricle, causing the wall to balloon out; sometimes requiring surgical excision or repair to prevent rupture. Carotid artery: Artery in the neck that supplies blood to the face, neck, and brain; there are two carotid arteries, one on the left and one on the right. Clavicle: A long bone present on either side of neck that links the upper limb to the thorax; it is also called the collarbone and is the only horizontal long bone in the body. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. Occlusive disease: A disease in which the arteries throughout the body narrow and finally completely block. Patch, patch graft: Artificial material, autologous tissue from the patient’s own body, or preserved tissue from a donor used to cover a defect or replace removed tissue or a portion of a structure. Pseudoaneurysm: Leakage of blood from the wall of an artery and then contained by surrounding tissue; also called false aneurysm. Sternocleidomastoid muscle: Long, thick muscle on each side of the neck that helps in turning and nodding of the head. Subclavian arteries: Major arteries of the upper extremities that pass beneath the clavicle and carry oxygen rich blood to the arm. Tips Use 35002 if the provider repairs a ruptured aneurysm by graft. Read Less

short_description: Thromboendarterectomy, including patch graft, if performed; carotid, vertebral, subclavian, by neck incision
lay_term: The provider removes thrombus and plaques from a carotid, vertebral, or subclavian artery through a neck incision. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the neck to access the abnormal lining of the affected carotid, vertebral, or subclavian artery. If she needs to harvest a vein to make a graft, she makes an incision over the vein, excises the graft, ties off the donor vein ends, and preps the graft. She places vascular clamps on the carotid, vertebral, or subclavian as needed and opens the artery. The provider then performs an endarterectomy to remove the portion of the artery where the thrombus or atherosclerosis has formed. She removes the intima, or the inner lining, of the artery to maintain a normal inner diameter of the artery over the affected area. She then removes the shunt and clamp to return normal blood flow and closes the skin incision in layers after ensuring hemostasis. lay_term: In this add–on procedure, the provider creates a composite graft, or a conduit, made out of two vein segments from two distal sites for use as a bypass graft. Explanation To create an autogenous composite graft, a provider harvests segments of vein from different locations, often a limb other than that undergoing bypass. As the patient is already under anesthesia, the provider incises the area of the first vein, dissects surrounding tissue and removes the vein. He then repeats the procedure to harvest another segment of vein from another location. After the provider harvests the veins and closes the sites, he then constructs the graft using fine sutures to attach the vein segments. He tests the suture lines for patency and adds sutures as necessary. He then uses this longer composite vein for a separately reportable bypass procedure to complete a distal arterial bypass. Terminology Arteriosclerosis: An abnormal thickening and hardening of the walls of the arteries. Atherosclerosis: A specific type of arteriosclerosis where the artery walls thicken and become narrowed or blocked due to the deposit of plaques inside the arteries, which restricts blood flow. Autogenous tissue graft, autologous tissue graft: Tissue harvested from the patient’s own body used to replace diseased, damaged, or missing tissue. Bypass graft: A healthy vessel taken from one area and grafted, or connected, to a blocked or severely narrowed vessel in another area to permit blood flow to bypass, or flow around, the obstruction. Conduit: A connection, such as an anastomosis, created to connect one tubular structure such as a vessel or ventricle to another structure; a tube–shaped graft. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure’s point of attachment. Tips Report this code when a provider harvests and combines two healthy vein segments from two other areas of the patient’s body to form the composite graft. You may see this in patients who have had previous cardiac procedures or lower extremity bypass procedures. The provider may use a composite graft when the vein is unsuitable because of anatomical reasons such as multiple branching or due to sclerosis. short_description: Transposition and/or reimplantation; vertebral to carotid artery

The provider performs this service to improve arterial blood flow. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises above the clavicular area over the vertebral and carotid arteries. He then re implants the vertebral artery to the subclavian artery at the chosen site to avoid the area of blockage of blood flow. He attaches the arteries in an end to side manner. This allows blood to flow normally. Finally, he may check the patency of the graft through an arteriography or ultrasound probe. He then closes the incisions and places a drain. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider reoperates on an arterial bypass graft more than a month after the initial procedure to place the graft. This service is done to open a stricture in a graft or to replace the graft that bypasses around a damaged or obstructed portion of an artery. He uses this code to report the additional work necessary to reaccess and repair or replace a graft. Explanation In a previous surgery, the provider performs a standard bypass procedure in the patient's lower extremities. This procedure will have included the provider using either healthy veins or arteries that he harvests from other areas of the body or limb, or he will have used a synthetic bypass on the blocked artery. The provider will have grafted the healthy pieces into the artery to bypass the blocked portion. The introductory incision will have been sutured and the patient will have been released. If during a postoperative examination the provider finds that the artery needs further repair or revision, the provider repeats the procedure on the appropriate location. This occurs one month or more after the initial procedure. The provider first performs an arteriography to assess the location and extent of the occlusion. Then when the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the location of the affected arteries to access and expose the arteries and the graft previously put in place. The provider is careful not to injure any branches from the femoral artery. The provider then incises the artery above the point of the graft attachment and inserts a balloon catheter to open a narrowing in the graft or to straighten the graft. If the graft requires replacement, the provider incises and reconstructs the graft. He may replace the entire construct after placing clamps above and below the affected portion or sutures the ends of a new graft to the sides of the artery, creating a bypass around the stricture. When the procedure is complete, he removes all clamps and instrumentation, checks for bleeding, and closes the incisions in layers. Bypass graft: A healthy vessel taken from one area and grafted, or connected, to a blocked or severely narrowed vessel in another area to permit blood flow to bypass, or flow around, the obstruction. Distal: The point furthest away from a given starting point. Femoral artery: The main blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood to the legs. short_description: Exploration not followed by surgical repair, artery; upper extremity (eg, axillary, brachial, radial, ulnar)
lay_term: The provider explores a previously operated area on the upper extremity to ascertain whether there is postoperative injury, clot, leaking blood vessels, or other abnormality in vessels such as the axillary, brachial, radial, or ulnar arteries. The exploration is not followed by surgical repair. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the upper extremity artery in question. She dissects down, being careful to preserve the vessels and structures surrounding the artery. She then frees the artery from any surrounding adhesions or scar tissue and examines the artery. In this service, the provider finds no injury for repair and closes the incision in layers. If, however, the provider finds during examination that the artery needs further repair or revision, she performs, documents, and reports the repair procedure, instead of this one, because the definition states, “not followed by surgical repair.” Terminology Axillary artery: A large blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood to the thorax, the axilla or armpit, and the upper limb. Brachial artery: Chief artery of the upper arm that is a direct continuation of the axillary artery and divides into the radial and ulnar arteries just below the elbow. Common femoral artery: Largest artery found in the femoral (thigh) region of the body. Deep femoral artery: Large deep branch of the femoral artery formed where it divides about two inches below the inguinal ligament. Lysis: The act of breaking down a structure; destroying cells or tissue using an agent or substance; in vascular surgery, instilling a clot–dissolving drug to break up a clot. Peroneal artery: A deep muscle artery that supplies the back of the fibula, the lateral bone of the leg that ends near the ankle; also known as the fibular artery. Popliteal artery: A continuation of the femoral artery that runs deep in the muscles along the back of the leg. Radial artery: Major vessel that supplies oxygenated blood to the forearm. Superficial femoral artery (SFA): Major vessel that supplies oxygenated blood to the lower legs. Tibial artery: Artery of the lower leg that originates from the popliteal artery and further divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries. Ulnar artery: Major vessel that supplies oxygenated blood to the forearm. Tips Report exploration only if no other service is performed. If an artery is examined through the same incision used for an open procedure performed during the same operative session, the exploration is part of the procedure and not reported separately. If the artery is examined and a defect is discovered and repaired, report the repair, not the exploration. For the same procedure on lower extremity arteries, see 35703, and for the same procedure on the neck arteries, see 35701. Read Less
