short_description: Exploration for postoperative hemorrhage, thrombosis or infection; neck
lay_term: The provider reopens a patient’s neck to find and correct the source of bleeding, clotting, or infection after a previous operation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin of the patient’s neck over the area for examination. She dissects down being careful to preserve underlying vessels and structures. She examines the site of hemorrhage, thrombosis, or infection related to blood vessels and controls the source of the bleeding or removes the thrombus or area of infection. For instance, for hemorrhage, she locates the hemorrhaging vessel and uses manual compression to keep the bleeding under control until she can apply clamps and then cauterizes, ligates, or sutures the vessel. She checks for additional areas of bleeding in the neck, particularly those near or related to the previous surgery. If a thrombosis is found, she incises the vessel and removes the blood clot. For an infection, the provider drains the area and may place a drain for ongoing removal of fluid. Upon completion of the procedure, she checks for return of normal blood flow in repaired vessels, irrigates the area, and closes the surgical wound, except when leaving the wound open for ongoing drainage of the infection. Terminology Cauterize: To burn tissue with heat or a chemical. Hemorrhage: Bleeding, typically used to refer to active or significant bleed. Infection: A disease condition that bacteria, viruses, or other microorganisms cause. Ligate: Close, tie off, repair, or encircle a vessel or other structure with sutures or wire. Thrombosis: Formation of a blood clot, also called a thrombus that remains blocked within a blood vessel where it forms. Tips Code 35800 differs from other excision or repair codes because it takes place in the circulatory system. This means the provider’s concern is with managing a hemorrhage via the blood vessels, rather than by exploring the source of the bleeding. Use codes 35800 to 35860 when the provider has to return the patient to the operating room for exploration for postoperative hemorrhage. That means you cannot use these codes for bleeding that occurs during the initial operative session. You may need to attach modifier 78, Unplanned return to the operating room by the same physician following initial procedure for a related procedure during the postoperative period, to 35800 to indicate that the service represents a return to the operating room for a related procedure during the postoperative period. short_description: Thrombectomy of arterial or venous graft (other than hemodialysis graft or fistula)
lay_term: The provider removes a clot from a vascular graft, other than one used for hemodialysis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the vascular graft. He dissects tissue to reach and visualize the graft. He clamps the vein or artery to stop blood flow through the graft. He may make an incision in the graft to take out the thrombus. He also may incise the vessel and then insert a balloon catheter, moving it past the clot, inflating the balloon, and then pulling the clots out of the graft and possibly the downstream vessels as he removes the balloon catheter. He sutures the graft or vessel closed, removes the clamps to restore blood flow, and then closes the other surgical incisions. This code does not apply to thrombectomy of a hemodialysis graft or fistula. Terminology Balloon catheter: A flexible tube with a balloon at the tip that can be inflated and deflated with a mechanism at the other end. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. Thrombectomy: Removal of a blood clot from a vessel. Thrombus: A blood clot. Tips If the provider performs thrombectomy with graft revision, see 35876, Thrombectomy of arterial or venous graft, other than hemodialysis graft or fistula; with revision of arterial or venous graft. short_description: Revision, lower extremity arterial bypass, without thrombectomy, open; with vein patch angioplasty Notes: Codes 35879 and 35881 describe open revision of graft-threatening stenoses of lower extremity arterial bypass graft(s) (previously constructed with autogenous vein conduit) using vein patch angioplasty or segmental vein interposition techniques. For thrombectomy with revision of any noncoronary arterial or venous graft, including those of the lower extremity, (other than hemodialysis graft or fistula), use 35876. For direct repair (other than for fistula) of a lower extremity blood vessel (with or without patch angioplasty), use 35226. For repair (other than for fistula) of a lower extremity blood vessel using a vein graft, use 35256.
lay_term: The provider opens a lower extremity arterial bypass graft and applies a venous patch to widen a narrowed area. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the lower extremity arterial bypass graft. He dissects tissue to reach and visualize the bypass graft. He confirms the site of narrowing, such as by Doppler. He obtains a venous graft from another area by incision of the skin over the donor site, ligation of the vein ends, and excision of the vein for graft. He clamps the bypass graft on either side of the narrowed area and then incises the bypass graft to open it. He then takes the vein he harvested, opens it, and prepares it to fit in the needed space in the bypass graft to widen the narrowed area. He sutures the vein in as a patch. He removes the clamps and checks for proper blood flow. He then closes the surgical incisions. Terminology Doppler ultrasound: Use of reflected sound waves to observe blood flow through a vessel; ultrasound is when the provider uses high–frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Patch, patch graft: Artificial material, autologous tissue from the patient’s own body, or preserved tissue from a donor used to cover a defect or replace removed tissue or a portion of a structure. Thrombectomy: Removal of a blood clot from a vessel. short_description: Arterial catheterization or cannulation for sampling, monitoring or transfusion (separate procedure); cutdown
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes an incision in the skin to locate the artery and then inserts a catheter into the artery. He uses this catheter for the purpose of sampling, transfusion, or continuous real time blood pressure and heart rate monitoring. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin and retracts the soft tissue to locate the target artery, usually the radial or ulnar artery. Next, he inserts a needle to puncture the artery and then using the needle inserts a catheter or cannula. He then removes the needle once the catheter is in the appropriate position. Next, he uses the catheter to sample, transfuse, or conduct real time cardiovascular monitoring. When the procedure is complete, the provider removes the catheter and sutures the artery. He then closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Arterial catheter or cannula: A thin plastic tube that a provider inserts into an artery; the radial artery in the wrist is the most common choice for the purpose of arterial catheterization. Artery: A blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood from heart to different part of the body. Cannula: A small tube that a provider inserts into the body through which a trocar, a hollow pointed puncturing device, can be inserted to enable the placement of other instruments into a cavity to draw off fluid or introduce medication. Catheter: A catheter is a tube that can be inserted into a body cavity, duct, or vessel; catheters thereby allow drainage, administration of fluids or gases, or access by surgical instruments; the process of inserting a catheter is called catheterization. Catheterization: The process of inserting a catheter. Radial artery: Major artery in the forearm that supplies the arm and hand with oxygenated blood from the lungs. Sampling: Collecting the blood sample for the purpose of laboratory investigation. Transfusion: A process of adding blood products such as plasma, red blood cells to patient’s own blood intravenously, through a vein. Ulnar artery: Main blood vessel in the forearm carrying oxygenated blood, ending in the superficial palmar arch where it joins the superficial branch of the radial artery. Tips The descriptor for code 36625 indicates it is a separate procedure, meaning that you cannot report this code separately with a related procedure when a provider performs this service in an anatomically related region through the same skin incision. If the provider performs the 36625 procedure with an unrelated procedure, you may need to append modifier 59, Distinct procedural service to 36625. Use 36620, Arterial catheterization or cannulation for sampling, monitoring or transfusion; separate procedure; percutaneous, when the provider percutaneously inserts a catheter through the skin into an artery and uses this catheter for the purpose of sampling, transfusion, or blood pressure and heart rate monitoring. Use 36640, Arterial catheterization for prolonged infusion therapy, chemotherapy, cutdowns, when the provider makes an incision in the skin to locate the artery and then inserts a catheter into the artery for the purpose of prolonged infusion therapy. short_description: Catheterization, umbilical artery, newborn, for diagnosis or therapy Notes: (Do not report modifier 63 in conjunction with 36660)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider inserts a catheter into one of the two arteries of the umbilical cord of a newborn. The provider performs this procedure to either collect blood for diagnostic purposes or to quickly administer medication directly into circulation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider prepares the umbilical stump by sterilizing it with antiseptic solution and grasps it with a pair of forceps. He ties a short piece of umbilical tape around the base of the stump. He then grasps the stump with forceps and uses a scalpel to incise the cord. He next identifies the umbilical artery and inserts the catheter into an opening in the artery. He uses radiological imaging to confirm the positioning of the catheter. He ensures the patency of the catheter by checking for an easy withdrawal of blood. The provider uses the catheter then to collect blood specimens or to administer medication. Catheterization: The process of inserting a catheter. Forceps: A two bladed instrument used to compress or grasp. Patent: Open or unobstructed. Umbilical artery: A paired artery present in the umbilical cord of the fetus or new born. Umbilical cord: A cord connecting fetus with placenta of mother and transports nutrients from mother and waste from fetus. short_description: Insertion of cannula for hemodialysis, other purpose (separate procedure); vein to vein
lay_term: The provider inserts a cannula into two veins for hemodialysis, a process in which a dialysis machine removes harmful wastes, salt, and fluids from the blood and reinfuses the purified blood back into the patient's circulation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider chooses an access point on the arm or forearm for tube insertion. He first cleans the area with antiseptic solution and then inserts a needle into two veins in the arm or forearm. Then using the needle or a guide wire, he inserts an end of a single cannula into each vein. The cannula then allows vein–to–vein access for the performance of hemodialysis. The patient's blood flows out of one end of tube, into a dialysis machine, and back into the body through the other end of tube. The provider may leave the cannula in place for several days. Terminology Cannula: A small tube that a provider inserts into the body through which a trocar, a hollow pointed puncturing device, can be inserted to enable the placement of other instruments into a cavity to draw off fluid or introduce medication. Dialysis machine: A machine that a provider uses for hemodialysis that filters a patient’s blood of harmful wastes that occur as a result of kidney failure. Vein: A blood vessel that carries the deoxygenated blood in the body. lay_term: The provider inserts one or more cannulas into an artery and vein to perform isolated extracorporeal circulation in patients along with heated or nonheated regional chemotherapy perfusion to an extremity. Extracorporeal circulation is the diversion of the patient’s blood through an external device that takes over the work normally performed by a normal heart and lung. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider identifies the artery and vein of the extremity he wants to use to selectively isolate the blood flow in. He then inserts the cannula, into the selected artery and vein. This tube in the vein acts as an exit point of the oxygen–depleted blood from the extremity into an external device that acts as an artificial lung, or oxygenator. Similarly, the tube in the artery acts as an entry point for the oxygenated blood returning from the device thereby providing for isolated extracorporeal circulation. The blood returning to the patient may also be heated by the external device to match the patient’s body temperature. The provider also then through the external device administers a high dose chemotherapy agent into the blood that targets and kills the cancer cells in the extremity in combination with the heat. Once, the provider completes the chemotherapy procedure, he removes the cannula and closes the puncture sites in the artery and the vein. Chemotherapy: Use of chemical agents that provider administers directly into circulation through a vein or artery to kill fast–growing cells in the body, typically cancer. short_description: Creation of arteriovenous fistula by other than direct arteriovenous anastomosis (separate procedure); autogenous graft Notes: (For direct arteriovenous anastomosis, use 36821)
lay_term: The provider surgically creates an arteriovenous fistula, a connection between an artery and a vein, using an autogenous vein graft from the patient. This service is done to allow for hemodialysis treatments. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision and locates the vein and an artery using radiological imaging. He clears the area around the artery and the vein and dissects them free. He then attaches a vessel clamp on each to stop the blood flow. Next, he makes an incision in the thigh or calf area and obtains a vein to use as a graft. He sutures the graft to the artery and the vein that he has freed. To create the fistula, he pulls the graft through a tunnel that he creates just under the skin and attaches one end to the artery and the other end to the vein. He removes the clamps from the blood vessels allowing the blood to flow freely through the graft. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissues in layers. In a normal arteriovenous connection, blood flows from the artery and into blood capillaries before passing into the vein. If the capillary connection is bypassed, tissues in the affected area receive less than the necessary blood supply. This connection is also important in cases where hemodialysis is necessary. The physician needs to establish that connection via arteriovenous anastomosis. Artery: A blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the heart to different parts of the body. Autogenous tissue graft: Tissue a provider harvests from the patient’s own body and uses to replace diseased, damaged, or missing tissue. Fistula: Connection between an organ, vessel, or other structure. Hemodialysis: Treatment for advanced, permanent kidney failure; during typical hemodialysis, a dialysis machine removes the harmful wastes, salts, and fluid from the blood that would normally be eliminated in urine. Vein: A blood vessel that carries deoxygenated blood in the body. Tips Report 36825 when a provider creates the arteriovenous graft he uses for anastomosis from material taken from the patient's own body. If the provider performs the 36825 procedure with an unrelated procedure, you may need to append modifier 59, distinct procedural service to 36825. Be sure the documentation supports the procedure as a separate procedure and not part of some other related procedure. Do not append modifier 59 when a more specific modifier, such as XE (same date, separate encounter), XP (different practitioner), XS (separate organ or structure), or XU (service does not overlap with the usual components of the main service). Documentation must support the use of the modifier. Do not confuse modifier 59 with modifier 51 for multiple procedures (e.g., same procedure on different anatomic sites, related procedures on the same anatomic site, or the same procedure multiple times on the same anatomic site). short_description: Insertion of Thomas shunt (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider inserts an arteriovenous shunt between an artery and vein. He most often places this shunt in a patient who will receive hemodialysis treatments. Hemodialysis is a process in which a dialysis machine removes harmful wastes, salt, and fluids from the blood and reinfuses the purified blood back into the patient's circulation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the vein and artery in the targeted site. He first dissects the vein and the artery and attaches clamps to each to stop the bleeding. He next inserts a needle into the vessel and threads a guidewire into the blood vessel using the needle. He then inserts the Thomas shunt into the vessel using the guidewire, placing one end into an artery and the other into a vein. He then removes the guidewire. The Thomas shunt provides end to end anastomosis between the artery and the vein. Artery: A blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the heart to the different parts of the body. Shunt: A shunt forms the bypass channel or passageway in the blood circulation connecting two blood vessels and diverts blood from one region to another. Vein: A blood vessel that carries deoxygenated blood in the body. Read Less

short_description: Distal revascularization and interval ligation (DRIL), upper extremity hemodialysis access (steal syndrome) Notes: (Do not report 36838 in conjunction with 35512, 35522, 35523, 36832, 37607, 37618)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses distal revascularization and interval ligation, or DRIL, to surgically correct a dialysis access induced ischemia of the lower part of the upper extremity, also known as Steal syndrome. The provider restores the blood supply to the hand and preserves the access site. The aim of this surgical intervention is to maintain the vascular supply of the forearm and hand while preserving the blood flow towards the hemodialysis access location. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider initially explores the hemodialysis access site in the patient's upper extremity and uses a vein bypass graft, or vein, from another location of the patient's body to increase the blood supply to the arteries of the lower arm. He carries the vein graft from a portion of the upper arm, above to the hemodialysis fistula, and joins it to the artery below the access site for hemodialysis. This restores the blood supply to the hand. In addition to the revascularization procedure, the provider also segregates and binds a part of a brachial artery between the distal joining of the bypass graft and hemodialysis fistula location. This part of the procedure is called ligation. The provider performs this to ensure an appropriate vascular supply to the lower portion of the upper extremity without interrupting the blood flow to the site of hemodialysis access. Brachial artery: A major artery located in the upper arm that supplies blood to the arm, forearm and hand. short_description: Introduction of needle(s) and/or catheter(s), dialysis circuit, with diagnostic angiography of the dialysis circuit, including all direct puncture(s) and catheter placement(s), injection(s) of contrast, all necessary imaging from the arterial anastomosis and adjacent artery through entire venous outflow including the inferior or superior vena cava, fluoroscopic guidance, radiological supervision and interpretation and image documentation and report Notes: (Do not report 36901 in conjunction with 36833, 36836, 36837, 36902, 36903, 36904, 36905, 36906)
lay_term: The provider introduces a needle and/or catheter under fluoroscopic guidance (live X–rays that can be viewed on a monitor) and injects intravenous contrast material to visualize and record images of the entire dialysis circuit to assess blood flow or locate an obstruction; radiological supervision, interpretation, image capture, and report are included in this code. Explanation The patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized. Using fluoroscopic guidance, the provider introduces a needle and/or a catheter through the skin over a surgically created connection between an artery and a vein (arteriovenous graft, fistula, or anastomosis) that serves as the dialysis access point. He injects contrast material (a special dye used in radiology imaging) to visualize the circulation throughout the arterial and venous components of the entire dialysis circuit, including the superior and/or inferior vena cava. The superior vena cava carries blood from the upper parts of the body, the inferior vena cava from the lower parts of the body, and both empty into the right atrium of the heart. He withdraws the needle and/or catheter and puts pressure over the access point to control bleeding. The provider supervises the procedure, documents the images, interprets the findings and prepares a report. Terminology Angiography: A medical imaging technique in which the provider injects a dye into blood vessels and uses plain X–rays, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging to visualize the inside, or lumen, of the vessels; more specific terms include arteriography when performed on the arteries or venography when performed on the veins; angiography can also be used to study blood supply to organs such as the heart, kidneys, and liver. Arteriovenous anastomosis: An abnormal connection between an artery and a vein made either surgically, as a result of trauma or a medical condition, or congenital; also be referred to as an arteriovenous fistula or graft. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Dialysis: The process of purification of blood by using a dialysis machine as a substitute for the normal function of the kidneys, which are paired organs found in the back of the abdomen that filter waste products from the blood and then excrete the toxins in the form of urine. Stent: A tubelike device used to maintain the opening of a tubular structure. Transluminal balloon angioplasty: A surgical procedure in which the provider passes a catheter with a balloon at its tip to an area of obstruction or narrowing in an artery; he inflates the balloon, which flattens the plaque and intima (the innermost layer of the wall of a vessel) back up against the wall and increases the diameter of the lumen (open interior of the vessel). Tips This procedure includes angiography, including radiological supervision and interpretation, image documentation and report, as well as image guidance and monitoring for both the diagnostic and therapeutic portions of the procedure, so do not report these procedures separately. Do not report this code more than once per session. For the same procedure including angioplasty of the peripheral dialysis segment, report 36902. For the same procedure with placement of a stent instead of angioplasty, report 36903. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Definitions Dialysis circuit: The arteriovenous (AV) dialysis circuit is designed for easy and repetitive access to perform hemodialysis. It begins at the arterial anastomosis and extends to the right atrium. The circuit may be created using either an arterial-venous anastomosis, known as an arteriovenous fistula (AVF), or a prosthetic graft placed between an artery and vein, known as an arteriovenous graft (AVG). The dialysis circuit is comprised of two segments, termed the (1) peripheral dialysis segment and (2) central dialysis segment. Both are defined as follows. Peripheral dialysis segment: The peripheral dialysis segment is the portion of the dialysis circuit that begins at the arterial anastomosis and extends to the central dialysis segment. In the upper extremity, the peripheral dialysis segment extends through the axillary vein (or entire cephalic vein in the case of cephalic venous outflow). In the lower extremity, the peripheral dialysis segment extends through the common femoral vein. The peripheral dialysis segment includes the historic "peri-anastomotic region" (defined below). Central dialysis segment: The central dialysis segment includes all draining veins central to the peripheral dialysis segment. In the upper extremity, the central dialysis segment includes the veins central to the axillary and cephalic veins, including the subclavian and innominate veins through the superior vena cava. In the lower extremity, the central dialysis segment includes the veins central to the common femoral vein, including the external iliac and common iliac veins through the inferior vena cava. Peri-anastomotic region: A historic term referring to the region of a dialysis circuit near the arterial anastomosis encompassing a short segment of the parent artery, the anastomosis, and a short segment of the dialysis circuit immediately adjacent to the anastomosis. The peri-anastomotic region is included within the peripheral segment of the dialysis circuit. Performed through dialysis circuit: Any diagnostic study or therapeutic intervention within the dialysis circuit that is performed through a direct percutaneous access to the dialysis circuit. Code 36901 includes direct access and imaging of the entire dialysis circuit. Antegrade and/or retrograde punctures of the dialysis circuit are typically used for imaging, and contrast may be injected directly through a needle or through a catheter placed into the dialysis circuit. All dialysis circuit punctures required to perform the procedure are included in 36901. Occasionally, the catheter needs to be advanced further into the circuit to adequately visualize the arterial anastomosis or the central veins, or selective catheterization of a venous branch may be required. All manipulation(s) of the catheter for diagnostic imaging of the dialysis circuit is included in 36901. Advancement of the catheter to the vena cava to adequately image that segment of the dialysis circuit is included in 36901 and is not separately reported. Code 36901 also includes catheterization of additional venous side branches communicating with the dialysis circuit, known as accessory veins. Advancement of the catheter tip through the arterial anastomosis to adequately visualize the anastomosis is also included in the service described by 36901 and is not separately reported. Evaluation of the peri-anastomotic portion of the inflow is an integral part of the dialysis circuit angiogram and is included in 36901. For the purposes of reporting dialysis access maintenance services, the arterial inflow to the dialysis circuit is considered a separate vessel. If a more proximal arterial inflow problem separate from the peripheral dialysis segment is suspected, additional catheter placement and imaging required for adequate evaluation of the artery may be separately reported. If a catheter is selectively advanced from the dialysis circuit puncture beyond the peri-anastomotic segment into the inflow artery, an additional catheterization code may be reported. For example, 36215 may be used to report image-guided retrograde catheter placement into the inflow artery and into the aorta, if necessary (36200 is not reported in addition to 36215 in this example). Note that 75710 may also be reported if contrast injection for diagnostic arteriography is performed through this catheter and radiological supervision and interpretation and imaging documentation is performed. Ultrasound guidance for puncture of the dialysis circuit access is not typically performed and is not included in 36901, 36902, 36903, 36904, 36905, 36906. However, in the case of a new (immature) or failing AVF, ultrasound may be necessary to safely and effectively puncture the dialysis circuit for evaluation, and this may be reported separately with 76937, if all the appropriate elements for reporting 76937 are performed and documented. For radiological supervision and interpretation of dialysis circuit angiography performed through existing access(es) or catheter-based arterial access, report 36901 with modifier 52. Dialysis Circuit Interventions (AV Grafts and AV Fistulae): For the purposes of coding interventional procedures in the dialysis circuit (both AVF and AVG), the dialysis circuit is artificially divided into two distinct segments: peripheral dialysis segment and central dialysis segment (see definitions). Codes 36901, 36902, 36903 and 36904, 36905, 36906 are built on progressive hierarchies that have more intensive services, which include less intensive services. Report only one code (36901, 36902, 36903, 36904, 36905, 36906) for services provided in a dialysis circuit. Code 36901 describes the diagnostic evaluation of the dialysis circuit, and this service is included in the services described by 36901, 36902, 36903, 36904, 36905, 36906. All catheterizations required to perform diagnostic fistulography are included in 36901. All catheterizations required to perform additional interventional services are included in codes 36902, 36903, 36904, 36905, 36906, 36907, 36908, 36909 and not separately reported. All angiography, fluoroscopic image guidance, roadmapping, and radiological supervision and interpretation required to perform each service are included in each code. Closure of the puncture(s) by any method is included in the service of each individual code. Code 36902 includes the services in 36901 plus transluminal balloon angioplasty in the peripheral segment of the dialysis circuit. Code 36902 would be reported only once per session to describe all angioplasty services performed in the peripheral segment of the dialysis circuit, regardless of the number of distinct lesions treated within that segment, the number of times the balloon is inflated, or the number of balloon catheters or sizes required to open all lesions, and includes angioplasty of the peri-anastomotic segment when performed. Code 36903 includes the services in 36902 plus transcatheter stent placement in the peripheral segment of the dialysis circuit. Code 36903 is reported only once per session to describe placing stent(s) within the peripheral segment, regardless of the number of stent(s) placed or the number of discrete lesion(s) treated within the peripheral segment. If both angioplasty and stenting are performed in the peripheral segment, including treatment of separate lesions, report 36903 only once. Code 36904 describes percutaneous transluminal mechanical thrombectomy and/or infusion for thrombolysis in the dialysis circuit (all thrombus treated in both the peripheral and central dialysis circuit segments) and includes diagnostic angiography (36901), fluoroscopic image guidance, catheter placement(s), and all maneuvers required to remove thrombus from the peripheral and/or central segments, including all intraprocedural pharmacological thrombolytic injection(s)/infusion(s). It is never appropriate to report removal of the arterial plug during a declot/thrombectomy procedure as an angioplasty (36905). Removal of the arterial plug is included in a fistula thrombectomy, even if a balloon catheter is used to mechanically dislodge the resistant thrombus. Codes 36905 (angioplasty) and 36906 (stent) describe services in the peripheral circuit when performed in conjunction with thrombolysis/thrombectomy. Code 36905 includes the services in 36904 plus transluminal balloon angioplasty in the peripheral segment of the dialysis circuit. Code 36905 may be reported only once per session to describe all angioplasty performed in the peripheral segment of the dialysis circuit, regardless of the number of distinct lesions treated within that segment, the number of times the balloon is inflated, or the number of balloon catheters required to open all lesions. Code 36906 includes the services in 36905 plus transcatheter stent placement in the peripheral segment of the dialysis circuit. Code 36906 is reported only once per session to describe placing stent(s) within the peripheral segment, regardless of the number of stent(s) placed or the number of discrete lesion(s) treated within the peripheral segment. Codes 36907 and 36908 describe procedures performed through puncture(s) in the dialysis circuit. Similar procedures performed from a different access (eg, common femoral vein) may be reported using 37248, 37249 or 37238, 37239. Code 36907 is an add-on code used in conjunction with 36901, 36902, 36903, 36904, 36905, 36906 to report angioplasty within the central dialysis segment when performed through puncture of the dialysis circuit, and is reported once per session independent of the number of discrete lesions treated, the number of balloon inflations, and number of balloon catheters or sizes required. These additional services should be clearly documented in the patient record, including the recorded images. Code 36907 may be reported only once per session with 36901, 36902, 36903, 36904, 36905, 36906, as appropriate. Report 36907 once for all angioplasty performed within the central dialysis segment. Code 36908 is an add-on code used in conjunction with 36901, 36902, 36903, 36904, 36905, 36906 to report stenting lesion(s) in the central dialysis segment when performed through puncture of the dialysis circuit. It is reported once, regardless of the number of discrete lesions treated or the number of stents placed. Code 36908 includes the services in 36907; therefore, 36908 may not be reported with 36907 in the same session. Code 36908 may be reported only once per session with 36901, 36902, 36903, 36904, 36905, 36906, as appropriate. Code 36909 is an add-on code used to report endovascular embolization or occlusion of the main vessel or side branches arising from (emptying into) the dialysis circuit. Code 36909 may only be reported once per therapeutic session, irrespective of the number of branches embolized or occluded. Embolization or occlusion of the main vessel or these side branches may not be reported with 37241. If open dialysis circuit creation, revision, and/or thrombectomy (36818-36833) are performed, completion angiography is bundled, as is peripheral segment angioplasty and/or stent placement (36901, 36902, 36903) and, therefore, not separately reported. lay_term: The provider introduces a needle and/or catheter under fluoroscopic guidance (live X–rays that can be viewed on a monitor) and injects contrast material into the dialysis access point to visualize and record images of the entire dialysis circuit; he finds an obstructed segment, which he dilates and opens up using a balloon expanded within the vessel lumen. Radiological supervision and interpretation for both components of the procedure and image capture and report for the angiography are included in this code. Explanation The patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized. Using fluoroscopic guidance, the provider introduces a needle and/or a catheter through the skin over a surgically created connection between an artery and a vein (arteriovenous graft, fistula, or anastomosis) that serves as the dialysis access point. He injects contrast material (a special dye used in radiology imaging) to visualize the circulation throughout the arterial and venous components of the entire dialysis circuit, including the superior and/or inferior vena cava. The superior vena cava carries blood from the upper parts of the body, the inferior vena cava from the lower parts of the body, and both empty into the right atrium of the heart. lay_term: Under fluoroscopic guidance (live X–rays that can be viewed on a monitor), the provider introduces a catheter into a vessel in the dialysis circuit and extracts a blood clot (hematoma) with special instruments (thrombectomy) and/or injects a drug to dissolve the clot (pharmacological thrombolytic injection); he also finds a narrowed segment in the outer area of the circuit, which he dilates and opens up using a balloon expanded within the vessel lumen (channel). The procedure includes diagnostic angiography and radiological supervision and interpretation. Explanation The patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized. Using fluoroscopic guidance, the provider introduces a catheter through the skin over a surgically created connection between an artery and a vein (arteriovenous graft, fistula, or anastomosis) that serves as the dialysis access point. He injects contrast material (a special dye used in radiology imaging) to visualize the circulation throughout the arterial and venous components of the dialysis circuit. He sees a clot in one of the vessels comprising the dialysis circuit. He uses any type of method or device (such as coil, aspiration, or stent retrieval device) to break up and retrieve the clot. Alternatively, he may inject a thrombolytic agent to break down or dissolve the clot and suction out the debris with an aspiration unit. He may use both techniques. He also sees a narrowing or obstruction in the peripheral segment. He inserts a balloon through the catheter into the narrowed area and expands the balloon, which opens up the lumen (interior diameter) of the vessel. Dialysis: The process of purification of blood by using a dialysis machine as a substitute for the normal function of the kidneys, which are paired organs found in the back of the abdomen that filter waste products from the blood and then excrete the toxins in the form of urine. Stent: A tubelike device used to maintain the opening of a tubular structure. Transluminal balloon angioplasty: A surgical procedure in which the provider passes a catheter with a balloon at its tip to an area of obstruction or narrowing in an artery; he inflates the balloon, which flattens the plaque and intima (the innermost layer of the wall of a vessel) back up against the wall and increases the diameter of the lumen (open interior of the vessel). lay_term: During a primary procedure on a patient's dialysis circuit, the provider finds an obstructed central segment, which he dilates and opens up using a balloon expanded within the vessel lumen (channel). Radiological supervision and interpretation for any imaging procedure required to carry out the balloon angioplasty is included with this code. Under imaging guidance, he inserts a balloon through a previously inserted catheter into the narrowed area and expands the balloon. The balloon stretches the internal lining of the vessel (intima) and leaves a ragged surface on the interior wall after the balloon is deflated. This triggers a healing response and breaks up the plaque, deposits of cholesterol and other lipid material in the lining of the arteries. He withdraws the catheter and balloon after confirming that the vessel is now open. He continues with the primary procedure, at the end of which he withdraws the catheter and puts pressure on the incision to control the bleeding. lay_term: During a primary procedure on a patient's dialysis circuit, the provider finds it necessary to perform permanent endovascular occlusion or embolization to deliberately occlude (block) the dialysis circuit due to a malfunction. Radiological supervision and interpretation for any imaging procedure required to carry out the embolization or occlusion is included with this code. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized and during a primary procedure on the dialysis circuit, the provider discovers that the dialysis access is malfunctioning in some way. He decides to block the dialysis access using permanent embolization techniques or other means to occlude the circuit. He may insert an endovascular device of some sort to block blood flow or tie off the vessel(s). He continues with the primary procedure, at the end of which he withdraws the catheter and puts pressure on the incision to control the bleeding. Terminology Angiography: A medical imaging technique in which the provider injects a dye into blood vessels and uses plain X–rays, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging to visualize the inside, or lumen, of the vessels; more specific terms include arteriography when performed on the arteries or venography when performed on the veins; angiography can also be used to study blood supply to organs such as the heart, kidneys, and liver. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Dialysis: The process of purification of blood by using a dialysis machine as a substitute for the normal function of the kidneys, which are paired organs found in the back of the abdomen that filter waste products from the blood and then excrete the toxins in the form of urine. Endovascular: Within a blood vessel, as in a surgical procedure in which the provider places a catheter into the blood vessel. Image guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a television monitor; ultrasound, high frequency sound waves to view tissues; or other forms of imaging during surgical procedures. Percutaneous transluminal mechanical thrombectomy: Extraction of a blood clot hematoma or thrombus) using specialized instruments inserted through a catheter, which is inserted into the blood vessel through a small puncture or incision in the skin. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Definitions Dialysis circuit: The arteriovenous (AV) dialysis circuit is designed for easy and repetitive access to perform hemodialysis. It begins at the arterial anastomosis and extends to the right atrium. The circuit may be created using either an arterial-venous anastomosis, known as an arteriovenous fistula (AVF), or a prosthetic graft placed between an artery and vein, known as an arteriovenous graft (AVG). The dialysis circuit is comprised of two segments, termed the (1) peripheral dialysis segment and (2) central dialysis segment. Both are defined as follows. Peripheral dialysis segment: The peripheral dialysis segment is the portion of the dialysis circuit that begins at the arterial anastomosis and extends to the central dialysis segment. In the upper extremity, the peripheral dialysis segment extends through the axillary vein (or entire cephalic vein in the case of cephalic venous outflow). In the lower extremity, the peripheral dialysis segment extends through the common femoral vein. The peripheral dialysis segment includes the historic "peri-anastomotic region" (defined below). Central dialysis segment: The central dialysis segment includes all draining veins central to the peripheral dialysis segment. In the upper extremity, the central dialysis segment includes the veins central to the axillary and cephalic veins, including the subclavian and innominate veins through the superior vena cava. In the lower extremity, the central dialysis segment includes the veins central to the common femoral vein, including the external iliac and common iliac veins through the inferior vena cava. Peri-anastomotic region: A historic term referring to the region of a dialysis circuit near the arterial anastomosis encompassing a short segment of the parent artery, the anastomosis, and a short segment of the dialysis circuit immediately adjacent to the anastomosis. The peri-anastomotic region is included within the peripheral segment of the dialysis circuit. Performed through dialysis circuit: Any diagnostic study or therapeutic intervention within the dialysis circuit that is performed through a direct percutaneous access to the dialysis circuit. Code 36901 includes direct access and imaging of the entire dialysis circuit. Antegrade and/or retrograde punctures of the dialysis circuit are typically used for imaging, and contrast may be injected directly through a needle or through a catheter placed into the dialysis circuit. All dialysis circuit punctures required to perform the procedure are included in 36901. Occasionally, the catheter needs to be advanced further into the circuit to adequately visualize the arterial anastomosis or the central veins, or selective catheterization of a venous branch may be required. All manipulation(s) of the catheter for diagnostic imaging of the dialysis circuit is included in 36901. Advancement of the catheter to the vena cava to adequately image that segment of the dialysis circuit is included in 36901 and is not separately reported. Code 36901 also includes catheterization of additional venous side branches communicating with the dialysis circuit, known as accessory veins. Advancement of the catheter tip through the arterial anastomosis to adequately visualize the anastomosis is also included in the service described by 36901 and is not separately reported. Evaluation of the peri-anastomotic portion of the inflow is an integral part of the dialysis circuit angiogram and is included in 36901. For the purposes of reporting dialysis access maintenance services, the arterial inflow to the dialysis circuit is considered a separate vessel. If a more proximal arterial inflow problem separate from the peripheral dialysis segment is suspected, additional catheter placement and imaging required for adequate evaluation of the artery may be separately reported. If a catheter is selectively advanced from the dialysis circuit puncture beyond the peri-anastomotic segment into the inflow artery, an additional catheterization code may be reported. For example, 36215 may be used to report image-guided retrograde catheter placement into the inflow artery and into the aorta, if necessary (36200 is not reported in addition to 36215 in this example). Note that 75710 may also be reported if contrast injection for diagnostic arteriography is performed through this catheter and radiological supervision and interpretation and imaging documentation is performed. Ultrasound guidance for puncture of the dialysis circuit access is not typically performed and is not included in 36901, 36902, 36903, 36904, 36905, 36906. However, in the case of a new (immature) or failing AVF, ultrasound may be necessary to safely and effectively puncture the dialysis circuit for evaluation, and this may be reported separately with 76937, if all the appropriate elements for reporting 76937 are performed and documented. For radiological supervision and interpretation of dialysis circuit angiography performed through existing access(es) or catheter-based arterial access, report 36901 with modifier 52. Dialysis Circuit Interventions (AV Grafts and AV Fistulae): For the purposes of coding interventional procedures in the dialysis circuit (both AVF and AVG), the dialysis circuit is artificially divided into two distinct segments: peripheral dialysis segment and central dialysis segment (see definitions). Codes 36901, 36902, 36903 and 36904, 36905, 36906 are built on progressive hierarchies that have more intensive services, which include less intensive services. Report only one code (36901, 36902, 36903, 36904, 36905, 36906) for services provided in a dialysis circuit. Code 36901 describes the diagnostic evaluation of the dialysis circuit, and this service is included in the services described by 36901, 36902, 36903, 36904, 36905, 36906. All catheterizations required to perform diagnostic fistulography are included in 36901. All catheterizations required to perform additional interventional services are included in codes 36902, 36903, 36904, 36905, 36906, 36907, 36908, 36909 and not separately reported. All angiography, fluoroscopic image guidance, roadmapping, and radiological supervision and interpretation required to perform each service are included in each code. short_description: Venous anastomosis, open; portocaval Notes: (For peritoneal-venous shunt, use 49425)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises a patient’s thoracic and abdominal area and creates a portocaval venous anastomosis, or a connection between the portal vein of the liver and the inferior vena cava. The provider performs this procedure as a treatment for portal hypertension, which often occurs due to a narrowing or blockage of the portal vein. This procedure lowers the pressure in the veins of the stomach and esophagus, or food pipe, and prevents serious bleeding in the gastrointestinal tract. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision extending from chest to abdomen. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue exposing the liver and inferior vena cava. He then identifies the portal vein of the liver and attaches a clamp over the vein to stop blood flow. He does the same to the inferior vena cava and attaches a clamp over the inferior vena cava. Next, he incises some portion of both the portal vein and the inferior vena cava along their length. He then connects the portal vein to the inferior vena cava by suturing them together, creating an anastomosis between the two. He then removes the clamps and checks the blood flow to ensure that there is no blood leakage. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He may place a chest tube for drainage. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two structures, anatomical or surgically created, such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end to side and side to side. Portal hypertension: High blood pressure in the veins and branches of the portal venous system, a system of vessels that drains blood from the gastrointestinal tract into the liver. Portal vein: A vein that carries deoxygenated blood from the stomach, the intestine, the spleen, the gall bladder, and the pancreas to the liver. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. Veins: Vessels that carry oxygen poor blood from the body to the heart. Vena cava: The major trunks of the venous circulatory system; the superior vena cava brings blood back to the heart from the upper body circulation, while the inferior vena cava brings it back from the lower body circulation. Tips Use 37145, Venous anastomosis, open; renoportal, when the provider creates an anastomosis between the renal vein and the portal vein. The renal vein is a vein that drains blood from the kidney. Use 37160, Venous anastomosis, open; caval mesenteric, when the provider creates an anastomosis between the superior mesenteric vein and the inferior vena cava. The superior mesenteric vein is a vein that drains the blood from the small intestine. Use 37180, Venous anastomosis, open; splenorenal, proximal, when the provider creates an anastomosis between the upper end of the splenic vein and the renal vein. The splenic vein is a vein that drains blood from the spleen, an organ located in the left upper part of the abdomen and is responsible for immunity. Use 37181, Venous anastomosis, open; splenorenal, distal, selective decompression of esophagogastric varices, any technique, when the provider creates an anastomosis between the lower end of the splenic vein and the renal vein. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider restores the blood supply in a narrowed or blocked unilateral femoral or popliteal artery through an endovascular, open or percutaneous approach. He performs this procedure with atherectomy, a surgical procedure to remove plaque from the blood vessel. This code includes an angioplasty procedure when the provider performs it within the same vessel. Explanation The provider accesses the lumen of the diseased vessel through an open or percutaneous approach to treat an area of arterial occlusion. In an open approach, the provider performs a vertical incision over the femoral triangle, an anatomical region in the upper inner thigh, to access to the femoral artery. In the case of a popliteal artery occlusion, the provider extends the incision through the femoral triangle and down to reach the back of the knee to expose the stenosed, or narrowed, popliteal artery. In a percutaneous approach, the provider punctures the artery through the skin to reach the occlusion. Next, the provider grasps the obstructed artery by using a vascular clamp, and then he performs an arterial irrigation by infusing a heparin saline into the occluded artery. Next, he passes a balloon catheter through a guidewire into the artery to reach the area of vessel obstruction. He then re expands the lumen of the affected artery by dilating the stenosed, or narrowed, artery using the balloon. Next, he removes the balloon catheter through the site of access. The provider then inserts another rotational atherectomy device, or burr catheter, under radiological guidance to the site of treatment with the assistance of the guidewire. He then dislodges the atherosclerotic plaque from the inner wall of the diseased artery using the burr catheter. This code includes an angioplasty procedure when provider performs it within same vessel during this procedure. Use this code when the provider performs this procedure on each additional vessel. Explanation In this add–on procedure, the provider restores the blood supply in additional unilateral tibial or peroneal arteries with atherectomy. The provider may use an open or percutaneous approach to treat an area of arterial occlusion. In an open approach, the provider performs incision over the compartments of the leg to gain access to the target artery. However, in the percutaneous approach, the provider punctures the artery through the skin to reach the occlusion. In either approach, the provider grasps the obstructed artery by a vascular clamp. He then performs an arterial irrigation by infusing heparin saline into the occluded artery. Next, he passes a balloon catheter through a guidewire into the arterial lumen to reach the area of vessel obstruction. He then re expands the lumen of the affected artery by dilating the stenosed, or narrowed, arterial area through the catheter balloon. Next, he removes the balloon catheter through the site of access and inserts another rotational atherectomy device, or burr catheter, under radiological guidance to the site of treatment with the assistance of the guidewire. He then dislodges the atherosclerotic plaque from the inner wall of the diseased artery using the burr catheter. The provider checks the patency of the occluded vessel and extent of revascularization through an angioscope at the end of the treatment session. Finally, he withdraws the atherectomy catheter system through the site of access and stops all bleeding by the application of a compression bandage over the puncture location, when the provider uses a percutaneous approach, or he repairs the incision by suturing the soft tissue in layers in an open procedure. Terminology Angioplasty: A surgical procedure to widen the artery narrowed or blocked artery Angioscope: A catheter with camera at the end for viewing the lumen of a blood vessel. Artery: A blood vessel that supplies oxygenated blood to the body tissues. Atherectomy: A surgical procedure to remove a plaque from the blood vessel. Catheter: A catheter is a tube that the provider inserts into a body cavity, duct, or vessel; catheters allow drainage, administration of fluids or gases, or access for surgical instruments; the process of inserting a catheter is called catheterization. Endovascular: A medical procedure in which the provider introduces a catheter containing medication or instrument into a blood vessel to treat the vascular disorder. Femoral artery: One of the main arteries in the human body that supplies oxygenated blood to the legs. Heparin: A drug that a provider uses to treat and prevent blood clot. Lumen: The interior, open area of a vessel or organ; a tubular like cavity. Occlusion: Blockage of a passage such as a blood vessel. Percutaneous: Through the skin. Peroneal artery: A blood vessel that supplies oxygenated blood to the outer portion of legs. Recanalization: A process of restoring the blood flow in an obstructed blood vessel. Revascularization: A surgical intervention a provider performs for the restoration and reestablishment of the blood supply to a particular body structure or organ. Rotational atherectomy device: A burr or a small drill threaded onto a catheter that a provider usually inserts through the femoral artery. Tibial artery: A major artery that supplies oxygenated blood to the front and back of the leg and the foot. Transluminal: Passing across the lumen of a blood vessel. short_description: Transluminal balloon angioplasty (except lower extremity artery(ies) for occlusive disease, intracranial, coronary, pulmonary, or dialysis circuit), open or percutaneous, including all imaging and radiological supervision and interpretation necessary to perform the angioplasty within the same artery; initial artery
lay_term: Using an open incision or a percutaneous (small incision in the skin) approach, the provider places a balloon–tipped catheter into the lumen (interior) of an artery. He expands the balloon as many times and at as many points as necessary within the same artery to open up the artery and improve blood circulation. The procedure includes all imaging guidance and diagnostic imaging necessary to carry out the angioplasty and all radiological supervision and interpretation (RS&I); do not report this code for this procedure on the dialysis circuit or the lower extremity, intracranial, coronary, or pulmonary arteries. Explanation With the patient prepped and anesthetized appropriately for an open or percutaneous procedure, the provider inserts a needle into the femoral artery, the main artery that provides oxygenated blood to the tissues of the leg. He places a guide wire through the needle and removes the needle. He threads an introducer over the guide wire and removes the wire after which he inserts a different–sized guide wire. Next, he advances a catheter over the guide wire into the vessel to be repaired, and then removes that guide wire. He may use imaging guidance for these procedures. He may also inject a contrast dye into the vessel and observe the blood flow on a monitor in order to determine the areas that need to be angioplastied. When he finds a blockage, he exchanges the first catheter, which was a diagnostic catheter, for a guiding catheter and again inserts a guide wire, which he advances across the area of blockage. He advances another catheter with a balloon at its tip over the guide wire to the area of blockage. He inflates the balloon, which compresses the plaque (yellowish deposits of cholesterol and other fatty material in the lining, or intima, of the arteries) up against the vessel wall. He deflates the balloon. He may repeat this procedure until he is satisfied with the result, using angiography with contrast injections to assess the blood flow. He may repeat this procedure at other points along the vessel until he has addressed all areas of blockage or narrowing. When the artery is open, and he determines that blood flow is satisfactory, he removes the catheter, checks for bleeding, and completes the procedure as appropriate for an open or percutaneous approach. Terminology Angiography: A medical imaging technique in which the provider injects a dye into blood vessels and uses plain X–rays, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging to visualize the inside, or lumen, of the vessels; more specific terms include arteriography when performed on the arteries or venography when performed on the veins; angiography can also be used to study blood supply to organs such as the heart, kidneys, and liver. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Image guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a television monitor; ultrasound, high frequency sound waves to view tissues; or other forms of imaging during surgical procedures. Open incision: A surgical approach that involves making a large enough incision that the provider can directly visualize the target anatomy. Tips This procedure includes radiological supervision and interpretation (RS&I) for any imaging procedures performed during transluminal balloon angioplasty procedure. Do not report the imaging procedure or RS&I separately. For the same procedure on each additional artery, report +37247 (Transluminal balloon angioplasty...; each additional artery [List separately in addition to code for primary procedure]). For the same type of procedure on veins (except dialysis circuit), report 37248 (Transluminal balloon angioplasty [except dialysis circuit], open or percutaneous, including all imaging and radiological supervision and interpretation necessary to perform the angioplasty within the same vein; initial vein). lay_term: After performing transluminal balloon angioplasty on the initial vein, the provider places a balloon through a catheter into the lumen (interior) of one or more additional veins (except for the dialysis circuit) and expands the balloon as many times and at as many points as necessary within the same vein to open up the vein and improve blood circulation. The procedure includes all imaging guidance and diagnostic imaging necessary to carry out the angioplasty and all radiological supervision and interpretation (RS&I). Explanation With the patient prepped and anesthetized appropriately for an open or percutaneous procedure and already having undergone TBA on one vein, the provider inserts a needle into another vein. He places a guide wire through the needle and removes the needle. He threads an introducer over the guide wire, removes the wire, and advances a catheter with a balloon at its tip through the introducer to the area of blockage. He may use imaging guidance for these procedures. He may also inject a contrast dye into the vessel and observe the blood flow on a monitor in order to determine the areas that need to be angioplastied. He inflates the balloon, which dilates the vein and presses the material causing the blockage up against the vessel wall. He deflates the balloon. He may repeat this procedure until he is satisfied with the result, using angiography with contrast injections to assess the blood flow. He may repeat this procedure at other points along the vessel until he has addressed all areas of blockage or narrowing. When the vein is open and he determines that blood flow is satisfactory, he removes the catheter, checks for bleeding, and completes the procedure as appropriate for an open or percutaneous approach. Terminology Angiography: A medical imaging technique in which the provider injects a dye into blood vessels and uses plain X–rays, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging to visualize the inside, or lumen, of the vessels; more specific terms include arteriography when performed on the arteries or venography when performed on the veins; angiography can also be used to study blood supply to organs such as the heart, kidneys, and liver. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Image guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a television monitor; ultrasound, high frequency sound waves to view tissues; or other forms of imaging during surgical procedures. Open incision: A surgical approach that involves making a large enough incision that the provider can directly visualize the target anatomy. Tips This procedure includes radiological supervision and interpretation (RS&I) for any imaging procedures performed during transluminal balloon angioplasty procedure. Do not report the imaging procedure or RS&I separately. Code +37249 is an add–on code; it must be reported with an appropriate primary code, 37248 (Transluminal balloon angioplasty [except dialysis circuit], open or percutaneous, including all imaging and radiological supervision and interpretation necessary to perform the angioplasty within the same vein; initial vein). lay_term: The provider inserts a stent in an artery using a catheter. Access may be either open or percutaneous. It includes any radiologic imaging to complete the procedure and if the provider performs angioplasty within the same vessel. This code does not apply to stent placement in the lower extremity, cervical carotid, intracranial, and coronary arteries. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, if the physician uses an open technique; he makes an incision in the skin over the vessel for exposure; then he incises the vessel longitudinally to access the area requiring a stent. If the provider employs a percutaneous transcatheter stent placement technique, he makes a small incision in the skin over an area proximal or distal to the area requiring a stent. Using a needle and guide wire to enter the vessel, he advances a catheter over the guide wire toward the area requiring treatment. The provider injects contrast material into the vessel to locate the exact area of narrowing and determine the extent of the narrowing. He may perform an angioplasty to prepare the site. He then delivers the stent to the site of the occlusion to increase the diameter of the stenosed vessel and keep it open. He uses radiological guidance to place the stent inside the vessel lumen. The provider withdraws the catheter when he determines that the vessel is sufficiently open. He then closes the access site using pressure, an arterial closure device, or suture. Terminology Angioplasty: Removal of plaque, the buildup of atherosclerotic fatty material in the lining of an artery; techniques include balloon and laser angioplasty. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Cervical carotid artery: Artery of the neck which supplies the neck, scapula, and shoulder blade. Coronary arteries: Vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle, such as the right or left coronary artery, left anterior descending, posterior descending, and circumflex. Extracranial vertebral artery: Artery outside the skull that supplies the muscles of the neck and upper vertebrae. Occlusive disease: Narrowing of arteries that obstruct blood flow. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Stent: A thin expandable tube placed through a narrowed area of a tubular structure, such as the esophagus, small intestine, or a vessel, to prevent obstruction and provide support after dilation. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Codes 37241-37244 are used to describe vascular embolization and occlusion procedures, excluding the central nervous system and the head and neck, which are reported using 61624, 61626, 61710, and 75894, and excluding the ablation/sclerotherapy procedures for venous insufficiency/telangiectasia of the extremities/skin, which are reported using 36468, 36470, and 36471. Embolization and occlusion procedures are performed for a wide variety of clinical indications and in a range of vascular territories. Arteries, veins, and lymphatics may all be the target of embolization. The embolization codes include all associated radiological supervision and interpretation, intra-procedural guidance and road-mapping, and imaging necessary to document completion of the procedure. They do not include diagnostic angiography and all necessary catheter placement(s). Code(s) for catheter placement(s) may be separately reported using selective catheter placement code(s), if used consistent with guidelines. Code(s) for diagnostic angiography may also be separately reported, when performed according to guidelines for diagnostic angiography during endovascular procedures, using the appropriate diagnostic angiography codes. Report these services with an appropriate modifier (eg, modifier 59). Please see the guidelines on the reporting of diagnostic angiography preceding 75600 in the Vascular Procedures, Aorta and Arteries section. Code 37241 is used to report endovascular embolization or occlusion procedures performed for venous conditions other than hemorrhage or hemodialysis access. Examples include embolization of venous malformations, capillary hemangiomas, varicoceles, and visceral varices. (For endovascular embolization or occlusion of side branch[es] of an outflow vein[s] from a hemodialysis access, use 36909.) Code 37242 is used to report vascular embolization or occlusion performed for arterial conditions other than hemorrhage or tumor such as arteriovenous malformations and arteriovenous fistulas whether congenital or acquired. Embolizations of aneurysms and pseudoaneurysms are also reported with 37242. Tumor embolization is reported with 37243. Note that injection to treat an extremity pseudoaneurysm is correctly reported with 36002. Sometimes, embolization and occlusion of an artery are performed prior to another planned interventional procedure; an example is embolization of the left gastric artery prior to planned implantation of a hepatic artery chemotherapy port. The artery embolization is reported with 37242. Code 37243 is used to report embolization for the purpose of tissue ablation and organ infarction or ischemia. This can be performed in many clinical circumstances, including embolization of benign or malignant tumors of the liver, kidney, uterus, or other organs. When chemotherapy is given as part of an embolization procedure, additional codes (eg, 96420) may be separately reported. When a radioisotope (eg, Yttrium-90) is injected as part of an embolization, then additional codes (eg, 79445) may be separately reported. Uterine fibroid embolization is reported with 37243. Code 37244 is used to report embolization for treatment of hemorrhage or vascular or lymphatic extravasation. Examples include embolization for management of gastrointestinal bleed, trauma-induced hemorrhage of the viscera or pelvis, embolization of the thoracic duct for chylous effusion and bronchial artery embolization for hemoptysis. Embolization of the uterine arteries for management of hemorrhage (eg, postpartum hemorrhage) is also reported with 37244. Intravascular stents, both covered and uncovered, are a class of devices that may be used as part of an embolization procedure. As such, there is the potential for overlap among codes used for placement of vascular stents and those used for embolization. When a stent is placed for the purpose of providing a latticework for deployment of embolization coils, such as for embolization of an aneurysm, the embolization code is reported and not the stent code. short_description: Intravascular ultrasound (noncoronary vessel) during diagnostic evaluation and/or therapeutic intervention, including radiological supervision and interpretation; initial noncoronary vessel (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure)
lay_term: In this add–on procedure, the provider inserts a specially designed catheter with an ultrasound transducer, a device that sends high–frequency sound waves through the tissues and detects their returning echoes to provide information about the underlying structures, into the vessel and examines its interior during a diagnostic or interventional therapeutic procedure, such as stent placement to treat an obstruction or blockage. This procedure is for the first vessel that is not a heart vessel (noncoronary) and includes radiologic supervision and interpretation of the intravascular ultrasound. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the skin over the vessel. He then inserts a sheath and places a guide wire through the sheath. Next, he inserts an ultrasound catheter over the guide wire into the vessel; the transducer emits and records high–frequency sound waves that a computer converts to images on a video screen, which the provider uses to examine the interior of the vessel. He removes the catheter and the guide wire once the procedure is complete. The provider stops the bleeding and closes the skin incision. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Intravascular stent: An expandable mesh tube to open a stenosed or narrowed vessel; the provider inserts the deflated stent into the narrowed portion of the vessel and then expands it against the wall of the vessel to open it; once expanded, the stent remains in position to keep the vessel open. Introducer sheath: A tube that a provider inserts into the body through which another instrument can be placed. Stent: A thin expandable tube placed through a narrowed area of a tubular structure, such as the esophagus, small intestine, or a vessel, to prevent obstruction and provide support after dilation. Therapeutic: For treatment purposes, as opposed to diagnostic, which refers to procedures performed for the purpose of determining the type of disease and its causes. Tips This code is for intravascular ultrasound of the first noncoronary vessel; when the provider performs intravascular ultrasound for each additional noncoronary vessel, use +37253, Intravascular ultrasound, noncoronary vessel during diagnostic evaluation and/or therapeutic intervention, including radiological supervision and interpretation; each additional noncoronary vessel. (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure, to report this service.) Because +37252 is an add–on code, payers will not reimburse you if you report it without an appropriate primary code, which is at the provider's discretion. Some payers may consider intravascular ultrasound of noncoronary vessels investigational, and it may not be covered. Check with the Medicare provider or private carrier to determine their policies. Even if not covered, you should still report the procedure for statistical purposes. Read Less

A provider performs this procedure most commonly for the treatment of an internal or common carotid artery aneurysm or injury. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the side of the neck, and incises down through the muscles. He accesses the internal or common carotid artery under direct visualization, separates it from the nearby structures, and places gradual occluding clamps. He then checks the effect of the reduction of the blood supply on the brain due to the clamps before placing sutures. After the confirmation, he then places the sutures to ligate the artery. After ligation, he secures the artery back to its original position, and sutures the surgical wound in layers. short_description: Ligation and division of long saphenous vein at saphenofemoral junction, or distal interruptions Notes: (Do not report 37700 in conjunction with 37718, 37722) (For bilateral procedure, report 37700 with modifier 50)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes multiple incisions over the affected areas of the thigh and along the long saphenous vein, and he ligates, or ties off, and divides, or separates, the diseased vein at the point where the saphenous and femoral veins meet and along the upper leg as necessary. He performs this procedure most commonly to treat varicose veins. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes incisions over the affected areas at the saphenofemoral junction or along the distal ends of the long saphenous vein. He exposes the vein at the targeted areas, applies clamps, then divides the affected areas, and ligates the remaining ends of the vein with sutures. After ligation at each place along the leg, he removes the clamps, secures the vein back, and sutures each of the surgical wounds in layers. Terminology Division of vein:To separate the vein from the area of disease. Femoral vein: The main blood vessel found in the upper thigh and pelvic region that carries blood back to the heart from the lower extremities. Ligation: Using sutures or wire to close, tie off, repair, or encircle a vessel or other structure. Saphenous vein: Vein of the lower extremities that a provider frequently harvests and uses for anastomosis. Saphenofemoral junction: The point where the saphenous and the femoral vein meets just below the knee joint. Varicose vein: Swollen, twisted veins that you can see just under the surface of the skin; these enlarged blood vessels are due to failure of valves throughout the length of the vein that let the blood flow in one direction toward the heart, so the blood starts to flow in the reverse direction, causing the vessels to swell and create problems such as pain, discoloration of skin, and ulcers. Tips Use 37700 when a provider divides and ligates only part of the affected long saphenous vein. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes incisions to access the short saphenous vein and remove it with the help of a stripping device.
