short_description: Ligation and division and complete stripping of long or short saphenous veins with radical excision of ulcer and skin graft and/or interruption of communicating veins of lower leg, with excision of deep fascia Notes: (Do not report 37735 in conjunction with 37700, 37718, 37722, 37780) (For bilateral procedure, report 37735 with modifier 50)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes incisions to access the long or short saphenous vein, ligates and divides the vein, and then removes the vein with the help of a stripping device. The provider also excises an ulcer including the deep fascia and nearby soft tissues and places a skin graft over the site. He may tie off superficial veins that connect with deeper veins. This procedure is most commonly done to treat varicose veins. Explanation In the case of the long saphenous vein, when the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the upper thigh area to access the saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction. He makes another incision in the lower leg area above the ankle and along the leg as necessary. He exposes the vein and divides the vein just below the affected area. He ligates the remaining end with sutures. Next, he inserts a stripping device at the lower incision, pushes it all the way to the upper end, and then attaches the end of the vein to the stripping device at the upper incision. He then pulls the vein out from the lower incision area. For the short saphenous vein, the provider makes an incision above the posterior knee joint area and accesses the short saphenous vein. He makes one more incision in the calf area over the short saphenous vein, exposes the vein, and divides the vein just below the affected area. He ligates the remaining end with sutures. Next, he inserts a stripping device from the upper incision and pushes it all the way to the lower end. He then attaches the end of the vein to the stripping device at the lower incision and pulls the vein out from the upper incision. In addition to either of the above procedures, the provider excises an ulcer that forms due to the varicose vein. He does this with the help of a sharp instrument, taking nearby soft tissue along with the ulcer, and may also choose to split and remove deep fascia where the superficial and deep veins connect to control the damage. Finally, he may repair the defect he causes by excision of the ulcer using a skin graft taken from another part of the patient’s body. Terminology Division of vein: To separate the vein from the area of disease. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. Communicating veins: Superficial veins found in the subcutaneous tissue such as the long or short saphenous vein that connect to the deep venous system, or the veins found underneath the deep fascia of the lower limb that travel along with the major arteries. Ligation: Using sutures or wire to close, tie off, repair, or encircle a vessel or other structure. Posterior: Backside of the body also known as the dorsal side. Radical: Directed at the root cause of a problem; in surgery, often used synonymously with major or extensive. Saphenous vein: Vein of the lower extremities that a provider frequently harvests and uses for anastomosis. Stripper: Surgical instrument used to cut, strip, and extract material, such as fascia or tendon grafts or varicose veins. Stripping: The process of removing a diseased vein, performed with the help of a stripper. Superficial: At the surface, especially on the surface of the skin or immediately below; the opposite of deep. Ulcer: A lesion, typically in the mucous lining of an organ, such as a gastric or peptic ulcer in the stomach or duodenum; ulcers that need to be treated surgically include ulcers that bleed or that erode or perforate through the wall of an organ; other types of ulcers include pressure or decubitus ulcers on the external skin caused when patients must remain in bed for a long time. Varicose vein: Swollen, twisted veins that you can see just under the surface of the skin; these enlarged blood vessels are due to failure of valves throughout the length of the vein that let the blood flow in one direction toward the heart, so the blood starts to flow in the reverse direction, causing the vessels to swell and create problems such as pain, discoloration of skin, and ulcers. Tips Code 37735 is among the CPT® codes for ligation performed on an artery or vein, and is most often done for removal of varicose veins in the legs. Many codes bundle into 37735, including some other ligation codes. Check the latest edits to see if the bundle may be broken with an appropriate modifier, such as 59, distinct procedural service. short_description: Ligation of perforator veins, subfascial, radical (Linton type), including skin graft, when performed, open,1 leg Notes: (For endoscopic procedure, use 37500)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes incisions along the affected vein and accesses the targeted perforator vein, a vein which connects the superficial vein to the deep veins. The provider incises through the fascia, excises the nearby diseased structures, and ligates the perforator vein, to treat varicose veins in one leg. The provider may also place a skin graft at the excision site to cover the wound. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes incisions over the, saphenous vein to access the targeted perforator vein and incises down to the level of the fascia. Then he separates the perforator vein by incising the fascial covering, and ligates the perforator vein with a suture or clip. He also excises the nearby diseased soft tissues. The provider then secures the ligated vein inside the fascia and sutures the fascia covering around it. At last, he repairs the defect created by the extensive tissue excision with the help of a skin graft. He may repeat the procedure if necessary on other veins of the same leg. Terminology Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. Ligation: Using sutures or wire to close, tie off, repair, or encircle a vessel or other structure. Perforator vein: A vein which connects the superficial veins to the deeper veins in the muscles. Radical: Directed at the root cause of a problem; in surgery, often used synonymously with major or extensive. Subfascial: Below the fascia. Superficial: At the surface, especially on the surface of the skin or immediately below; the opposite of deep. Varicose vein: Swollen, twisted veins that you can see just under the surface of the skin.; these enlarged blood vessels are due to failure of valves throughout the length of the vein that let the blood flow in one direction toward the heart, so the blood starts to flow in the reverse direction, causing the vessels to swell and create problems such as pain, discoloration of skin, and ulcers Tips Use this code only once for one leg. If the provider performs the procedure on both legs, code with modifier 50, Bilateral procedure, or according to the payer's guidelines for bilateral procedures. Do not report graft harvesting and placement separately. If the provider directly incises the skin to access the perforator vein under ultrasound guidance use 37761, Ligation of perforator veins, subfascial, open, including ultrasound guidance, when performed, 1 leg. short_description: Splenectomy; total (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider makes an incision into the abdominal cavity and performs a complete excision of the spleen. The provider performs this service for a patient with a traumatic rupture of the spleen, hemolytic anemia, or cancer of the spleen. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the abdomen just below the left ribs. He exposes the spleen and releases it from the surrounding structures. Next, the provider ligates the arteries and veins of the spleen, and divides them. Then he incises all the ligaments supporting the spleen to completely free it. He then removes the spleen in its entirety. After the procedure is complete, the provider irrigates the surgical site and may place a drain. Finally, he closes the wound in layers with sutures and applies a dressing. Terminology Anemia: Decrease in amount of red blood cells, which results in lack of oxygen in blood. Hemolytic anemia: Anemia caused by abnormal destruction of red blood cells. Ligation: Using sutures or wire to close, tie off, repair, or encircle a vessel or other structure. Rupture: A tear in a structure due to injury. Spleen: An abdominal organ which helps in blood cell production and immunity. Splenectomy: Surgical excision of the spleen. Tips Code 38100 is separate procedure, do not report this code if the provider performs any other major procedure in the same location and in same session. For laparoscopic approach use code 38120, Laparoscopy, surgical, splenectomy. Read Less

short_description: Splenectomy; total, en bloc for extensive disease, in conjunction with other procedure (List in addition to code for primary procedure)
lay_term: In this add–on procedure, the provider performs a complete excision of the spleen, while performing another extensive procedure that requires excision of abdominal organs. The provider performs this service most often on a patient due to trauma, or cancer of the abdominal organs. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes or extends an existing incision from another procedure. He identifies and inspects the area of disease and decides on the best approach to remove the diseased tissue. In addition to excision of other organs, he exposes the spleen and releases it from the surrounding structures. Next, the provider ligates the arteries and veins of the spleen, and incises them. Then he incises all the ligaments supporting the spleen to completely free it, and he removes the spleen in its entirety. After the procedure is complete, the provider irrigates the surgical site and closes the wound in layers with sutures. Terminology En bloc: French term for all together or as a whole. Ligation: Using sutures or wire to close, tie off, repair, or encircle a vessel or other structure. Rupture: A tear in a structure due to injury. Spleen: An abdominal organ which helps in blood cell production and immunity. Splenectomy: Surgical excision of the spleen. Whipple procedure: A procedure which the provider removes pancreas and duodenum in case of pancreatic cancer. Tips Code +38102 is an add–on code and a provider may only use it to identify removal of the spleen as part of a larger resection of diseased tissue. The number of codes that a provider may report 38102 with is extensive and so they are not specifically listed here. Typically, the en block splenectomy would be done with a total or subtotal excision of the pancreas, the stomach, or a combination of those procedures. Do not use 38102 alone. Because an en block splenectomy is part of a very extensive procedure it is not unusual for the entire operative session to require the use of a surgical assistant or co surgeons. A provider may report code 38102 with either of these modifiers; 80 (Assistant surgeon) or 62 (Two surgeons). However, if one surgeon performs the basic procedure, for example a Whipple procedure and the other performs the splenectomy, the surgeon who performs the splenectomy will not be able to bill code 38102 separately. Both surgeons will have to list both codes with modifier 62 for reimbursement. Read Less

short_description: Blood-derived hematopoietic progenitor cell harvesting for transplantation, per collection; allogeneic
lay_term: The provider harvests hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) from the blood of a donor using a technique known as apheresis. The provider performs this service using specially designed equipment for this task. Explanation The provider performs bone marrow and stem cell transplantation to treat various diseases of the blood and bone marrow as well as some other cancers. He may harvest stem cells from the blood as well as the bone marrow. The provider connects the blood circulation of a donor with a machine that circulates the collected blood and separates the stem cells from other components by a process called apheresis. The provider may perform multiple cycles to collect a sufficient amount of cells. After collecting the cells he transplants the cells into another person and the rest of the blood is returned to the donor. Harvesting of blood–derived stem cells is very much like a normal blood donation and does not require much provider intervention. Terminology Allogenic: Use of body tissue of one individual for another individual. Apheresis: A procedure in which the blood of a donor or patient is passed through an apparatus that separates out one particular constituent and returns the remainder to the circulation. Bone marrow: Substance within the internal cavity of a bone; a source of stem cells, which ultimately develop into red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs): Specialized blood–forming cells found in the bone marrow that can develop itself into different types of blood cells. Stem cells: Cells found in most, if not all, multicellular organisms; they are characterized by the ability to renew themselves through cell division and to differentiate into a diverse range of specialized cell types. Tips For harvesting of hematopoietic progenitor cells from the patient’s own blood, use code 38206. Read Less

short_description: Transplant preparation of hematopoietic progenitor cells; cryopreservation and storage Notes: (For diagnostic cryopreservation and storage, use 88240)
lay_term: The provider manages the preservation and storage of harvested hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs). He assures cell preservation according to current protocols for future transplantation of the cells. Explanation The proper preservation of HPCs that a provider obtains from blood or umbilical cells is essential to maintain the viability of the cells. The provider assures cell preservation in a solution, known as a cryoprotective solution. The solution prevents ice crystallization at very low temperatures. The provider cools the cells slowly and keeps them in special vials or bags that can tolerate the cryogenic substance. They may be kept in a laboratory freezer or in a nitrogen liquid or vapor. The provider maintains a temperature range from minus 80 degrees Celsius to minus 120 degrees Celsius, depending upon the estimate of storage duration. If preservation is necessary for a longer period of time then cells require a lower temperature. Terminology Cryoprotective solution: A solution that helps prevent tissue damage due to low temperatures. Hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs): Specialized blood–forming cells found in the bone marrow that can develop itself into different types of blood cells. Read Less

short_description: Transplant preparation of hematopoietic progenitor cells; specific cell depletion within harvest, T-cell depletion
lay_term: The provider prepares the hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) in such a way that it has minimal numbers of T cells to minimize the chances of rejection. Explanation After the provider harvests, preserves, and thaws the cells, he prepares the solution for transplant in a patient where there is a greater probability of rejection of the hematopoietic progenitor cells. To lower the chance of rejection, the provider uses various techniques to reduce the number of T cells in the transplant preparation, because T cells are primarily responsible for the rejection of a graft from another person. There are multiple methods for depleting T cells like elutriation, agglutination, and a CD34–positive cell enrichment technique in which the provider uses CD34, a positive antigen, to separate the T cells from the rest of the cells. Terminology Agglutination: Abnormal clumping of particles of any substances, most commonly in case of abnormal clumping of blood cells due to contact between incompatible blood groups. CD34 positive cell enrichment: Process by which the provider isolates CD34 cells from all the other cells, including the targeted cells the provider wants to remove in the hematopoietic progenitor solution; the provider is then able to remove the unwanted cells, including such cells as T cells, or tumor cells. Elutriation: A process of separating particles of a solution on the basis of particle size. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. Hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs): Specialized blood–forming cells found in bone marrow that can develop itself into different types of blood cells. T cell: A type of blood cell in a human, which provides immunity. Thawing: Process of liquefying a frozen solution with the help of increased temperatures. Tips Report this service only once per day. Read Less

short_description: Transplant preparation of hematopoietic progenitor cells; tumor cell depletion
lay_term: The provider prepares the hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) using a combination of enrichment and depletion techniques to remove the most tumor cells possible to minimize the chances of reintroduction of tumor cells into the recipient. Explanation After the provider harvests, preserves, and thaws the hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs), he prepares the solution for transplant into a patient from whom the provider harvested the cells. The provider reduces the number of tumor cells left in the HPC solution using multiple methods such as elutriation, agglutination, and CD34–positive cell enrichment technique in which the provider uses CD34, a positive antigen, to separate the tumor cells from the rest of the cells. For this service, he combines these techniques, usually applying the C34–cell enrichment technique first and then following with a depletion technique such as elutriation for additional removal of tumor cells. Terminology Agglutination: Abnormal clumping of particles of any substances, most commonly in case of abnormal clumping of blood cells due to contact between incompatible blood groups. CD34–positive cell enrichment: Process by which the provider isolates CD34 cells from all the other cells, including the targeted cells the provider wants to remove in the hematopoietic progenitor solution; the provider is then able to remove the unwanted cells, including such cells as T cells or tumor cells. Elutriation: A process of separating particles of a solution on the basis of particle size. Hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs): Specialized blood–forming cells found in bone marrow that can develop itself into different types of blood cells. Tumor cell: An abnormal cell with a capacity to multiply in an uncontrolled manner. Tips Report this service only once per day. Read Less

short_description: Transplant preparation of hematopoietic progenitor cells; platelet depletion
lay_term: The provider prepares the hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) solution to reduce the number of platelets left and prevent any clumping of the HPC solution. Explanation After the provider harvests, preserves, and thaws the hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs), he prepares the solution for transplant using techniques to ensure there are as few platelets left as possible. This process helps to minimize the risk of the solution clumping as platelets are comparatively large in size and dead platelets create bulk in solution, which can cause problems in the transplantation process. The provider may perform centrifugation, apheresis, or he may use cell washers, most commonly buffered saline, to separate cells and plasma from the rest of the HPCs solution. Terminology Agglutination: Abnormal clumping of particles of any substances, most commonly in case of abnormal clumping of blood cells due to contact between incompatible blood groups. Apheresis: A procedure in which the blood of a donor or patient is passed through an apparatus that separates out one particular constituent and returns the remainder to the circulation. Centrifuge: Use of centrifugal force to separate solids suspended in a liquid medium. Hematopoietic progenitor cell (HPCs): Specialized blood–forming cells found in bone marrow that can develop into different types of blood cells. Platelets: One of three primary cell types in blood, which aids in clot formation to stop bleeding. Tips Report this service only once per day. Read Less

short_description: Transplant preparation of hematopoietic progenitor cells; plasma (volume) depletion
lay_term: The provider prepares the hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) in such a way that the solution has minimal plasma volume left. The provider performs this service to facilitate the transplantation process with a smaller volume of HPC solution. Explanation After the provider harvests, preserves, and thaws the hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs), he prepares the solution for transplant by reducing the volume of plasma. This process helps minimize the risk of toxicity due to the cryoprotective solution the provider uses in freezing and storing the cells, as more plasma volume leads to more cryoprotective solution in the HPCs. Conversely, a smaller plasma volume results in fewer blood cells and blood proteins available, which may cause incompatibility. The provider may perform centrifugation, apheresis, or he may use cell washers, most commonly buffered saline, to separate cells and plasma from the rest of the HPCs solution. Terminology Agglutination: Abnormal clumping of particles of any substances, most commonly in case of abnormal clumping of blood cells due to contact between incompatible blood groups. Apheresis: A procedure in which the blood of a donor or patient is passed through an apparatus that separates out one particular constituent and returns the remainder to the circulation. Centrifuge: Use of centrifugal force to separate solids suspended in a liquid medium. Hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs): Specialized blood–forming cells found in bone marrow that can develop itself into different types of blood cells. Plasma: The liquid portion of blood that typically suspends blood cells; plasma usually accounts for more than half of blood volume and contains important components such as proteins, electrolytes, hormones, and coagulation factors. Platelets: One of three primary cell types in blood, which aids in clot formation to stop bleeding. Tips Report this service only once per day. Read Less

lay_term: The provider inserts a long, large–bore needle into the sternum or pelvic bone and aspirates (sucks out) bone marrow tissue. This procedure is used for diagnostic purposes only. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a specially designed needle with an attached syringe through the skin, typically in the sternum of the chest or iliac crest in the pelvic area, and pushes the needle in a rotating manner into the bone marrow. After confirming the needle position, he aspirates (withdraws) the soft bone marrow tissue through the bore of the needle and transfers it to a container or slides for analysis. Finally, he removes the needle slowly and controls the bleeding with pressure at the needle insertion site. The procedure usually takes place in a minor procedure room or special suite for bone marrow procedures. Terminology Aspiration: To withdraw fluid from a body cavity or a mass, such as a cyst, with a needle and a syringe. Bone marrow: The spongy tissue inside the large bones; it is the place where new blood cells are produced. Iliac crest: Upper rounded portion of the pelvic bone. Pelvis: The hip bone, sacrum, the large triangular bone at the lower end of the spinal column, and coccyx or tailbone; often used to refer to the hip bones alone; may be used to refer to the pelvic cavity. Sternum: Breastbone, at the front of the rib cage. Tips The provider reporting this code obtains bone marrow for diagnostic purposes only. This procedure does not involve obtaining a sufficient amount of bone marrow for transplant purposes. Do not separately report this code if a provider performs this service at the same time as harvesting bone marrow for transplantation. If a provider performs multiple aspirations at the same insertion site, report code 38220 only one time. However, if he aspirates it from separate sites, such as one sample from the iliac crest and another from the sternum, then report code 38220 with modifier 59, distinct procedural service, for the additional site. Some payers, however, may limit reporting this code to only one time per day. If the provider performs a bone marrow biopsy for diagnostic purposes, see 38221, but if he performs a combined aspiration/biopsy, see 38222. Read Less

short_description: Bone marrow harvesting for transplantation; allogeneic
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider inserts a long needle or trocar in the sternum or pelvic bone to take a sufficient amount of bone marrow tissue from the body of a donor for transplantation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a specially designed needle or trocar. He inserts the needle or trocar through the skin, most commonly in the sternum of the chest or the iliac crest in the pelvic area, and pushes the needle into the bone marrow. After confirmation of the needle position, he aspirates, scrapes, or excises out the bone marrow tissue and transfers it to a container for transplant. Finally, he removes the needle or trocar slowly and controls the bleeding with pressure at the insertion site. The procedure usually takes place in a minor procedure room or special suite for bone marrow procedures. Terminology Allogeneic: A tissue graft harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also called allograft and homograft. Bone marrow: The spongy tissue inside the large bones; it is the place where new blood cells are produced. Iliac crest: Upper rounded portion of the pelvic bone. Sternum: Breastbone, at the front of the rib cage. Trocar: A hollow pointed puncturing device, typically part of a cannula and trocar combination, usually in crisscross shape. Read Less

short_description: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy; harvesting of blood-derived T lymphocytes for development of genetically modified autologous CAR-T cells, per day
lay_term: The provider uses specialized equipment to withdraw blood from the patient and extract T lymphocytes (white blood cells) for use in CAR–T therapy (use of the patient’s modified cells to attack cancer cells). Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider inserts a needle through the skin into a vein (venipuncture). The provider also performs needle insertion at a second site. Tubes connect the needles to a leukapheresis machine. Blood flows from one site into the leukapheresis machine, which separates out the T lymphocytes (white blood cells involved in immunity) using centrifugation, a process that rotates a mixture at a high speed to separate it into its component parts. The machine then returns the remaining blood to the patient. When the desired volume of T lymphocytes is collected, the provider discontinues the procedure and removes the needles. The provider performs this service as part of chimeric antigen receptor T–cell (CAR–T) therapy, a cancer treatment where a lab modifies a patient’s own immune cells to better recognize and attack cancer cells. Report this code per day. Tips See 38225 to 38228 for various elements of CAR–T therapy services. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Cellular and gene therapies involve the collection, processing and handling of cells or other tissues, genetic modification of those cells or tissues, and administration of the genetically modified cells or tissues with the intent to treat, modify, reverse, or cure a serious or life-threatening disease or condition. Codes 38225, 38226, 38227, 38228 describe the various steps required to collect, prepare, transport, receive, and administer genetically modified T cells. The collection and handling code (38225) may be reported only once per day, regardless of the number of collections or quantity of cells collected. Similarly, the administration code (38228) may only be reported once per day, regardless of the number of units administered. The development of genetically modified cells is not reported with this family of codes. Chimeric antigen receptor therapy (CAR-T) with genetically modified T cells begins with the collection of cells from the patient by peripheral blood leukocyte cell harvesting. The cells are then cryopreserved and/or otherwise prepared for processing or shipping to a manufacturing or cell-processing facility, if applicable, where gene modification and expansion of the cells are performed. When gene modification and expansion of the cells by the manufacturer are complete, the genetically modified cells are returned to the physician or other qualified health care professional when additional preparation occurs, including thawing of the cryopreserved CAR-T cells, if necessary, before the cells are administered to the patient. The procedure to administer CAR-T cells includes physician or other qualified health care professional monitoring of multiple physiologic parameters, verification of cell processing, evaluation of the patient during, as well as immediately before and after the administration of the CAR-T cells, direct supervision of clinical staff, and management of any adverse events during the administration. Care on the same date of service that is not directly related to the service of administration of the CAR-T cells (eg, care provided after the administration is complete, care for the patient’s underlying condition or other medical problems) may be separately reported using the appropriate evaluation and management code with modifier 25. Management of uncomplicated adverse events (eg, nausea, urticaria) during the infusion is not reported separately. The fluid used to administer the cells and other infusions for incidental hydration (eg, 96360, 96361) are not reported separately. Similarly, infusion(s) of any supportive medication(s) (eg, steroids) concurrently with the CAR-T cell administration are not reported separately. However, hydration or administration of medications (eg, antibiotics, opioids) unrelated to the CAR-T administration may be reported separately with modifier 59. (For administration of drugs, agents and biologic response modifiers, see Chemotherapy and Other Highly Complex Drug or Highly Complex Biologic Agent Administration) (For transplant services/procedures, see Bone Marrow or Stem Cell Services/Procedures)

short_description: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy; preparation of blood-derived T lymphocytes for transportation (eg, cryopreservation, storage)
lay_term: The provider prepares T lymphocytes (white blood cells) that were previously extracted from the patient’s blood and places them in a proper container for transportation to a lab. This service is related to CAR–T therapy (use of the patient’s modified cells to attack cancer cells). Explanation The provider prepares the patient’s previously extracted T lymphocytes (white blood cells involved in immunity) for transportation to a lab where they will be modified for chimeric antigen receptor T–cell (CAR–T) therapy, a cancer treatment where a lab modifies a patient’s own immune cells to better recognize and attack cancer cells. As an example, the provider may mix the T lymphocytes with a cold protective solution to freeze the blood and then place it in a subzero temperature storage container for transport to a laboratory. Tips See 38225 to 38228 for various elements of CAR–T therapy services. Read Less

short_description: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy; receipt and preparation of CAR-T cells for administration
lay_term: The laboratory receives cryopreserved T lymphocytes (white blood cells) and genetically modifies them so that they can be administered to the patient at a separate service as part of CAR–T therapy. Explanation The lab provider receives and genetically modifies T lymphocytes (white blood cells involved in immunity) previously harvested from the patient. The process uses a “disarmed” virus to create a cell that has receptors on the surface that can bind to certain proteins (antigens) on tumor cells to fight the cancer as part of chimeric antigen receptor T–cell (CAR–T) therapy. The lab provider applies a process that multiplies the number of genetically modified cells to the hundreds of millions. Tips See 38225 to 38228 for various elements of CAR–T therapy services. short_description: Hematopoietic progenitor cell (HPC); allogeneic transplantation per donor
lay_term: Lay Term
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) refers to the infusion of hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPC) obtained from bone marrow, peripheral blood apheresis, and/or umbilical cord blood. These procedure codes (38240-38243) include physician monitoring of multiple physiologic parameters, physician verification of cell processing, evaluation of the patient during as well as immediately before and after the HPC/lymphocyte infusion, physician presence during the HPC/lymphocyte infusion with associated direct physician supervision of clinical staff, and management of uncomplicated adverse events (eg, nausea, urticaria) during the infusion, which is not separately reportable. HCT may be autologous (when the HPC donor and recipient are the same person) or allogeneic (when the HPC donor and recipient are not the same person). Code 38241 is used to report any autologous transplant while 38240 is used to report an allogeneic transplant. In some cases allogeneic transplants involve more than one donor and cells from each donor are infused sequentially whereby one unit of 38240 is reported for each donor infused. Code 38242 is used to report a donor lymphocyte infusion. Code 38243 is used to report a HPC boost from the original allogeneic HPC donor. A lymphocyte infusion or HPC boost can occur days, months or even years after the initial hematopoietic cell transplant. HPC boost represents an infusion of hematopoietic progenitor cells from the original donor that is being used to treat post-transplant cytopenia(s). Codes 38240, 38242, and 38243 should not be reported together on the same date of service. If a separately identifiable evaluation and management service is performed on the same date of service, the appropriate E/M service code, including office or other outpatient services, established (99211-99215), hospital inpatient or observation care services (99221-99223, 99231-99239), and inpatient neonatal and pediatric critical care (99471, 99472, 99475, 99476), may be reported using modifier 25 in addition to 38240, 38242 or 38243. Post-transplant infusion management of adverse reactions is reported separately using the appropriate E/M, prolonged service or critical care code(s). In accordance with place of service and facility reporting guidelines, the fluid used to administer the cells and other infusions for incidental hydration (eg, 96360, 96361) are not separately reportable. Similarly, infusion(s) of any medication(s) concurrently with the transplant infusion are not separately reportable. However, hydration or administration of medications (eg, antibiotics, narcotics) unrelated to the transplant are separately reportable using modifier 59.

short_description: Suture and/or ligation of thoracic duct; thoracic approach
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs the thoracic duct. The provider accesses the duct through the thorax by incising either the breastbone or ribs. The most common reason for repair is penetrating trauma of the chest. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider enters the chest by splitting the sternum, or breast bone, in an approach called a median sternotomy or by a large incision between the ribs called a thoracotomy. He carefully dissects either the sternum or the ribs to reach the thoracic duct. Depending on the approach, the provider must carefully preserve the lungs, heart, and great vessels during the procedure. The provider identifies the area of concern and depending on the condition he is treating, uses sutures to repair the damage or to encircle the duct and tie it off. If he splits the sternum, he closes the bone with surgical wire. Finally, he reapproximates the tissues in layers and closes the skin and subcutaneous tissues. Terminology Endoscope: Medical instrument consisting of a long, thin, flexible, or rigid tube which has a light and a video camera used to view or image the inside of the body. Great vessels: Large vessels that bring blood to and from the heart. Mediastinoscopy: A surgical procedure to examine the mediastinum which is the area of the upper chest between and in front of the lungs. Reapproximates: Brings them together again. Ribs: Pairs of bones, extending from the spine or towards the breastbone. Scope: An instrument which the provider uses to look inside the body; it may be rigid or flexible. Subcutaneous tissue: The deepest layer of skin. Thoracic duct: The main vessel passing upwards in front of the spine and draining into the vein near the base of the neck. Thorax: The part of the body between the neck and the abdomen; it includes the cavity which contains the ribs, breastbone, chest, and the heart; this cavity is the thoracic cavity. Tips Separate codes exist for procedures on the thoracic duct via cervical, thoracic, and abdominal approaches. The approaches require different work so the provider must assign the code carefully after reviewing the documentation for the approach. All codes are for an open approach. There are no codes for an endoscopic approach. For example, if a provider performs a mediastinoscopy to the thoracic duct and if the provider uses a scope to perform the procedure, report 38999, Unlisted procedure, hemic or lymphatic system. lay_term: The provider excises or biopsies lymph nodes lying near the surface of the body using a needle. The provider commonly performs this procedure to identify and diagnose the cause of disease in the lymph node or surrounding tissues. The provider can excise any superficial node, but more often the nodes in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal areas. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the underlying lymph node. Typically, the procedure will address a lymph node near the surface of the skin. The provider can visualize or palpate the lymph node so he usually needs no guidance. The provider may use radiologic guidance though when necessary. The provider identifies the target lymph node or nodes. The provider then injects a local anesthetic and inserts a large needle into the node. He then removes a sample. He may take multiple specimens of the same lymph node. The provider applies pressure to stop bleeding from the site and applies a bandage. Terminology Axilla: The armpit. Biopsy: Examination of tissue a provider removes from a living body to discover the cause or severity of a disease. Inguinal biopsy: Biopsy through the groin. Lymph node: A knot or swelling at various spots along the circulation of the lymph system; the lymph system maintains fluid balance by returning fluid from the spaces between tissues back to the blood stream and supports the immune system. Superficial lymph node: A lymph node that lies near the surface of the body. Tips If the provider uses guidance to localize the node report the guidance separately if there is documentation of visualization of the target area and if a permanent image is kept. Report 38505 only once no matter how many specimens a provider obtains from the same node or how many nodes he biopsies in the same area. However, if the provider performs biopsies in other areas, report the code again with modifier 59, Distinct procedural service to indicate that a different area was tested. Biopsies on the contralateral or opposite side may be coded with modifier 50, Bilateral procedure. Read Less

short_description: Biopsy or excision of lymph node(s); open, deep cervical node(s) with excision scalene fat pad
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes the lymph nodes in the deep tissues of the neck and the scalene fat pad through an open incision. He may send them to the laboratory for analysis. The provider performs the procedure as an investigation or treatment of tumors in the neck or chest. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider may position the patient supine with the neck extended and turned to the opposite side to improve access to the target area. The provider makes a 10 cm incision in the front of the neck, just 2 cm above the collarbone. He cuts through the sternocleidomastoid, the oblique prominent muscle in front of the neck. He then retracts the platysma and omohyoid muscles to gain a view of the lymph nodes to be excised. He separates the tissue overlying the target node or nodes with care to preserve critical structures like the phrenic nerve and the thoracic duct in the area. The provider excises the lymph node or nodes and dissects out the scalene fat pad. He may send them for biopsy. After controlling bleeding, he places a drain and closes the wound in layers. Terminology Lymph nodes: Small nodules at various points along the circulation of the lymph system; the lymph system returns fluid from the spaces between tissues (interstitial fluid) back to the blood stream and supports the immune system. Omohyoid: A small muscle used to move the hyoid bone, a tiny bone in the front of the neck. Platysma: A sheet–like muscle in the front of the neck. Phrenic nerve: One of the seven major peripheral nerves that extend from the left and right side of the neck and down to the lungs to control the function of the diaphragm muscle which is important for breathing. Scalene fat pad: A thick layer of fatty tissue beneath the skin in the lower neck to protect the deeper structures. Sternocleidomastoid muscle: A neck muscle that helps turn and bend the neck, so named because it originates at the top of the sternum and the clavicle (cleido–) and has its insertion at the mastoid process of the temporal bone of the skull. Thoracic duct: The main vessel passing upwards in front of the spine and draining into the vein near the base of the neck. Tips Code 38520 is for excision of one or more neck lymph nodes identified as possibly diseased and for excision of other node–bearing tissue to treat extensive disease. Use 38520 only once no matter how many nodes the provider biopsies in the same area. Add modifier 50 for biopsies performed on the opposite side. Additional Info This code is for excision of a lymph node that has been identified as possibly diseased. It may be identified visually or it might be taken due to its proximity to other diseased tissue. The code can be used for any deep node in the neck. Deep nodes lie under a layer of muscle and/or bone. One method of identifying lymph nodes for excision is by injection of a dye into a known area of disease and allowing the dye to drain into the lymphatic system. The node that picks up the most dye is the first node to filter fluids from the diseased area; this is referred to as a sentinel node. If it is sampled and no disease is found then no further lymphadnectomy is needed. If it is found to be diseased, additional nodes can be removed as needed. This process is called a sentinel node biopsy. Read Less

short_description: Excision of cystic hygroma, axillary or cervical; without deep neurovascular dissection
lay_term: The provider removes a cystic hygroma in the armpit or neck by surgical excision. This procedure does not involve deep dissection or involvement of the critical nerves and blood vessels in the area. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider adjusts the neck of the patient to improve access to the target area. For an axillary hygroma, or a hygroma in the armpit, the provider may turn the patient in a lateral, or sideways, position or may pad the shoulder to improve exposure. The provider then uses a scalpel to dissect the tissue overlying the cyst or cysts, which are primarily superficial and require no deep dissection or extra work to preserve critical nerves or blood vessels in the area. The provider excises the cyst completely, if possible, and reapproximates the tissues in layers. The provider then closes the incision with sutures and covers the incision with a sterile bandage. He may place a drain if necessary and suture it to the skin to drain blood or other fluids while the wound heals. Terminology Axilla: The armpit. Cyst: An abnormal closed saclike structure containing gas, fluid, or semisolid material, that has its own membranous lining delineating it from the surrounding tissue. Cystic hygromas: Single or multiple cysts found mostly in the neck region or armpit but may also be found in the head or chest; they are often present from birth but may develop later in life; also known as a lymphangioma. Neurovascular dissection: Excision of the nerves and blood vessels. Tips Cystic hygromas are most often found in the neck and are typically congenital, although they may not be found until later in life. The most effective treatment of cystic hygromas is complete excision. However, in some cases excision may be impossible due to the involvement of the cysts in the critical nerves and or blood vessels of the area. Considering that cystic hygromas are benign, the decision may be made to leave the structures or it may only be possible to remove part of the hygroma. Whether a provider removes all or part of the cystic hygroma at the same surgical session, the provider still reports this service with 38550. Code 38550 also includes removal of one or more cystic structures during the same session. If the provider only removes part of the hygroma, it is likely to grow back and require further treatment, including possible reexcision, which a provider would also report with 38550. If the hygroma requires reexcision or if the patient has had other neck surgery in the same area it may be appropriate to apply modifier 22, Increased procedural services to describe any extra work the provider has to perform due to scarring or alterations in the anatomy. The provider should document the extra time and effort and quantify it as much as possible. Do not report this service, with modifier 50, Bilateral procedure. If the procedure is performed on both the right and left axillae, you may be able to report it with modifier 51 for multiple procedure or LT/RT; check with the payer to be sure. Read Less

short_description: Limited lymphadenectomy for staging (separate procedure); pelvic and para-aortic Notes: (When combined with prostatectomy, use 55812 or 55842) (When combined with insertion of radioactive substance into prostate, use 55862)
lay_term: The provider excises lymph nodes (lymphadenectomy) from the pelvic area or near the aorta to identify the stage of cancer in the pelvis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a laparotomy incision and explores the abdomen and pelvis for evidence of cancer. She excises lymph nodes in the pelvis and or para–aortic area and sends the samples to pathology for examination. Using the pathology results, she identifies the number and location of nodes with metastatic cancer and determines the stage using this information. In cases of extensive metastatic cancer, the provider may also sample lymph nodes in adjacent areas in order to identify the extent of the disease and plan treatment. The provider then approximates the tissues in layers and closes the laparotomy wound. Terminology Aorta: The largest artery in the body, which arises from the left ventricle of the heart and supplies oxygenated blood to the rest of the body; it consists of an ascending and descending aorta that serve the upper and lower parts of the body respectively. Laparotomy: A large incision through the abdominal wall to gain access to the abdominal cavity. Lymph nodes: Small nodules at various points along the circulation of the lymph system; the lymph system returns fluid from the spaces between tissues (interstitial fluid) back to the bloodstream and supports the immune system. Lymphadenectomy: Surgical removal of one or more groups of lymph nodes; also known as lymph node dissection. Metastatic cancer: Cancer that has spread from its original location to another place in the body. Tips Code 38562 describes a sampling of the lymph nodes specifically for the purposes of staging. This procedure is typically performed at a separate operative session. Do not use code 38562 in addition to other excisions to describe lymphadenectomy to treat disease as code 38562 bundles into other procedures that include lymphadenectomy. If the staging procedure occurs in the global period of a previous procedure to remove or debulk a tumor, you may need to add modifier 58, Staged or related procedure or service by the same physician or other qualified healthcare professional during the postoperative period, to indicate that this is a staged activity. short_description: Suprahyoid lymphadenectomy Notes: (For bilateral procedure, report 38700 with modifier 50)
lay_term: The provider excises the lymph nodes from the top of the hyoid bone, a small bone in the midline near the base of the tongue and above the thyroid. In cases of metastatic cancer it may also be necessary to remove the lymph nodes and other tissue in the area of the jaw and upper neck. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider adjusts the head and neck of the patient to improve access to the target area. The provider makes an incision that starts just below the ear and curves to the top of the hyoid, a small bone in the midline near the base of the tongue and above the thyroid. The provider then extends this incision towards the chin. He takes care to preserve critical nerves, blood vessels, and other structures in the area. The provider identifies and removes the submandibular gland. He also removes the submental and submandibular lymph nodes and inspects the tissues in the area for evidence of disease. He removes any suspicious tissue he finds. The provider ensures hemostasis. Finally, he closes the incision in layers and may place a drain. Terminology Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Lymph node: A knot or swelling at various spots along the circulation of the lymph system; the lymph system to maintain fluid balance by returning fluid from the spaces between tissues back to the blood stream and supports the immune system. Lymphadenectomy: Surgical removal of one or more groups of lymph nodes; it is also called a lymph node dissection. Metastatic cancer: Cancer that has spread from the original site where it first started to another place in the body. Submandibular: Situated below the jaw or mandible. Submental: Located under the chin. Suprahyoid: Above the hyoid bone, a small bone in the midline near the base of the tongue and above the thyroid that supports the tongue and the larynx, or voice box. Thyroid: A gland in the neck which secretes hormones regulating growth and development. Tips Code 38700 describes removal of the submandibular and submental lymph nodes as well as the submandibular gland and other tissue in the top of the neck. The provider may perform this procedure in conjunction with other procedures that do not include lymphadenectomy in this area. It may also be billed separately for recurrent or advancing disease. If a provider performs this procedure in the global period of another resection, the provider may need to append modifier 58, Staged or related procedure or service by the same physician during the postoperative period, to indicate that the procedure was a planned or staged procedure. short_description: Cervical lymphadenectomy (modified radical neck dissection)
lay_term: The provider excises the lymph nodes and any diseased soft tissue he finds in the cervical area. He takes care to dissect free and preserve the spinal accessory nerve, the jugular vein, and the sternocleidomastoid muscle during the procedure. This service is done to excise the diseased lymph nodes, and prevent an extensive disease from spreading further. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider adjusts the head and neck of the patient to provide better exposure of the target area. The provider makes a long incision starting under the ear and extending down the neck and out to the chin. He identifies the areas of disease, excises the lymph nodes, and any other tissues involved in or near the area of disease. He takes extra time and effort to carefully dissect out and preserve the spinal accessory nerve, the jugular vein, and the sternocleidomastoid muscle. He reapproximates the tissues and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Biopsy: Examination of tissue a provider removes from a living body to discover the cause or severity of a disease. Cervical lymphadenectomy: Also called a radical neck dissection, this procedure involves removing all of lymph nodes and additional muscle and soft tissue; the provider may also excise nerves and blood vessels if involved in the disease process. Jugular vein: Any of several large veins in the neck, carrying blood from the head and face to the heart. Lymph node: A knot or swelling at various spots along the circulation of the lymph system; the lymph system to maintain fluid balance by returning fluid from the spaces between tissues back to the blood stream and supports the immune system. Lymphadenectomy: Surgical removal of one or more groups of lymph nodes; it is also called lymph node dissection. Modified radical neck dissection: Procedure to remove the lymph nodes and additional muscle and soft tissue in the neck but with extra work to dissect free and preserve the spinal accessory nerve, jugular vein, and sternocleidomastoid muscle. Radical neck dissection: Surgical procedure in which the provider removes a mass such as a tumor from the neck, along with an additional edge of tissue which seems normal; he also removes the lymph nodes from the neck. Spinal accessory nerve: Either of the eleventh pair of cranial nerves, that conveys impulses to the upper chest, back, and shoulders. Sternocleidomastoid muscle: Muscle situated in area of the collar bone, and serves to turn and nod the neck. Tips Code 38724 bundles into many other procedures for treatment of extensive cancer of the head and neck. If the provider performs radical neck dissection in the global period of another procedure to remove the actual tumor, then the provider may need to append modifier 58, Staged or related procedure or service by the same physician during the postoperative period, to code 38724. lay_term: In this add on procedure, the provider incises the chest and removes thoracic and mediastinal lymph nodes. He commonly removes the lymph nodes for cancer of the breast, lung, or chest wall. The provider performs this procedure along with another primary procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest through a thoracotomy incision. The provider then splits and retracts the sternum or spreads the ribs depending on the thoracic approach. After the provider performs a primary procedure such as to remove a tumor mass, he then inspects the mediastinum. The provider also carefully inspects the mediastinal lymph nodes for disease, and removes the affected nodes. In cases of extensive metastatic cancer, it may be necessary to remove all the lymph nodes in the area of the disease. The provider then ensures that he stops all bleeding. If the sternum is split, he wires it together. Next, he reapproximates the subcutaneous tissues and closes the incision in layers. He may make a separate stab incision to place a chest tube to drain any fluids during healing. short_description: Retroperitoneal transabdominal lymphadenectomy, extensive, including pelvic, aortic, and renal nodes (separate procedure) Notes: (For excision and repair of lymphedematous skin and subcutaneous tissue, see 15004-15005, 15570-15650)
lay_term: The provider performs extensive surgical excision of the lymph nodes from the retroperitoneal area and throughout the abdomen. He also excises pelvic, aortic, and renal lymph nodes. The provider removes the pelvic, aortic, renal, and other lymph nodes in the lower abdomen for cancer in the lower abdomen. Explanation When the patient is prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a long incision from the distal tip of the sternum, or breastbone, to the umbilicus, or navel. The provider thoroughly inspects the abdominal cavity for signs of disease. He removes any adhesions. He may use suction to evacuate fluid from the abdomen. The provider removes the pelvic, aortic, and renal lymph nodes. He may also remove other nodes or tissues involved in or near the area of disease. In cases of extensive metastatic cancer, it may be necessary to remove all of the lymph nodes in area of the disease. The provider ensures hemostasis and closes the abdominal incision in layers. Terminology Aorta: The main artery of the body, which arises from the heart and supplies oxygenated blood to the rest of the body; in humans it passes from the left ventricle of the heart and runs down to the backbone. Aortic lymph nodes: Lymph nodes in the aortic area. Distal: Located far from the point of origin. Hemostasis: Stoppage of blood flow. Lymph node: A knot or swelling at various spots along the circulation of the lymph system; the lymph system to maintain fluid balance by returning fluid from the spaces between tissues back to the blood stream and supports the immune system. Lymphadenectomy: Surgical removal of one or more groups of lymph nodes; it is also called lymph node dissection. Metastatic cancer: Cancer that has spread from the place where it first started to another place in the body. Renal lymph nodes: Lymph nodes near the kidney. Retroperitoneal: Behind and outside the peritoneum. Transabdominal: Across the abdomen. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider injects the lymphatic ducts for examination. The provider performs a two stage lymphangiography, a procedure in which he first injects a dye into the lymphatic ducts and follows with an X–ray examination of the vessels of the lymphatic system. Explanation The provider identifies the target lymphatic ducts and makes a small incision over the duct in order to access it. He injects a contrast, or radiopaque dye into the duct. He takes X–rays and examines the duct for leakage, blockage, or other problems. He applies pressure to stop any bleeding. He closes the small incision with a suture. Terminology Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Lymph nodes: Small bodies located particularly in the neck, armpit, and groin that filter bacteria and foreign bodies from the lymph fluid; during infection, lymph nodes may become swollen and activated. Lymphatic ducts: Lymphatic vessels, which are part of the lymphatic system. Lymphatic system: A network of organs, lymph nodes, ducts, and vessels that make lymph, a colorless fluid containing white blood cells that drains from the tissues into the blood. lay_term: The provider injects a contrast, or radioactive tracer into the target tissues and massages the tissue to move the dye into the lymphatic system. He performs this procedure to identify the sentinel node, and locate any traces of tumor draining into the node. This service is most often done for melanoma or breast cancer. Explanation The provider injects dye into the tissues near the resected tumor and massages the tissue to facilitate the spread into the lymphatic system. For breast cancer sentinel node, identification the injection is made in the subareolar area of the breast. The provider then examines the nodes in the target area and identifies the node that has picked up the most dye. The provider reports the removal of the primary node, or nodes separately. The provider usually performs this procedure at the time of a tumor resection. Terminology Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Lymph nodes: Small bodies located particularly in the neck, armpit, and groin that filter bacteria and foreign bodies from the lymph fluid; during infection, lymph nodes may become swollen and activated. Lymphatic system: A network of organs, lymph nodes, ducts, and vessels that make lymph, a colorless fluid containing white blood cells that drains from the tissues into the blood. Periareolar, subareolar: Below or beneath the areola of the breast, the circular, pigmented area around the nipple of the breast. Sentinel nodes: The first few lymph nodes into which a tumor drains. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass, can be benign or cancerous. Tips Code 38792 involves injection of radioactive material. short_description: Cannulation, thoracic duct
lay_term: The provider inserts a cannula inside the thoracic duct, administers medication, and then removes the cannula. He commonly performs this procedure to address anomalies of the thoracic duct and to inject substances for therapeutic or diagnostic purposes. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest or abdomen. The provider then exposes the thoracic duct for cannulation. He makes a small incision in the thoracic duct and inserts a catheter or cannula into the duct. The provider then injects medication or dye and removes the cannula. The provider ensures that he stops all bleeding. Finally, he closes the incision in layers. The provider often performs this procedure at the time of another procedure. Terminology Cannula: A small tube not as flexible as a catheter, but that a provider inserts into the body so that he can pass instruments into the cavity, draw off fluid, or introduce medication. Catheter: A catheter is a tube that the provider inserts into a body cavity, duct, or vessel; catheters allow drainage, administration of fluids or gases, or access for surgical instruments; the process of inserting a catheter is called catheterization. Lymphatic system: A network of organs, lymph nodes, ducts, and vessels that make lymph, a colorless fluid containing white blood cells that drains from the tissues into the blood. Thoracic duct: The main lymphatic channel in the body that passes upwards in front of the spine and drains into a vein near the base of the neck; it receives interstitial fluids collected and filtered by the lymphatic system and returns those fluids to the cardiovascular system. lay_term: The provider injects a nonradioactive dye into the tissues surrounding the lymph nodes. The provider examines the lymph nodes during the procedure to detect the presence of disease and identify the primary lymph nodes to which the tumor drains. The provider often performs this procedure at the time of a lymph node biopsy or tumor resection. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider injects dye into the tissues near the target area or resected tumor and massages the tissue to facilitate the spread into the lymphatic system. The provider then examines the lymph nodes in the target area, called roadmapping. He follows the path of the dye, and identifies the primary lymph nodes to which the tumor drains. He then removes the node for biopsy, which the provider reports separately. The biopsy samples are sent to the laboratory for testing and determination of the presence of disease. The provider often performs this procedure at the time of a lymph node biopsy or tumor resection. Terminology Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, open. Lymphatic system: A network of organs, lymph nodes, ducts, and vessels that make lymph, a colorless fluid containing white blood cells that drains from the tissues into the blood. Nonradioactive tracer: A substance that can be detected and estimated by virtue of some property other than radioactivity, such as colour. Sentinel nodes: The first few lymph nodes into which a tumor drains. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass of cells, can be benign or cancerous. lay_term: The provider inserts a thin rigid or flexible instrument through a small incision in the neck or upper chest to look inside the mediastinum, the central part of the chest cavity between and in front of the lungs. The procedure includes excision of one or more samples of any abnormal–looking tissue mass for analysis to determine the presence of cancer or other disease, when performed. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the lower neck above the collarbone or near the upper part of the breastbone and inserts a mediastinoscope, a lighted tubular instrument, through the incision. He examines the mediastinum through the scope and may remove one or more pieces of tissue from any abnormal–looking masses for further examination. The provider controls any bleeding, withdraws the scope, and closes the small incision in layers. Terminology Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, open. Tips This code is for mediastinoscopy with or without biopsy of suspicious masses in the chest; when the provider performs mediastinoscopy with biopsy of a lymph node, use 39402, Mediastinoscopy, with lymph node biopsy or biopsies, e.g., lung cancer staging. short_description: Repair, diaphragmatic hernia (other than neonatal), traumatic; chronic
lay_term: The provider surgically repairs a recurrent hernia of the diaphragm due to a chronic traumatic injury to the diaphragm. This code is not applicable for repair of a neonatal hernia. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider may approach the diaphragm from the anterior or posterior area, or through the abdomen, or the thorax, or chest. The provider carefully inspects the organs that have herniated into the chest. If the provider finds any damaged or nonviable tissues, he may separately excise or repair them. The provider also inspects the damage to the diaphragm. The provider repairs any adhesions or damage due to the chronic nature of the injury and then repairs the diaphragm using suture material or mesh. When the procedure is complete, he closes the incision in layers. Terminology Chronic injury: A very old injury or one that is persistent and long lasting, or constantly recurring over time. Diaphragm: The membrane dividing the abdominal and chest, or thoracic, cavities. Diaphragmatic hernia: Bulging of abdominal or structures from behind the peritoneum through the diaphragm. Suspensory ligament: A fibrous membrane suspending an organ or part of it in the body. Torsion: The action of twisting; torsion of a blood vessel causes lack of blood supply to the organ the blood vessel supplies blood to. Tips Code 39541 describes chronic traumatic diaphragmatic hernia and includes additional reimbursement associated with repair of a chronic wound. When organs herniate into a different area of the body they may become damaged or their suspensory ligaments may be stretched or torn. Additionally, the organs may die due to compression or torsion of the blood vessels. A provider reports repair or removal of damaged organs separately. This code only includes replacing the organs into the appropriate cavity. For repair of a neonatal hernia, see 39503, Repair, neonatal diaphragmatic hernia, with or without chest tube insertion and with or without creation of ventral hernia. Read Less

The provider may approach this procedure through the thorax, in a transthoracic approach, or through the abdomen, in a transabdominal approach. The diaphragm may be paralyzed. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider may approach the diaphragm from the anterior or posterior area, or through the abdomen, or the thorax, or chest. He inspects the diaphragm and identifies the area or areas of damage. The provider returns the abdominal contents back into the abdomen. He then folds the connective tissue attaching the diaphragm to the chest wall and sutures it to return the diaphragm to its anatomic, or natural original position. Finally, he closes the incision in layers. Terminology Diaphragm: The membrane dividing the abdominal and chest, or thoracic, cavities. Diaphragmatic hernia: Bulging of abdominal or structures from behind the peritoneum through the diaphragm. Eventration of diaphragm: The term used to describe a condition of relaxation of the diaphragmatic dome; it may present at birth as a congenital condition due to a defect of diaphragmatic development or in a later stage of life as an acquired condition such as diaphragmatic paralysis. Imbrication: The surgical overlapping of tissues to close a wound or repair a defect. Read Less

short_description: Resection, diaphragm; with complex repair (eg, prosthetic material, local muscle flap)
lay_term: The provider resects the diaphragm and repairs it using an involved repair technique. He may insert a prosthetic material or close the diaphragm using a local muscle flap. He commonly performs this procedure to excise diseased tissue from a spread of a tumor into the area. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the chest and or abdomen, and opens the area to provide the best exposure to the disease. The provider divides and moves structures as necessary, then places retractors to allow optimal visualization of the space. The provider then excises the area of disease often using electrocautery. He then repairs the area using a complex repair technique to correct the defect and connect the remaining diaphragm to the costal margin. He may insert a prosthetic material or close the diaphragm using a local muscle flap. He then closes the chest incision in layers. Terminology Complex repair: Surgical repair that involves more than layered closure often including additional work such as debriding the wound, excising scar tissue, placement of stents and other preparations of the area before closure. Costal margin: The lower edge of the chest or thorax. Diaphragm: The membrane dividing the abdominal and chest, or thoracic, cavities. Electrocautery: An instrument using heat produced by a high frequency electric current for destruction of tissue. Flap: Tissue for grafting, typically removed from one place on the body and positioned in another; however, it may remain anchored and rotated from one side of an area to another. Prosthesis: An artificial or manmade replacement for a body part. Resection: Surgical removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also called excision. Retractors: Retractor: Surgical instrument used to retract (hold back) wound edges or deeper tissues to give better visualization and access to the provider performing surgery. Read Less
